<b>Beyond the COPs</b>

- Courts
  <toggle>
  ICJ opinion

  - 23 July 2025 (Vanuatu-led): states have legal duties to cut emissions; failure can be an internationally wrongful act → reparations
  - <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81eb-b2bd-fafe2e9e61d3/4251111b-206d-81ca-a066-001cf6d602a1">ITLOS 2</span>024: GHG emissions = marine pollution under UNCLOS
  - India argued CBDR + no new duties beyond UNFCCC and Paris · limit: advisory, not binding
  </toggle>
- Trade
  <toggle>
  CBAM

  - EU carbon tax on imports from 1 Jan 2026: steel, cement, aluminium, fertiliser, hydrogen, electricity
  - India: cost ≈0.05% of GDP (CSE) + hits MSMEs + heavy paperwork → "disguised protectionism", against CBDR
  </toggle>

<b>Gaps</b>

- <b>P</b>: pledges not binding + no fossil-fuel phase-out text
- <b>I</b>: technology locked behind IPR
- <b>F</b>: \$100 billion never fully met + new goal counts loans + adaptation finance tripled but with no clear baseline
- <b>C</b>: North–South trust deficit + unilateral trade measures (CBAM)

<b>Fixes</b>

- CBDR-RC to guide timelines and finance + grant-based finance + technology access as a right + NDC 3.0 with economy-wide targets + fund loss and damage and the TFFF
</toggle>

<toggle>
OLD way

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 NATURAL CAUSES OF CC

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: climate changes that happen without any human role, mostly over thousands to millions of years
- <b>Pillars / key features</b>: 1. Continental Drift (affect because of change pod physical features over time)
- 2\. Variation of the Earth’s orbit
- 3\. <span color="green_bg">Milankovitch</span> cycles (Milankovitch cycles are long-term, predictable variations in Earth's orbit, axial tilt, and wobble that alter the distribution and intensity of sunlight reaching our planet. These astronomical shifts operate over tens of thousands of years and are the primary natural drivers behind Earth's historical climate phases, including the onset and retreat of major ice ages)
- 4\. Plate tectonics
- 5\. Volcanic Activity
- 6\. Ocean Currents:Ocean current is one of the major components of the climate [system.It](http://system.It) is driven by horizontal winds causing the movement of the water against the sea surface.The temperature differences of the water influence the climate of the region.
- 7\. Solar Variability: Sunspot activity can alter incoming solar radiation + Volcanic Eruptions: E.g., Mount Pinatubo (1991) injected aerosols into the stratosphere, causing a short-term cooling of \~0.5°C (Milankovitch cycles work over \~100,000 years, driving cold and warm periods)
- <b>Significance</b>: explain past ice ages, but not the fast warming since 1950 → IPCC AR6: warming is <span color="green_bg">unequivocally</span> human-caused
- <b>Examples</b>: Mount Pinatubo, 1991 (\~0.5°C cooling for about two years) + <span color="green_bg">Maunder Minimum</span> (1645–1715, few sunspots) during the Little Ice Age
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Anthropogenic Factors

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2022

- <b>2022 Q17 (15 marks):</b> Discuss global warming and mention its effects on the global climate. Explain the control measures to bring down the level of greenhouse gases which cause global warming, in the light of the Kyoto Protocol, 1997.
</toggle>

- 1\. Greenhouse Gases (water vapour, Co2, CFC, Methane (formed via decomposition of organic matter), Nitrous oxide)
- 2\. Change in land use patterns (From the satellite imagery, it is seen that the clearing of forest cover for agriculture and irrigated farming in arid and semi-arid lands can increase solar energy absorption and the amount of moisture evaporated into the atmosphere)
- 3\. Atmospheric aerosols: what are aerosols ? They are organic and inorganic matter like dust, volcanic ash, water from transpiration, agricultural dust or vehicular emissions, they are very small in size Atmospheric aerosol can: Scatter and absorb the solar and infrared radiation, change microphysical and chemical properties of the clouds, Solar radiation, when scattered, cools the planet
- <b>Examples</b>: Indo-Gangetic Plain winter haze (stubble + vehicles + industry → <span color="green_bg">aerosols</span> cut sunshine and change local climate) + south-east Amazon (2021 study: deforestation turned it into a net <span color="green_bg">carbon source</span>)
- <b>India's response</b>: 3rd largest emitter but low per-capita → <span color="green_bg">CBDR</span> + NDC 2035 + <span color="green_bg">CCTS</span> carbon market + LiFE (see Legal & Policy, <span color="green_bg">Panchamrit</span>)
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Legal & Policy Developments

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2025

- <b>2025 Q18 (15 marks):</b> Write a review on India’s climate commitments under the Paris Agreement (2015) and mention how these have been further strengthened in COP26 (2021). In this direction, how has the first Nationally Determined Contribution intended by India been updated in 2022?
</toggle>

- <span color="green_bg">MK Ranjitsinh</span> vs. Union of India case (2024): Right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change under Articles 14 and 21.
- India’s enhanced NDC submitted in August 2022, which includes reducing emissions intensity by 45%, achieving 50% non-fossil energy capacity by 2030, and targeting <span color="green_bg">net-zero</span> by 2070.
  - NDC 2031–35 (third NDC): emissions intensity −47% by 2035 (from 2005) + 60% non-fossil power capacity + extra <span color="green_bg">carbon sink</span> 3.5–4 bn t CO₂e
  - Where India stands: intensity −36% by 2020 + 52.57% non-fossil capacity (Feb 2026) + 2.29 bn t sink added by 2021
  - Gaps: \~\$250 bn a year needed till 2047 (NITI) + 50% of capacity but \<30% of generation is non-fossil + coal still \~71% of electricity generated (43% of capacity, \~55% of primary energy) + battery minerals imported
  - Way forward: CBDR-RC finance (green bonds, blended finance) + hybrid solar–wind–storage + agroforestry for sink
- However, on the implementation front, India has already achieved 50% non-fossil electricity capacity as of June 2025—five years ahead of schedule—and has reduced its GDP emission intensity by 36% between 2005 and 2020.
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Urgency of Climate Change

<ul>
<li>
<b>Definition & India's status</b>: WHY change is esseential right now ? Because there is seen an acceleration in warming, 0.18 degree from 1990-2015 and then 0.26 degrees warming rate in 2015 to 2025.
</li>
<li>
<b>Examples</b>: 2024 = first calendar year above 1.5°C (WMO) + Wayanad landslides after extreme rain (Jul 2024)
</li>
<li>
<b>India's response</b>: <span color="green_bg">net zero</span> by 2070 + NDC 2035 (−47% intensity) + 50% non-fossil capacity reached Jun 2025, 5 years early (see <span color="green_bg">Panchamrit</span>)
</li>
<li>
<b>Challenges</b>: remaining <span color="green_bg">carbon budget</span> for 1.5°C nearly used up + coal still \~71% of India's power generation + finance gap
</li>
<li>
<b>Way forward</b>: Enhanced rock weathering ( basalt added to agri fields, rainwater and Co2 in air react with it to form sodium bicarbonates, locking it in for 10k years), <b>Direct Ocean Capture (DOC) (</b>Seawater holds roughly <b>140 times more CO2, CO2 per unit volume </b>than ambient air), elimate methan plumes (methane CH4 traps 80x heat), Feed additives like <b>3-NOP</b> and red seaweed (<i>Asparagopsis taxiformis</i>) inhibit methanogenic enzymes in cattle stomachs,cutting livestock methane by 30%–80%, High-altitude aircraft disperse reflective sulfate or calcium carbonate particles into the stratosphere (\~20 km up), mimicking the cooling effect of major volcanic eruptions like Mount Pinatubo in 1991, on legal front : 
</li>
</ul>
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Global Temperature Trends

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Rising Global Temperatures: Earth’s surface temperature has increased by \~1.1°C since 1850 (IPCC AR6). The last 8 years (2015–2023) were the warmest on record (WMO 2023), Doubling of CO₂ is likely to cause 2.5–4°C warming. (IPCC AR6)
- <b>Examples</b>: 2024 = warmest year on record and the first calendar year above <span color="green_bg">1.5°C</span> (WMO) + India's 2024 = warmest year since 1901 (IMD)
- <b>Significance</b>: every extra 0.5°C → more heat extremes, heavy rain and droughts (IPCC <span color="green_bg">SR1.5</span>)
- <b>India's response</b>: Heat Action Plans (first: Ahmedabad 2013) + net zero 2070 (see Panchamrit)
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Melting Glaciers & Ice Sheets

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2017

- <b>2017 Q17 (15 marks):</b> ‘Climate Change’ is a global problem. How India will be affected by climate change? How Himalayan and coastal states of India will be affected by climate change?
</toggle>

- Himalayan glaciers (which store Carbon sink (stores 5.4 billion tonnes of carbon) like Gangotri are retreating at \~20 m/year. Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets have lost over 4000 gigatonnes of mass since 1992, The Hindu Kush–Himalaya region is warming rapidly—0.2 °C per decade over the last 50 years—with projections that 30–67% of glaciers may vanish by 2100 under mid-to-high warming scenarios + Nepal’s Yala Glacier declared dead (if all glaciers melt sea level rise by 60m (NASA) + + Himalayan states reported a loss of 1,072 sq km of forest cover (2019 -2021) + HR (Himalayan region) records about 100 million tourists every year with 240 million expected by 2025. ( indian initiative : NMSHE)
- Melt rate doubled since 2000; Ganga basin −21%, Brahmaputra −16% (<span color="green_bg">ICIMOD</span>) + more dead glaciers: Ayoloco (Mexico 2021), Okjökull (Iceland 2019)
- Why faster: warming fastest at 4,500–6,000 m + <span color="green_bg">black carbon</span> + less seasonal snow + erratic western disturbances
- Effects: less <span color="green_bg">albedo</span> → more warming + about 0.75 mm/yr sea rise (2000–23, WMO) + GLOFs and debris flows (Chamoli 2021, Sikkim 2023, Dharali 2025)
- India: NMSHE + Himansh station + National GLOF Risk Mitigation Programme; World: 2025 Year of Glaciers' Preservation + Decade of Action for Cryosphere Sciences 2025–34
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Oceans & Heat Absorption

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Oceans absorb 90% of excess heat, threatening coral reefs and fisheries.
  - Stat: The oceans absorb approximately 30% of anthropogenic CO2.
  - 2025: oceans took in an extra 23 zettajoules of heat (record since the 1960s) + SST \~0.5°C above 1981–2010
- <b>Examples</b>: 2023–24 <span color="green_bg">marine heatwaves</span> → 4th global coral bleaching (NOAA 2024) + warmer Arabian Sea → stronger cyclones on the west coast (Tauktae 2021, Biparjoy 2023)
- <b>India's response</b>: <span color="green_bg">Deep Ocean Mission</span> (2021) + INCOIS ocean monitoring and cyclone/tsunami warnings + <span color="green_bg">MISHTI</span> mangroves + coral restoration + UNOC3, Nice 2025 (<span color="green_bg">Nice Ocean Action Plan</span>: SDG 14 is the least funded SDG <span color="pink">(Life Below Water) </span>+ UN Ocean Decade 2021–30
- <b>Challenges</b>: <span color="green_bg">ocean acidification</span> + oxygen loss + sea-level rise + acidification planetary boundary breached + stratification → less oxygen and nutrients
- <b>Way forward</b>: cut CO₂ + more marine protected areas + ocean goals in the NDC (Blue NDC Challenge: France + Brazil, before COP30)
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Extreme Weather Events

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Increase in Extreme Weather Events: India witnessed record-breaking heatwaves in 2022 and 2024.
- <b>Pillars / key features</b>: <span color="green_bg">ENSO</span>: El Niño and La Niña (ocean) + Southern Oscillation (air)
- El Niño: trade winds weaken → warm water moves to South America → weak
- Indian monsoon, drought + lower kharif yields (rice, sugarcane, oilseeds) + harsher summers
- La Niña: trade winds strengthen → good monsoon + cold winters in the north + more floods and Bay of Bengal cyclones
- <span color="green_bg">Super El Niño</span>: central/eastern Pacific >2°C above normal for a long time (one forecast for late 2026)
- Note: El Niño–monsoon link is weakening (see item 46)
- <b>Examples</b>: Cyclone Biparjoy (2023) and flooding in Himachal Pradesh (2023) reflect this volatility.
- <b>India's response</b>: IMD impact-based forecasts + <span color="green_bg">Mission Mausam</span> (2024) + NDMA heatwave and cyclone guidelines
- <b>Challenges</b>: local extremes (cloudbursts) still hard to forecast + weaker El Niño–monsoon link makes seasonal forecasts harder
- <b>Way forward</b>: Bharat Forecast System + <span color="green_bg">Early Warnings for All</span> (UN, by 2027) + heat and flood plans in every district
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 CO₂ Records

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: A continuous record of CO₂ concentrations since 1958, measured at Mauna Loa Observatory, Hawaii (it has never been 400 ppm in 1000’s of years).
  - In 2024, fossil CO₂ emissions hit an all-time high of 10.2 GtC (up 0.8% from 2023), driven by rising natural gas (+2.4%), oil, and coal use. While US and EU emissions declined, India’s emissions rose to 0.9 GtC.
- <b>Pillars / key features</b>: How does Co2 cause climate change : Longwave and short wave differentiation and CO2 absorbs longwave and releases
- <b>Examples</b>: Mauna Loa 2024 average 424.6 ppm, a record (NOAA) + 2023→2024 rise of 3.58 ppm, the fastest ever (Met Office; wildfires + El Niño)
- <b>India's response</b>: 3rd largest emitter, low per-capita → argues <span color="green_bg">carbon budget</span> fairness at COPs + <span color="green_bg">CCTS</span> carbon market (2023) + CCUS push (Budget 2026–27) + 500 GW non-fossil target
- <b>Challenges</b>: emissions still rising (record in 2024) + gas, oil and coal use all up
- <b>Way forward</b>: peak and cut emissions + <span color="green_bg">CCUS</span> for hard sectors + a working carbon market
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Economic Impacts

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: 1 Deg. Celsius warming reduces global GDP by 12 per cent.
- <b>Examples</b>: Kerala floods 2018 (\~₹31,000 cr needed to rebuild, PDNA) + Pakistan floods 2022 (\~\$30 bn <span color="green_bg">loss and damage</span>)
- <b>India's response</b>: SDRF/<span color="green_bg">NDRF</span> + PMFBY crop insurance + Odisha's <span color="green_bg">climate budget</span> tagging + <span color="green_bg">CDRI</span> for resilient infrastructure
- <b>Challenges</b>: adaptation finance gap + most disaster losses uninsured
- <b>Way forward</b>: climate budget tagging in every state + <span color="green_bg">parametric insurance</span> + resilient infrastructure
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Panchamrit – India’s COP26 Climate Goals

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2025, 2021

- <b>2025 Q18 (15 marks):</b> Write a review on India’s climate commitments under the Paris Agreement (2015) and mention how these have been further strengthened in COP26 (2021). In this direction, how has the first Nationally Determined Contribution intended by India been updated in 2022?
- <b>2021 Q17 (15 marks):</b> Describe the major outcomes of the 26th session of the Conference of the Parties (COP) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). What are the commitments made by India in this conference?
</toggle>

- <span color="green_bg">Panchamrit</span> refers to the five key climate goals announced by India at COP26 (Glasgow, 2021) to combat climate change and promote sustainability. They are:
  - Reach 500 GW of non-fossil fuel energy capacity by 2030.
  - Meet 50% of energy requirements from renewables by 2030.
  - Reduce total projected carbon emissions by 1 billion tonnes by 2030.
  - Cut emissions intensity of GDP by 45% by 2030 (from 2005 levels).
  - Achieve <span color="green_bg">net-zero</span> carbon emissions by 2070. (PIB)
  - NITI net-zero report: India 2.9 t CO₂e per person (world 6.7) + \$22.7 tn needed by 2070, gap \$6.5 tn + \~1.3 Gt CO₂e still left in 2070 (farms, cement, heavy industry)

|  | 2015 NDC (2030) | 2022 update (2030) | NDC 2035 | Progress |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Emissions intensity cut (vs 2005) | 33–35% | 45% | 47% | 36% by 2020 |
| Non-fossil power capacity | 40% | 50% | 60% | 52.57% (Feb 2026) |
| Extra <span color="green_bg">carbon sink</span> | 2.5–3 bn t | 2.5–3 bn t | 3.5–4 bn t | 2.29 bn t by 2021 |
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
⚪ Country-Specific Examples

- Canada (2023): Wildfires burned 18.5 million hectares and released 2 gigatonnes of CO₂, nearly three times the nation’s economic emissions and 23% of global wildfire emissions that year.

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Challenges & Solutions

- <b>Challenges</b>: Challenges in CC: GHG emissions (India 3rd largest), 8% gap in current policies and NDC’s pledges, the pace of renewable energy growth don’t meet its implementation (power still 70 % coal).
  - Steel sector accounts for about 12% of India’s CO₂. Also: cement \~6% + aluminium \~2.8% of India's GHG → refuse-derived fuel in cement (−80–85% by 2070) + round-the-clock RE for aluminium; EU <span color="green_bg">CBAM</span> makes it urgent
  - CBAM: EU carbon tax on imports from 1 Jan 2026 (cement, aluminium, fertiliser, steel, hydrogen, electricity) → India: trade barrier + cost \~0.05% of GDP (CSE) + hits MSMEs + heavy paperwork → India calls it "disguised protectionism" (see COP30)
  - Methane is responsible for \~30 % global temperature rise since the Industrial Revolution. (Global Methane Tracker, 2025 by International Energy Agency, IEA)
- <b>India's response</b>: Panchamrit + CCTS (2023) + Green Hydrogen Mission + PAT for industry
- <b>Way forward</b>: Solutions: Municipal green bonds (eg. Ahmedabad), move away from FF, invest in battery storage systems, local actions like pachathuruthu initiative (aims to create man-made mini-forests, or "green islands," across the state.), sponge cities (eg. China to avert CC’s flood effects).
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Climate Change & Sea Level Rise

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2023, 2022, 2017

- <b>2023 Q18 (15 marks):</b> The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change(IPCC) has predicted a global sea level rise of about one metre by AD 2100. What would be its impact in India and the other countries in the Indian Ocean region?
- <b>2022 Q18 (15 marks):</b> Explain the causes and effects of coastal erosion in India. What are the available coastal management techniques for combating the hazard ?
- <b>2017 Q17 (15 marks):</b> ‘Climate Change’ is a global problem. How India will be affected by climate change? How Himalayan and coastal states of India will be affected by climate change?
</toggle>

- Sea level rise occurred at 3.3 mm per year (1993 - 2017) in North Indian Ocean.
- Average ocean temprature increased 1.45 degree (water expands when hot leading to sea level rise).
- 2023 driest year for rivers on record.
- On India: Coastal erosion and chronic flooding threaten major cities like Mumbai, Chennai, and Kolkata. <span color="pink_bg">Over 36 million Indians may face persistent flooding by 2100 across a 7,500 km coastline.</span> Over <span color="pink">570,000 hectares could be submerged with a 1-meter rise, displacing about 7.1 million people</span>, while significant infrastructure losses are expected, especially in Odisha and West Bengal. <span color="green">The Sundarbans face serious threats: up to 80% of mangrove cover could vanish</span>, with islands already disappearing and shoreline retreating up to 200 meters annually. Intensifying cyclones like Amphan in 2020 highlight how sea-level rise magnifies storm surges—Amphan pushed seawater 25 km inland, severely impacting the Sunderbans delta. + distress movement eg. of Kosi river and climate change, how it is cutting nearby lands in Bihar, forcing people to relocate (no institutional support, false promises creates trust deficit, no rehabilitation). Lakshadweep faces land submergence risks: Kavaratti, Minicoy may lose 60% of land under RCP8.5.
- Maldives: With average elevations around 1.5 meters, the nation is at risk of becoming largely uninhabitable by 2100 unless adaptive measures are undertaken.
- Bangladesh: Low-lying delta regions could see 0.74 meters of sea rise by 2100, displacing over 2 million people. (Already started)
- Other IOR countries: Sri Lanka (Colombo, coastal belt) + Myanmar (Irrawaddy delta) + Pakistan (Indus delta: <span color="green_bg">seawater intrusion</span> in Sindh) + Indonesia (Jakarta sinking, capital moving to Nusantara) + Seychelles, Mauritius (beaches, reefs, tourism)
- What it means for India: climate migration from Bangladesh into Assam, West Bengal + shared fisheries hit + India as first responder (HADR) + role via <span color="green_bg">CDRI</span> and MAHASAGAR
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 International Court of Justice

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: ICJ case: The International Court of Justice (ICJ), in a landmark advisory opinion “Obligations of States in respect of Climate Change” led by Pacific Island law students (2019); led by Vanuatu, issued on 23 July 2025, declared that nations have a legal obligation under international law—including treaties and customary norms—to curb greenhouse gas emissions and avoid environmental harm. Failing to meet these duties may be deemed an internationally wrongful act, opening the door for reparations such as compensation, restoration, or guarantees against future harm.
- <b>Examples</b>: Vanuatu-led UNGA request (Mar 2023, by consensus) → ICJ opinion Jul 2025 + <span color="green_bg">ITLOS</span> advisory opinion (May 2024: GHG emissions = marine pollution under UNCLOS)
- <b>India's response</b>: at the ICJ hearings (Dec 2024) India argued <span color="green_bg">CBDR</span> + equity + historical emissions of the North → court should not add new duties beyond UNFCCC/Paris
- <b>Significance</b>: first world-court opinion on climate duties → backs <span color="green_bg">climate litigation</span> and loss-and-damage claims
- <b>Challenges</b>: advisory, so not binding + no enforcement
- <b>Way forward</b>: use it in NDCs and finance talks + national courts can rely on it (SC already sees a right against climate change, M.K. Ranjitsinh 2024)
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Migration & Vulnerable Nations

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Panama became the first country to migrate because of climate related effects.
- <b>Examples</b>: Ghoramara island, Sundarbans (failed: about half the island lost to erosion → people moved to Sagar island) + Tuvalu–Australia <span color="green_bg">Falepili Union</span> (2023, worked: climate visas for Tuvaluans)
- <b>India's response</b>: no law for <span color="green_bg">climate migrants</span> yet + resettlement left to states + HADR to neighbours (Bangladesh, Maldives, Sri Lanka)
- <b>Challenges</b>: Most disproportionately affected are small island developing nations (SIDS); had access to only 1 billion out of 100 billion pledged, lost \$153 Billion.
- <b>Way forward</b>: Solutions: Flood barriers (eg. Oyster beds), <span color="green_bg">storm surge</span> modelling and planning, and build flood resistant cities like in South Korea.
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Antarctic & OZONE

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Ozone: good in the stratosphere (blocks UV), a pollutant at ground level + ODS (CFCs, HCFCs) release chlorine/bromine that breaks ozone → Antarctic hole (Aug–Nov, polar vortex)
  - Recovery to 1980 levels: 2040 world + 2045 Arctic + 2066 Antarctic
- <b>Pillars / key features</b>: Treaties: Vienna Convention 1985 (first to name the problem) → <span color="green_bg">Montreal Protocol</span> 1987 (universal, ODS cut >98%) → <span color="green_bg">Kigali Amendment</span> 2016 (HFCs: not ozone-depleting but strong GHG, cut 80–85% by late 2040s)
  - Antarctica treaty (area south of 60 degree) (use Antarctica only for exploration)
- <b>Examples</b>: Montreal Protocol (worked: ozone layer on track to recover, UNEP–WMO 2023) + India phased out HCFC-141b in foam making by 1 Jan 2020 (among the first developing countries)
- <b>India's response</b>: India: CFCs, CTC, halons out by 2010 + ODS Rules 2000 + HCFC −67.5% + HFC phase-down 10% (2032) → 20% (2037) → 30% (2042) → 85% (2047) + no new HFC plant clearances beyond 2027 + (India operates Antarctic research stations—Dakshin Gangotri (1st), Maitri, and Bharati—and plans Maitri-II, reaffirming its commitment through the Indian Antarctic Act, 2022.)
- <b>Challenges</b>: HFC demand rising with ACs + rogue CFC-11 emissions found in 2018 (eastern China)
- <b>Way forward</b>: <span color="green_bg">India Cooling Action Plan</span> (2019: cooling demand −20–25% by 2037–38) + climate-friendly refrigerants
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Impacts – IPCC Draft Report

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: what warming is already doing to species, oceans, forests, health, gender, migration, farming and schooling (toggles below)
- <b>Examples</b>: Pakistan floods 2022 (1,700+ deaths, 8 million displaced) + Punjab excess rain Jul 2023 → paddy transplanting delayed (more in toggles)
- <b>India's response</b>: NAPCC (9 missions) + <span color="green_bg">State Action Plans on Climate Change</span> + heat action plans + climate-resilient crop varieties (ICAR) + health mission on climate (NPCCHH)
- <b>Challenges</b>: <span color="green_bg">adaptation gap</span>: finance far below need + many ecosystems near the limits of adaptation
- <b>Way forward</b>: National Adaptation Plan + locally led adaptation + early warnings for all

<toggle>
Species

- Extinction rates a thousand times higher than before the Anthropocene + at 2–3°C up to 54% of land and sea species threatened this century + freshwater fish: local biodiversity down up to 75% by 2°C + turtles: upper-range sea-level rise → 59% loss of green turtles’ Mediterranean nesting area, loggerhead 67%
</toggle>

<toggle>
Oceans

- Coral reefs: 70–90% die at 1.5°C + marine heatwaves at least 34% more frequent and 17% longer since 1925 + Arctic summer sea ice down 25% (\~2 million sq km) since late 1970s
</toggle>

<toggle>
Systems

- Permafrost: at 2°C, 15% lost by 2100, releasing 36–67 billion tonnes of carbon + many terrestrial, freshwater, ocean and coastal ecosystems already “near or beyond” their adaptive capacity
</toggle>

<toggle>
Forests

- Fire seasons extended, potential burnable area doubled + at 2°C severe drought in Brazil’s natural areas could quadruple + Arctic tundra burned area up ninefold (1996–2015) + high emissions, drought and wildfire could turn half the Amazon into grassland
</toggle>

<toggle>
Human Health

- Extreme heat, storms, floods → heat illness, injuries, waterborne diseases, mental health (elderly, children, pregnant women, chronically ill, low-income worst hit) + longer pollen seasons, more air pollution and wildfire smoke → asthma + pest-borne diseases spread (Lyme, Zika, West Nile)
- WHO: additional 250,000 deaths per year (2030–2050) + deaths due to non communicable diseases, 85% of it by CC (COP29 spl report)
- COP30: <span color="green_bg">Belém Health Action Plan</span> = first health adaptation plan (\$300 mn) + \~5 lakh heat deaths a year + 1 in 12 hospitals at risk of climate shutdown → early warnings + trained health workers + resilient hospitals
</toggle>

<toggle>
Gender-Based Violence

- UN Spotlight Initiative (2025): each 1°C rise → 4.7% more intimate partner violence (IPV) + femicide up 28% during heatwaves (reasons: extreme weather, displacement, food insecurity, economic instability) + women environmental defenders in Guatemala, Philippines face evictions and threats
- Successful examples: Mozambique mobile health clinics + Haiti & Vanuatu train midwives for green jobs and embed GBV services in climate response
</toggle>

<toggle>
Displacement

- World Migration Report 2024 (UN): over 216 million could be displaced within their countries by 2050 + Pakistan 2022 floods (1,700+ deaths, 8 million displaced) + Bangladesh 1.5 million (2022) + Brazil 700,000 (2022) + Colombia 281,000
- Poverty: floods and droughts push farm households into debt cycles + tribals hit hardest + 1 unit more services in GSDP → \~1.9% lower poverty odds (NISER)
</toggle>

<toggle>
Agriculture

- Coffee shifting from Wayanad to higher altitudes (heat stress) + rice = 8–12% of global methane + Punjab excess rain July 2023 → delayed paddy transplantation, yield loss
- Non-irrigated area → farmer incomes drop 17–18% (eco survey) + by 2050 rice yields −10–15%, wheat −20% unless adaptation + hurdles: cost, small land in adopting climate-resistant agriculture
- Climate-resilient agriculture: CC can cut yields 4.5–9% (\~1.5% of GDP a year) + half of sown area rainfed + India: <span color="green_bg">NICRA</span> (ACASA atlas) + NMSA + PKVY + Soil Health Card → way forward: heat-tolerant seeds (wheat DBW-187, rice CR Dhan) + climate-resilient villages nationwide + one nodal agency
</toggle>

<toggle>
Education

- Schools closed 75% of the time due to extreme heat + 1 degree rise → lower test scores + 4 mil girls can’t complete education (low and middle income countries) + rainfall shocks hurt vocab at age 5 and math at age 15 (UNESCO) → Solutions: Indonesia’s INARISK + Rwanda’s flood- and landslide-safe schools
</toggle>
