<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 India-Specific Legislations

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2014

- <b>2014 Q13 (12.5 marks):</b> Should the pursuit of carbon credits and clean development mechanisms set up under UNFCCC be maintained even though there has been a massive slide in the value of a carbon credit? Discuss with respect to India’s energy needs for economic growth.
</toggle>

- Carbon pricing instruments 5 (2005) → 80 now, covering about 29% of world GHG + USD 107 bn revenue (2025) (World Bank)
- <span color="green_bg">Article 6</span> (rules finished at COP29): 6.2 country-to-country trades + 6.4 UN-run market (replaces Kyoto's CDM) + 6.8 non-market cooperation
- Issues: carbon colonialism + weak MRV + <span color="green_bg">greenwashing</span> → fix: Core Carbon Principles + third-party verification + blockchain tracking
- The Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (<span color="green_bg">CCTS</span>), 2023 sets yearly GHG emission intensity targets for 9 big polluting sectors. If companies exceed limits, they must buy carbon credits from the Indian Carbon Market or face fines. Others outside these sectors can voluntarily run green projects to earn and sell credits.
- The GEI Target Rules, 2025 fix sector-specific limits on GHG emissions per unit of production for 4 high-energy sectors—aluminium, cement, chlor-alkali, and pulp & paper. Companies must meet these yearly targets or buy carbon credits; non-compliance attracts fines under the Environment Protection Act, 1986. → 2025: 4 more sectors (refinery, petrochemicals, textiles, secondary aluminium) → <span color="green_bg">208 units must cut 3–7% by 2026–27 + penalty = 2x credit price (CPCB enforces)</span>
- <span color="pink_bg">The Green Credit Programme (GCP), 2023</span> is a voluntary market scheme that rewards eco-friendly actions like tree planting, sustainable farming, waste management, and air pollution reduction. Credits earned can be traded domestically and used in ESG disclosures, with the Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education (ICFRE) managing the programme. Under EPA,1986. → new rule: credit only after 5 years + 40% canopy (1 credit = 1 tree) → concerns: buy credits instead of restoring + uses existing degraded forest, no new forest + weak survival checks
- The Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) Scheme is basically an energy-saving game for big industries (launched 2012 by BEE under NMEEE, which, if you recall our timeline, is one of the 8 original missions of NAPCC 2008, now 9 with Health) → reduces Specific Energy Consumption (SEC) of Designated Consumers (iron & steel, cement, fertilizers, thermal power plants)
  - The genius of the PAT scheme is that it doesn't just mandate cuts; it creates a profitable market for energy efficiency → Perform (target over a 3-year cycle) → Achieve (audit) → Trade: over-achievers earn Energy Saving Certificates (ESCerts), under-achievers buy ESCerts on the Indian Energy Exchange (IEX) or face heavy penalties
- National green hydrogen mission.
- Green steel.
- SVAGRIHA is an Indian green building rating system by IGBC (Indian Green Building Council) that promotes sustainable and eco-friendly construction for small residential projects.
- To reduce methane: Global methane pledge but in India national mission on sustainable agriculture and direct seeded rice.
  - Methane: <span color="green_bg">84x</span> CO₂ over 20 years, lives \~12 years + sources: livestock, rice, coal mines, gas leaks, landfills + India = 3rd biggest emitter, not in the Global Methane Pledge (−30% by 2030) + ISRO found landfill hotspots (Pirana, Deonar, Ghazipur) → fix: waste segregation + bio-CNG (GOBARdhan) + scientific landfills + bio-covers
- Here’s a concise 2-line summary of the types of greenwashing companies use:
- The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has issued 2024 guidelines (“Prevention and Regulation of Greenwashing and Misleading Environmental Claims, 2024’.”) to prevent greenwashing by ensuring environmental claims in advertisements are truthful, clear, and fully disclosed. This regulation aims to protect consumers from misleading claims, maintain public trust, and promote genuine sustainable practices. Companies engage in various greenwashing tactics like hiding true sustainability efforts (greenhushing), misleading with false labels (greenlabeling), shifting blame to consumers (greenshifting), or downplaying actions by hiding in groups (greencrowding) to appear environmentally friendly without real impact. They also change targets frequently (greenrinsing) or highlight small green features to distract from harmful practices (greenlighting).
- India has started its first cluster of five Carbon Capture and Utilisation (CCU) testbeds for the cement sector, using a Public-Private Partnership (PPP).
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 COP 3 (KYOTO PROTOCOL)

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2022, 2014

- <b>2022 Q17 (15 marks):</b> Discuss global warming and mention its effects on the global climate. Explain the control measures to bring down the level of greenhouse gases which cause global warming, in the light of the Kyoto Protocol, 1997.
- <b>2014 Q13 (12.5 marks):</b> Should the pursuit of carbon credits and clean development mechanisms set up under UNFCCC be maintained even though there has been a massive slide in the value of a carbon credit? Discuss with respect to India’s energy needs for economic growth.
</toggle>

<b>🌍 Global Architecture & Outcomes</b>

- Legally Binding Targets: Transitioned global climate action from voluntary pledges to binding emission cuts, placing the burden exclusively on industrialized nations (Annex I) based on their historical emissions.
- Flexible Market Mechanisms: Introduced foundational carbon market tools: the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM), Joint Implementation (JI), and International Emissions Trading.

<b>🇮🇳 India’s Strategic Stance & Gains</b>

- Defending Developmental Space: As a developing nation (Non-Annex I), India successfully negotiated an exemption from binding targets, arguing that poverty alleviation and economic growth were its overriding priorities.
- Championing <span color="green_bg">CBDR</span>: India strongly backed the protocol because it legally codified the principle of <span color="green_bg">Common But Differentiated Responsibilities</span> (CBDR), ensuring the Global North took the lead.
- Capitalizing on the CDM: Rather than just opting out, India proactively utilized the CDM to attract foreign direct investment and technology transfer. By selling carbon credits (Certified Emission Reductions), India became one of the world's largest beneficiaries, which helped kickstart its early domestic renewable energy projects.

<b>UNDESTANDING KYOTO</b>
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
⚪ COP 15 (COPENHAGEN) (2009)

- Political Accord, Not a Treaty: Copenhagen Accord = 11th-hour compromise shaped by BASIC (Brazil, South Africa, India, China) negotiating with the US + The 2°C Consensus (first formal recognition) + Voluntary Pledges (NAMAs): shift from Kyoto’s top-down mandates to bottom-up
- 🇮🇳 India: "Constructive Engagement" pivot, shed the "deal-breaker" image by anchoring BASIC + voluntarily pledged emissions intensity −20–25% by 2020 (vs 2005), agriculture excluded for food security + MRV win: domestically funded actions only under "International Consultation and Analysis" (ICA), no intrusive audits
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
⚪ COP 17 (DURBAN South Africa ) (2011)

- The ADP Mandate (Durban Platform): draft a post-2020 universal agreement by 2015 (became Paris) + Breaking the "Firewall": Kyoto-era Annex I / Non-Annex I split began to end, new deal "applicable to all Parties"
- 🇮🇳 India: The Battle for Equity (no binding cuts ignoring historical emissions) + The Vocabulary Victory: "a protocol, another legal instrument or an agreed outcome with legal force" → crucial wiggle room: commitments via domestic laws and policies, not an intrusive, punitive international treaty
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 COP 21 (PARIS)

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2025

- <b>2025 Q18 (15 marks):</b> Write a review on India’s climate commitments under the Paris Agreement (2015) and mention how these have been further strengthened in COP26 (2021). In this direction, how has the first Nationally Determined Contribution intended by India been updated in 2022?
</toggle>

<b>1. 🌍 Global Architecture & Key Outcomes</b>

- The Bottom-Up Paradigm: Replaced Kyoto’s rigid, top-down mandates with a flexible, universal system where every nation submits Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) based on their sovereign capacities.
- The Temperature Goal: Established a binding global consensus to hold the average temperature increase to "well below 2°C" above pre-industrial levels, actively pursuing 1.5°C.
- The "<span color="green_bg">Ratchet Mechanism</span>": Instituted a mandatory 5-year ambition cycle, requiring countries to submit increasingly ambitious NDCs over time to prevent backsliding.
- Enhanced Transparency Framework (ETF): Created a unified system for a "<span color="green_bg">Global Stocktake</span>" to track progress, while maintaining flexibility for developing nations.
- <span color="green_bg">Article 6</span> (New Carbon Markets): Laid the groundwork to replace Kyoto's Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) with decentralized, cooperative carbon market mechanisms.
- Article 8 (Loss and Damage): Formally recognized the irreversible impacts of climate change, though developed nations insisted on a strict clause excluding liability or financial compensation.
- Nuanced CBDR-RC: Retained the sacred principle of Common But Differentiated Responsibilities, but added the crucial phrase "in the light of different national circumstances," signaling that as developing nations grow, their obligations will increase.

<b>🇮🇳 India’s Strategic Stance & First NDCs (2015)</b>

- The Three Quantitative Targets: India submitted highly ambitious, measurable goals for 2030:
  - 1\. Reduce the emissions intensity of its GDP by 33–35% (from 2005 levels).
  - 2\. Achieve 40% cumulative electric power installed capacity from non-fossil fuel energy resources.
  - 3\. Create an additional carbon sink of 2.5 to 3 billion tonnes of CO2  equivalent through expanded forest and tree cover.
- Climate Justice: India masterfully framed the narrative around "Climate Justice" rather than "climate charity," emphasizing that developing nations have a fundamental right to poverty eradication and economic growth.
- Conditional Commitments: India made it clear that achieving its NDC targets was intrinsically linked to the successful delivery of climate finance (the \$100B/year promise) and technology transfer from the Global North.
- Global Leadership (The ISA): Transitioning from a protesting nation to a global rule-maker, India, alongside France, launched the International Solar Alliance (ISA) on the sidelines of the summit to accelerate global clean technology deployment.
  - ISA now (10 years, Mar 2026): 125 members, India re-elected President (2024–26), first inter-governmental body HQ'd in India + <span color="green_bg">Towards 1000</span> (\$1 tn solar investment, 1 bn people, 1 bn t CO₂ cut a year by 2030) + OSOWOG, STAR-C, SolarX, Global Solar Facility + VGF for LDCs/SIDS → "alternative OPEC", South-South tool + challenges: finance gap, US exit (2026), slow projects in Africa and islands, high tariffs on PV
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
⚪ COP 24 (KATOWICE)

- 🌍 Global Outcome: The summit adopted the Katowice Climate Package, effectively the "operating manual" for the Paris Agreement. It established the Enhanced Transparency Framework (ETF) to standardize how countries report their emissions and progress. 🇮🇳 India’s Stance: India negotiated hard to ensure the rulebook retained the principle of CBDR-RC. It secured "flexibility" for developing nations in reporting standards, arguing that the Global South requires financial and technical capacity-building before facing stringent, universal audit mechanisms.
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 COP 26 (GLASGOW)

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2025, 2021

- <b>2025 Q18 (15 marks):</b> Write a review on India’s climate commitments under the Paris Agreement (2015) and mention how these have been further strengthened in COP26 (2021). In this direction, how has the first Nationally Determined Contribution intended by India been updated in 2022?
- <b>2021 Q17 (15 marks):</b> Describe the major outcomes of the 26th session of the Conference of the Parties (COP) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). What are the commitments made by India in this conference?
</toggle>

- Global Outcome: The Glasgow Climate Pact
- COP26 was a critical implementation summit aimed at operationalising the <span color="green_bg">Paris Agreement</span> and enhancing 2030 ambition. Key outcomes included:
- Finalisation of the Paris Rulebook, particularly:
  - Operationalising <span color="green_bg">Article 6</span> carbon markets (including rules to prevent double counting and transition of CDM credits).
  - Strengthening the Enhanced Transparency Framework.
- A formal request for countries to revisit and strengthen 2030 NDCs to align with the 1.5°C pathway.
- For the first time in UNFCCC history, the text explicitly called for the “phase-down of unabated coal power” and reduction of inefficient fossil fuel subsidies.
- Renewed emphasis on climate finance, though without concrete fulfilment of the \$100 billion annual commitment.-
  - COP26 became one of India’s most consequential climate summits since Paris.
- 1️⃣ The <span color="green_bg">Panchamrit</span> – India’s Ambition Upgrade
- India announced a transformative five-point climate action framework (“Panchamrit”) → see 🟢 Panchamrit heading above
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 COP 27 (SHARM - EL - SHEIKH)

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt, Nov 2022 → the "implementation COP"
- <b>Pillars / key features</b> (Global Architecture & Outcomes)
- The <span color="green_bg">Loss and Damage</span> (L&D) Fund: The crowning achievement. After decades of resistance from the Global North, an agreement was finally reached to establish a dedicated fund to financially compensate vulnerable developing nations suffering from irreversible climate disasters. This was a monumental victory for <span color="green_bg">climate justice</span> and the G77 bloc.
- Sharm el-Sheikh Implementation Plan: The summit shifted the focus from "pledges" to "action," demanding accountability and rapid execution of the commitments made at Paris and Glasgow.
- Call for MDB Reform: For the first time, the final text explicitly called for the reform of Multilateral Development Banks (like the World Bank) to scale up climate finance and reduce the debt burden on developing nations.
- <b>Examples</b>: Pakistan floods 2022 (\~\$30 bn loss) → the push that won the <span color="green_bg">L&D fund</span> + Egypt's "implementation COP" still left the fund empty till COP28
- <b>India's response</b> (India’s Strategic Stance & Diplomatic Gains)
- The "All Fossil Fuels" Gambit: This is a crucial exam point. When developed nations heavily pressured India to phase out coal, India launched a brilliant diplomatic counter-offensive. India formally proposed that the final text should call for a phase-down of all fossil fuels (including the natural gas and oil heavily relied upon by the West), not just coal. This exposed the hypocrisy of the developed world and successfully defended India’s baseload energy security.
- Mainstreaming <span color="green_bg">Mission LiFE</span>: India successfully embedded the "Lifestyle for Environment" (LiFE) movement into the preamble of the Sharm el-Sheikh Implementation Plan.
  - Analytical Point: This was a strategic narrative shift. By focusing on mindful, sustainable consumption, India shifted a portion of the climate burden away from just "production emissions" (which developing nations need for growth) and pointed it at the unsustainable per-capita consumption patterns of the developed world.
- Submission of the LT-LEDS: India officially submitted its Long-Term Low Emission Development Strategy. If Glasgow (COP26) was the announcement of Net-Zero by 2070, the LT-LEDS was the roadmap. It provided a comprehensive, multi-sectoral strategy focusing on:
  - Rapid expansion of green hydrogen and nuclear power.
  - 20% ethanol blending in petrol.
  - A deliberate emphasis that this transition is fundamentally conditional on the Global North providing trillions in climate finance and technology transfer.
- <b>Challenges</b>: L&D fund set up with no money at first + no new mitigation ambition (no phase-down of all fossil fuels in the text)
- <b>Way forward</b>: fill the <span color="green_bg">L&D fund</span> + MDB reform + finance and tech for the South
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 COP 28 (DUBAI)

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Dubai, UAE, Nov–Dec 2023 → first Global Stocktake
- <b>Pillars / key features</b> (Global Architecture & Outcomes)
- The First <span color="green_bg">Global Stocktake</span> (GST): This was the realization of the <span color="green_bg">Paris Agreement</span>'s built-in "<span color="green_bg">Ratchet Mechanism</span>." The GST concluded that the world was severely off-track from the 1.5°C goal.
- The "UAE Consensus": For the first time in nearly 30 years of climate summits, the final text explicitly called for "transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems, in a just, orderly and equitable manner." (This language is critical—it avoided the strict "phase-out" demanded by the West, accommodating developing nations).
- Tripling Renewables & Doubling Efficiency: A global pledge was introduced to triple renewable energy capacity (to roughly 11,000 GW) and double the global average annual rate of energy efficiency improvements by 2030.
- Early Win on Loss & Damage: On Day 1, the Loss and Damage Fund (agreed upon at COP27) was officially operationalized and capitalized with initial pledges, a rare moment of immediate action.
- <b>Examples</b>: L&D fund \~\$700 mn pledged on Day 1 (vs hundreds of billions needed a year) + India and China stayed out of the tripling-renewables and <span color="green_bg">Global Cooling Pledge</span>
- <b>India's response</b> (India’s Strategic Stance & Diplomatic Gains)
- Protecting Sovereign Energy Security: India made a bold, calculated move. Despite having one of the world's fastest-growing renewable sectors, India (along with China) refused to sign the pledge to triple global renewable energy.
  - Why? The pledge contained hidden clauses aimed at halting investments in "unabated coal power." India fiercely maintained that while it is committed to scaling renewables (already meeting its NDC targets early), it cannot compromise its baseload power requirements essential for rapid industrialization and poverty eradication.
- The Green Credit Initiative: Moving beyond just "carbon credits," India launched the Global Green Credit Portal. This is a massive paradigm shift. It creates a market-based incentive system that rewards broader ecological actions—like water conservation, afforestation, and waste management—not just carbon emission reductions.
- Pitching for Global Leadership: Signaling ultimate confidence in its climate trajectory, Prime Minister Modi officially offered to host COP33 in India in 2028.
- Global Biofuel Alliance (GBA) Push: Following its launch at the G20 in New Delhi earlier that year, India used COP28 to heavily promote the GBA, positioning biofuels as the essential bridge for the Global South's energy transition.
- <b>Challenges</b>: "transition away", not phase-out + loopholes ("transitional fuels" = gas, CCS) + L&D pledges small
- <b>Way forward</b>: turn the stocktake into stronger <span color="green_bg">NDC 3.0</span> (2025 round) + finance to match
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 COP 29 (BAKU)

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: 1. COP 29 (Baku, 2024): The Finance COP & The Battle for Equity
- <b>Pillars / key features</b> (Global Architecture & Outcomes)
- The New Collective Quantified Goal (<span color="green_bg">NCQG</span>): The primary mandate of Baku was to replace the notoriously unmet \$100 billion/year target (set back in 2009) with a post-2025 finance framework.
- The \$300 Billion Compromise: After bitter negotiations, developed nations agreed to a target of mobilizing \$300 billion annually by 2035. However, this figure controversially includes private sector investments and multilateral loans, rather than just direct public grants from wealthy nations.
- Breakthrough on <span color="green_bg">Article 6</span>.4: After years of deadlock since the <span color="green_bg">Paris Agreement</span>, the summit finally adopted the rules for a centralized, UN-backed global carbon market. This mechanism allows countries and companies to trade carbon credits (representing emission reductions) to meet their climate targets, officially replacing the Kyoto-era CDM.
- Also at COP29: Enhanced Transparency Framework + first Biennial Transparency Reports completed + Baku Adaptation Roadmap launched + Sharm el-Sheikh mitigation programme continued + Baku Workplan (indigenous peoples) renewed + Lima Gender and Climate Change Programme extended by 10 years
- <b>Examples</b>: India's objection at the closing plenary (Chandni Raina: "optical illusion") → deal gavelled through anyway + Switzerland–Thailand (Bangkok e-buses), first <span color="green_bg">Article 6.2</span> credit transfer (Jan 2024)
- <b>India's response</b> (India’s Strategic Stance & Diplomatic Masterstrokes)
- The Voice of the Global South (LMDC & BASIC): India did not just negotiate for itself; it acted as the shield for the Like-Minded Developing Countries (LMDC) and the broader Global South, aggressively calling out the structural inequity of the final deal.
- Calling Out the "Optical Illusion": India registered a fierce formal protest on the plenary floor, unequivocally rejecting the \$300 billion pledge as an "abysmally poor" and "paltry sum." India pointed out that delaying this target to 2035 severely undermines the urgency of the 2030 NDC targets.
- Quality over Quantity (The Debt Trap Warning): India fundamentally challenged the nature of the finance. It argued that forcing developing nations to take on market-rate loans to fund green transitions is not "climate finance"—it is a recipe for a widespread sovereign debt crisis. India demanded that the core of the NCQG must be concessional, grant-based public finance.
- The \$1.3 Trillion Demand: India maintained that based on independent economic assessments, the developing world requires at least \$1.3 trillion annually to realistically transition away from fossil fuels, adapt to climate impacts, and cover loss and damage.
- India's stance also: \$600 billion of the \$1.3 trillion as grants or similar support + opposed changes to the Mitigation Work Programme, wanted the pre-2020 emission gap of developed countries recognised + just transition respecting developing countries' right to develop + opposed follow-up mechanisms for the Global Stocktake, wanted Party-submitted adaptation indicators + Global South voice via CDRI and ISA
- <b>Challenges</b>: \$300 bn far below the \$1.3 tn need + counts loans and private money + target only by 2035
- <b>Way forward</b>: Baku-to-Belém Roadmap to \$1.3 tn + <span color="green_bg">concessional</span> grant-based finance at the core
- <b>Extra (COP29 side outcome)</b>: Declaration on Green Digital Action (GDA) adopted, Leveraging Digital Technologies: To support climate action + Mitigating the impact of Digitization on climate: Establishing metrics + Fostering Sustainable Innovation: By facilitating investments, (reasons : ICT sector is estimated to have accounted for 1.5– 3.2 % of global GHG emissions in 2020, Increase in online shoppers has led to a 30 % rise in digital-related waste from 2010 to 2022, reaching 10.5 million tonnes globally, In 2022, Global data centres alone consumed 460 terawatts hours (expected to double by 2026), Demand for minerals required for digitalisation like graphite, lithium, and cobalt could surge by 500 % to 2050.
- (Significance of digital tech in sustainable Dev: E.g., AI has been trained to measure changes in icebergs 10,000 times faster than a human, Informed decision making: Data analytics, Sustainable Design approaches: Stress on circular economy model, Promoting Open data sources (DPI’s like India Stack); Climate monitoring using AI, internet to mobilise opinion.
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 COP 30 (BELEM)

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Belém, Brazil, Nov 2025 → 10 years after Paris, held at the edge of the Amazon
- <b>Pillars / key features</b> (Global Architecture & Outcomes: The Belém Package)
- The <span color="green_bg">Tropical Forests Forever Facility</span> (TFFF): A paradigm-shifting, \$125 billion multilateral investment fund. Unlike previous grant-based models, the TFFF operates on market logic—creating a massive trust fund that pays dividends to tropical nations for successfully conserving their forests. Crucially, it mandates that 20% of all funds must go directly to Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities.
- Tripling Adaptation Finance: While previous COPs focused heavily on mitigation (cutting emissions), COP30 delivered a vital political signal to triple adaptation finance by 2035, recognizing that vulnerable nations are already suffering irreversible climate impacts.
- The <span color="green_bg">Just Transition</span> Mechanism (Belém Action Mechanism - BAM): Formalized a UN mechanism to ensure that the global shift away from fossil fuels is equitable. It guarantees technical and financial support so that workers and fossil-fuel-dependent communities in developing nations are not left behind during the green transition.
- <span color="green_bg">Global Goal on Adaptation</span> (GGA) Indicators: The summit finalized a comprehensive set of 59 indicators to finally measure and track global progress on climate resilience (e.g., water security, infrastructure readiness).
- <span color="green_bg">Belém Package</span> (195 Parties): Belém Mission to 1.5°C (COP29–31 troika) + Baku-to-Belém Roadmap to \$1.3 tn/yr by 2035 + adaptation finance tripled to \$120 bn/yr (within the \$300 bn NCQG) + Baku Adaptation Roadmap 2026–28 + Belém 4x Pledge on sustainable fuels by 2035 (India among launchers) + Belém Health Action Plan (first health adaptation plan, \$300 mn) + PACT (coal transitions) + J-REDD+ + Gender Action Plan
- Also at Belém: Systematic Observation Impact Bond (first bond for weather data; \$200 mn for LDCs and SIDS) + Beat the Heat drive (72 nations in Global Cooling Pledge: cooling emissions −68% by 2050) + Food Waste Breakthrough (halve food waste by 2030) + No Organic Waste (methane from organic waste −30% by 2030) + Utilities for Net Zero Alliance (\~\$1 tn by 2030)
- <b>Significance</b>: pledges → implementation ("COP of Implementation", "Forest COP", 10 years of Paris) + TFFF = forest model not tied to carbon markets + \$1.3 tn = biggest finance goal yet + all 195 Parties adopted the package
- <b>Examples</b>: TFFF launch (\~\$5.5 bn pledged: Norway up to \$3 bn as loans, Brazil and Indonesia \$1 bn each → far from the \$125 bn goal) + 53 countries endorsed the TFFF declaration
- <b>India's response</b> (India’s Strategic Stance & Diplomatic Masterstrokes)
- Combating "Disguised Protectionism" (The CBAM Pushback): This is India's most critical diplomatic intervention at COP30. Utilizing the BRICS coalition, India launched a fierce condemnation of unilateral, extraterritorial trade measures—specifically targeting the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). India successfully framed these carbon taxes as "disguised protectionism" that violates the sacred principle of CBDR-RC by unfairly penalizing the exports of developing economies.
- Defending Economic Sovereignty: India powerfully argued on the plenary floor that the Global North is using trade barriers to evade its historical financial responsibilities, essentially forcing the Global South to pay for the developed world's climate guilt.
- Strategic Observer in TFFF: While not a tropical rainforest nation in the Amazonian sense, India strategically joined the TFFF as an Observer. India used this platform to highlight its own massive domestic success: creating an additional carbon sink of 2.29 billion tonnes of CO2  equivalent between 2005 and 2021 through expanded forest and tree cover.
- Championing the Just Transition: India strongly welcomed the new Just Transition Mechanism, reiterating that the burden of climate change mitigation cannot be shifted onto the shoulders of those who have the least historical responsibility for causing the problem.
- India's stance also: <span color="green_bg">Article 9.1</span> finance = legal duty of developed countries + asked for a clear definition of climate finance + "COP of Adaptation" + developed nations to reach net zero earlier + technology access is a right, not a bargaining tool (IPR barriers) + via G77+China, BASIC, LMDC
- <b>Challenges</b>: no fossil-fuel roadmap in the final text + adaptation tripling has no clear baseline + CBAM-type trade measures still coming
- <b>Way forward</b>: Brazil-led fossil-fuel and deforestation roadmaps + NDC 3.0 with economy-wide absolute targets + finalise GGA indicators + CBDR to guide timelines and finance + fund the TFFF + finance on the <span color="green_bg">Baku-to-Belém Roadmap</span>
</toggle>
</toggle>
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h1">
3\. Pollution

<callout icon="💡">
Impact Thinking Framework: EEH (Environment, Economy, Health) Solutions: Recover, Recycle, Reuse, Finance, Governance Calculation: Green GDP = Net Domestic Product - (Cost of Depletion of Natural Resources + Cost of Degradation of Ecosystem)
</callout>

<toggle heading="h3">
POLLUTIONS

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Air

<b>Causes</b>

- <b>P</b>: <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-819e-86e9-dbd151717f46/4251111b-206d-818d-9883-001c17ae9e19">weak standards: India</span>'s PM2.5 limit (40) is 8x WHO's
- <b>I</b>: monitoring thin in small towns and villages
- <b>N</b>: winter inversion + low wind + north-westerly dust trap pollution
- <b>C</b>: open waste burning (Ghazipur landfill fires)
- <b>H</b>: vehicles + construction dust + stubble + coal plants (Delhi PM2.5: transport 23%, biomass burning 20%, dust 15%, industry 9%, CAQM)
  <toggle>
  Photochem smog

  - Classical smog: coal SO₂ + smoke + fog → grey haze, cold humid winters
  - Photochemical smog: NOx + VOCs (vehicles, industry) + strong sunlight → ground-level ozone → brown haze, warm sunny cities
  - Effects: lungs and eyes + SO₂ and NO₂ erode buildings (yellowing Taj) + acid rain
  - Fix: cut NOx an<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8105-8f9f-e72f5ac4267b/4251111b-206d-8169-926e-001cfd77d5a3">d VOCs</span> at source + regional caps (Gothenburg)
  </toggle>
- <b>C</b>: about <span color="green_bg">⅔ of Delhi's PM2.5 comes from outside Delhi</span>

<b>Effects</b>

- Health: 2nd biggest death risk after high BP + ≈15% of Delhi deaths (2023)
- Environment: acid rain + urban heat island
- Economy: ≈9.5% of GDP lost (Lancet 2025)
- Governance: 66 of the world's 100 most polluted cities are Indian (IQAir 2025)
- Society: the poor and outdoor workers breathe it most

<b>Solutions</b>

- <b>P</b>: raise standards to WHO level
  <toggle>
  WHO AQG 2021

  - First update since 2005, tighter for most pollutants
  - PM2.5 annual 10 → 5 + PM2.5 24-hour 25 → 15 + PM10 annual 20 → 15 + NO₂ annual 40 → 10
  - New: 24-hour NO₂, peak-season ozone, 24-hour CO limits
  - <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81e4-aebd-ffda4854febf/4251111b-206d-8172-ad2c-001c4cbc317f">India's NAAQS (2009): PM2.5 annual 40 = 8x the new WHO level →</span> revise NAAQS
  </toggle>
- <b>P</b>: implement better, target PM2.5 not just PM10
  <toggle>
  NCAP

  - 2019: cut particulate pollution 40% by 2026 (vs 2017) in 131 <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8137-9bb3-f7c8de735d6e/4251111b-206d-81ba-bebc-001c4d6bdc0f">non-attainment cities t</span>hrough city action plans
  - Who: CPCB monitors, SPCBs and ULBs implement, MoEFCC funds
  - Problems: P chases PM10, not PM2.5 · N city by city, not airshed · H root causes untouched · F money spent on water sprinkling for dust
  - Fix: target PM2.5 + airshed plan<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-810e-9759-ec18bf638cf8/4251111b-206d-8176-a1d0-001c363af8ef">s + source apportionment</span> in every city + health-based targets
  </toggle>
- <b>I</b>: monitors from 25 to 1,600 + <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-814f-b0e8-e2f4e5e64428/4251111b-206d-8128-8d20-001cd8974c04">SAFAR</span> real-time tracking + cloud seeding trials
  <toggle>
  Cloud seeding

  - Silver iodide, potassium iodide or dry ice sprayed from aircraft → nuclei that pull water vapour into rain · hygroscopic (liquid clouds) vs glaciogenic (supercooled clouds)
  - India: IIT Kanpur trial over Delhi to wash out pollution · World: Dubai for rain
  - Uses: clear smog and dust + rain in drought areas + less hail, wildfire control, more winter snow
  - Concerns: floods and landslides + disturbs natural weather + silver iodide may be toxic + costs unclear → fix: research + environmental safeguards + clear rules
  </toggle>
- <b>N</b>: scale Delhi's GRAP to other airsheds, move to an <span color="green_bg">airshed approach</span>
  <toggle>
  Delhi model

  - <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-816e-9559-dd389a6d004e/4251111b-206d-8152-ac5f-001ced60c571">CAQM Act 2021 (replaced EPCA) r</span>uns GRAP for the whole NCR
  - <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81fd-97cd-c6296dde2120/4251111b-206d-8110-8d02-001c08bf52dc">GRAP: 4 stages</span> by AQI: Poor (201–300) → Very poor (301–400) → Severe (401–450) → Severe+ (450+)
  - Beijing model: average PM2.5 cut from 144 to 92 (2015–2024)
  - Polluter pays: environmental compensation (SC, Lodhi Property case)
  </toggle>
- <b>C</b>: awareness + end open waste and stubble burning
- <b>H</b>: clean the source: EVs (7.6% share in 2024 → 30% by 2030) + CNG + cleaner industrial fuels + phase out old vehicles
- <b>F</b>: <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8118-8fc8-fddc20e4bb5b/4251111b-206d-8114-aec1-001ca3397aa4">emissions trading (Surat</span> 2019, best practice)
- <b>C</b>: NCR states' joint annual plans + regional caps
  <toggle>
  <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8167-ae5d-ddbd5fcb8f64/4251111b-206d-81f7-9747-001cf133f51d">Gothenburg 1999</span>

  - Under UNECE Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution
  - Caps on SO₂, NOx, VOCs and ammonia
  - Lesson: air crosses borders, so caps must be regional, not city-wise
  </toggle>
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Water

- Frame: <span color="green_bg">water bankruptcy</span> = long-term use > what nature refills (UNU-INWEH) + India has 18% of people, 4% of fresh water

<b>Causes</b>

- <b>P</b>: weak checks on industry and cities + Draft National Water Policy 2020 still not adopted
- <b>I</b>: aquifers mapped late (NAQUIM), little real-time data
- <b>N</b>: climate change (groundwater depletion may triple by 2080)
- <b>N</b>: sea-level rise + storm surges push seawater into coastal aquifers
  <toggle>
  Seawater intrusion

  - What: saline seawater moves into coastal freshwater aquifers when freshwater pressure falls; risk along the 7,500 km coast (Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Andhra, Kerala) (new, CivilsDaily)
  - Causes: over-pumping near coasts + sea-level rise, cyclones, storm surges + wetland loss and sand mining (Chennai lost 85% of its wetlands, WWF) + less silt to deltas (dams, river linking)
  - Fix: artificial recharge (recharge wells, subsurface dykes) + caps and licensing on coastal borewells + mangroves + salt-tolerant crops (ICAR-CSSRI rice) (new, CivilsDaily)
  </toggle>
- <b>C</b>: overuse + nitrogen fertiliser overuse (nitrate now the most widespread groundwater pollutant) + idol immersion during festivals
- <b>H</b>: untreated sewage (>60% enters rivers) + industry (sugar, paper, tanneries, dyeing)
  <toggle>
  Industrial pollution

  - Industry dumps heavy metals (lead, mercury, chromium) + dyes, phenols + hot water
  - Cases: Kali river, UP (sugar mills, distilleries, paper mills → black water, no aquatic life) + Noyyal, Tamil Nadu (Tiruppur dyeing units → farmland infertile, groundwater salty)
  - Fix: <span color="green_bg">zero liquid discharge</span> for textile units + CETPs + online effluent monitoring
  - Law: Water Act 1974 (2024 amendment: fines by adjudicating officers go to the Environment Protection Fund) + EPA 1986 + NGT
  </toggle>
- <b>H</b>: farms draw 87% of groundwater
  <toggle>
  Groundwater

  - Statu<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81cc-a10d-e15c722a26c5/4251111b-206d-8115-aeb6-001cac65268e">s (CGWB</span> 2025): 10.8% of units over-exploited (17.2% in 2017) + India ≈25% of world groundwater use
  - Why: <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81c9-a7a9-efdf24f8e7bb/4251111b-206d-81b4-8edb-001cae7a2bde">Easement Act 1882</span> ties water to land + cities seal recharge zones + land subsidence in 5 megacities
  - Pollution: 28.3% of samples exceed a BIS limit: nitrate → blue-baby syndrome, fluoride → fluorosis (Nalgonda technique), arsenic → cancers (<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8189-9e07-ffb222c170c2/4251111b-206d-8165-b5db-001c1c20d1d7">phytoremediation)</span> + uranium (Punjab, Haryana)
  - Steps: Atal Bhujal + <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81e2-8e7c-dbde41507ea9/4251111b-206d-8117-ad1b-001cc6933bf0">NAQUIM +</span> <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81e2-8e7c-dbde41507ea9/4251111b-206d-8111-9500-001cfcbec2f3">IN-GRES →</span> next: National Water Commission (Mihir Shah) + groundwater rights apart from land

  <toggle>
  Atal Bhujal

  - 2019, World Bank-backed, 7 water-stressed states: community-led groundwater management, gram panchayats make water security plans (new)
  </toggle>
  </toggle>
- <b>F</b>: sewage plants costly to build and run, so few get built
- <b>C</b>: water = State subject, inter-state rivers = Union (Art 262) → many agencies, states fight over water
  <toggle>
  Urban water governance

  - Indore contaminated tap-water crisis + many agencies, nobody accountable (Gurugram)
  - ≈38% of water lost as <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8182-afc1-e7dfcf5feabc/4251111b-206d-8182-bb6b-001c0787b3b7">non-revenue water (leaks, theft) + b</span>orewell and tanker dependence (Chennai 2019, Bengaluru 2024)
  - Best practice: Rajasthan's Mukhyamantri Jal Swavlamban Abhiyan ("four waters") → groundwater up ≈4%
  - Fix: 100% wastewater treatment and reuse + Integrated Urban Water Management + water budgeting + Jan Bhagidari
  </toggle>

<b>Effects</b>

- Health: cholera, typhoid + blue-baby syndrome, fluorosis, cancers
- Environment<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81f1-8852-cabe525dd1dc/4251111b-206d-812f-9183-001c19a39513">: eutrophication</span>, dead zones + 296 polluted stretches on 271 rivers (CPCB 2025)
- Economy: ≈3% of GDP lost (World Bank) + threat to 75% of wheat and 65% of rice (NITI 2019)
- Governance: city water crises (Chennai 2019, Bengaluru 2024) + inter-state disputes
- Society: women and girls spend 200 million hours collecting water (UNICEF, global) + 20% of households lack tap water

<b>Solutions</b>

- <b>P</b>: one national water law
  <toggle>
  NWP 2012

  - National Water Policy 2012 (earlier 1987, 2002): drinking water and sanitation first, then water as an economic good + minimum ecological flow + basin-level planning
  - Water Regulatory Authority in each state + pricing to save water + a national framework law
  - Draft NWP 2020 (Mihir Shah) not adopted: from building dams to managing demand + groundwater as a common resource
  - National Water Mission (NAPCC): water-use efficiency +20% + basin plans
  </toggle>
- <b>P</b>: clean rivers basin by basin
  <toggle>
  Namami Gange

  - NMCG implement<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8105-a404-f1495fbcc0bc/4251111b-206d-8110-a833-001c0c289fa0">s: 127 STPs working (Mar 2025) + CETPs</span> for industry
  - Earlier plans (<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8190-b2ec-e466a70bf97d/4251111b-206d-817c-8292-001c266e2328">GAP 1985</span>, GAP-II, NGRBA) faltered: P only sewage, not the whole basin · N no <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8190-b2ec-e466a70bf97d/4251111b-206d-81e1-b8a0-001c8b64c5d2">e-flow ·</span> H states didn't run STPs after building them
  - Now: I NGT 2022 found untreated waste in 60% of the Ganga · F only 69% of funds used till 2024–25
  - Quantum leaps: basin-level management with minimum e-flow + autonomous pollution boards + real-time AI tracking (Ganga digital twin)
  </toggle>
- <b>P</b>: tap water for every home
  <toggle>
  Jal Jeevan Mission

  - Tap water to every rural household + water-quality monitoring + Panchayats run and maintain it
  - Gap: 20% of households still lack tap water
  </toggle>

  <toggle>
  AMRUT 2.0

  - Water-secure cities: tap connections to all households in 500 AMRUT cities
  - Outcome-based funding + circular economy of water (treated wastewater reuse)
  </toggle>
- <b>I</b><span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-815b-bce6-fac702fda06b/4251111b-206d-810e-8c04-001cdea9d879">: GRACE satellite</span> for groundwater + IN-GRES + AI and GIS to site farm ponds + IoT sensors + <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-815b-bce6-fac702fda06b/4251111b-206d-81ae-a9ba-001c19d8e13b">RTDAS water-level data</span> (National Hydrology Project)
- <b>N</b>: plan by basin, keep minimum <span color="green_bg">e-flow</span> (EU Water Framework Directive), revive water bodies (Mission Kakatiya: 46,531 tanks)
  <toggle>
  Amrit Sarovar

  - 75 water bodies per district, built or revived with people's participation
  - 68,000+ completed (Mar 2025), 46,000 of them under MGNREGS
  </toggle>

  <toggle>
  River linking

  - <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8187-b7e3-d4749ee5c44f/4251111b-206d-81ba-a976-001cf6b6b786">NPP 1980 (NWDA)</span>: 30 links = 14 Himalayan + 16 Peninsular; Ken–Betwa is the first (MP + UP, Bundelkhand)
  - For: surplus to deficit basins → drought and flood relief + irrigation + hydropower + navigation
  - Against: forests drowned (Panna Tiger Reserve, ≈20,000 people affected) + less silt → deltas sink, seawater intrusion + costly, slow, states fight
  </toggle>
- <b>C</b>: community action: <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-811d-9b4e-ee8770398fed/4251111b-206d-8186-9ef9-001c6a5688d3">Jal Sanchay Jan Bhagidari</span> + Atal Bhujal + <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-811d-9b4e-ee8770398fed/4251111b-206d-81fe-a54d-001c3a9731d0">Neeru-Chettu</span> (Andhra: 1.2 lakh structures repaired)
- <b>H</b>: <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81d7-8632-cf86ba0ae9ca/4251111b-206d-81d7-b6ca-001c945030fb">clean the source: ZLD</span> + CETPs + less nitrogen fertiliser (natural farming) + drip and sprinkler
- <b>F</b>: water pricing + tradable pollution permits for water (like air emissions trading)
- <b>C</b>: National Water Commission <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81f8-a4cc-c7df4046048b/4251111b-206d-8143-bb03-001cc1fed67d">(merge CWC</span> + CGWB, Mihir Shah) + basin authorities
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Plastic

- Frame: India makes ≈4 million t of plastic waste a year (CPCB) + 3rd in the world in single-use plastic

<b>Causes</b>

- <b>P</b>: weak enforcement of the single-use plastic ban (thin bags back in markets)
- <b>I</b>: compostable or bio-based plastic is only 1.5% of plastic + few cheap alternatives
- <b>N</b>: plastic never breaks down, only fragments into microplastics
- <b>C</b>: throwaway habits: per-capita plastic waste doubled in 5 years
- <b>H</b>: packaging and FMCG (world makes 460+ million t of plastic a year) + informal recycling
  <toggle>
  Plastic types

  <image source="notion-file-block://4221111b-206d-803a-be38-de7b40fff058/378b7019-f2b3-48af-ae2a-d503744aa49f?space_id=3939cd2d-3e25-404f-9196-d463e4c2e65e&name=Major_Types_of_Plastics.png" />

  - PET: a pet dog drinking from a plastic bottle → everywhere, highly recyclable
  - PVC: plumbing pipes → industrial, toxins, low recyclability
  - PP: double P = Tupperware → goes in the microwave, heat resistant
  - PS: sounds like Styrofoam → crumbles, very low recyclability
  </toggle>
- <b>F</b>: plastic stays cheaper: tariffs on plastics cut to 7.2% while alternatives (bamboo) pay ≈14.4%
- <b>C</b><span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8104-8ece-ec625928bb17/4251111b-206d-81c7-b3d6-001c134f425c">: global plastics treaty talks stalled (INC adjourned</span> without consensus)

<b>Effects</b>

- Health: microplastics enter food and blood
- Environment: ≈20 million t of plastic leaks into nature every year (WEF)
- Society: waste pickers and coastal communities bear it

<b>Solutions</b>

- <b>P</b>: strict EPR audits + enforce the ban
  <toggle>
  SUP ban + EPR

  - PWM Amendment Rules 2021: single-use plastic items banned from Jul 2022 + <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8131-8dc5-e0b6feb3bf55/4251111b-206d-81c1-8462-001cd21aca0d">EPR on plastic packaging</span> (2022): producers, importers, brand owners answer for the whole life cycle
  - <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81d4-81db-e499c7c43741/4251111b-206d-8174-bde5-001cee6c09c3">PWM Rules 2024</span>: Panchayats assess local plastic waste + PWM Rules 2026: more recycled plastic in packaging
  - Worked: Sikkim (plastic bags banned in 1998) · Failed: 2022 ban (weak enforcement, few cheap alternatives)
  </toggle>
- <b>I</b>: cheap alternatives (KVIC's <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81b3-902b-c26ba78d3abe/4251111b-206d-8128-a825-001ca0d82f3d">Project REPLAN,</span> compostables) + National Dashboard on SUP
- <b>C</b>: carry-your-own-bag habits (Sikkim)
- <b>H</b>: replace at source: Mandatory Jute Packaging Act 2010 + recycled-content mandates
- <b>F</b>: <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8168-951e-d4041b1740b1/4251111b-206d-8176-a506-001c2dcd79a0">Plastic Parks (</span>10 approved, grants up to 50%) + fix tariffs so alternatives are cheaper
- <b>C</b>: industry pacts (<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81ff-8e09-d0e7928511a2/4251111b-206d-818f-a984-001cf4b35473">India Plastics Pact,</span> Un-Plastic Collective) + a global treaty covering the whole life cycle + <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81ff-8e09-d0e7928511a2/4251111b-206d-8192-97df-001c3e65f291">synergy with the BRS conventions</span>
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Oil Spills

- Frame: oil pollution = petroleum released into the sea from tankers, ship accidents, offshore rigs, pipelines and routine discharge (new)

<b>Causes</b>

- <b>P</b>: weak checks on cargo declarations and hazardous-goods handling
- <b>I</b>: little real-time detection at sea
- <b>N</b>: rough monsoon seas and cyclones sink ships (MSC ELSA 3 off Kochi, May 2025)
- <b>H</b>: tanker and cargo-ship accidents, fires, collisions + routine discharge
  <toggle>
  Maritime disasters

  - MSC ELSA 3 sank off Kochi + fire on MV Wan Hai 503 off Kerala (2025)
  - Mauritius, MV Wakashio (2020)
  - Problems: tangled ownership (Liberian flag, German owner, Cyprus manager) + insurance disputes delay clean-up
  - Rules: IMO conventions (SOLAS 1974<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81ca-856b-fb391af70f9f/4251111b-206d-818a-9583-001ce3a88ac8">, MARPOL</span>, IMDG Code) + Merchant Shipping Act 1958 + National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan (Coast Guard)
  </toggle>
- <b>F</b>: insurance disputes delay clean-up
- <b>C</b>: tangled ownership across countries, nobody answers

<b>Effects</b>

- Environment: oil film blocks light and oxygen → plankton and corals die + coats seabirds and turtles + toxins climb the food chain (new)
- Economy: fishing and coastal tourism lose
- Society: fishing communities lose livelihoods
- Why worse for India: 7,500 km coast + most crude arrives by sea + fragile mangroves (Sundarbans), coral reefs (Gulf of Mannar), turtle nesting beaches (Odisha) (new)

<b>Solutions</b>

- <b>P</b>: enforce SOLAS + polluter pays + honest cargo declaration
- <b>I</b><span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8163-954d-dad9feb8a43f/4251111b-206d-81be-92d2-001ce6addccb">: electronic cargo tracking + satellite detection (RISAT)</span>
- <b>N</b>: <span color="green_bg">bioremediation</span> (<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81ee-a557-dfd744a076b2/4251111b-206d-81d9-8d73-001c0614f390">Oilzapper</span>, Oilivorous-S by TERI) + natural sorbents (milkweed fibre)
- <b>H</b>: booms and skimmers + standard safety SOPs
- <b>C</b>: National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan (Coast Guard) + MARPOL, UNCLOS
</toggle>
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h3">
WASTE

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Solid Waste

- Frame: 62 million t a year generated, 43 collected, only 12 treated (TERI) → 165 million t by 2030

<b>Causes</b>

- <b>P</b>: rules not implemented + no political will + no designated sites → open dumps and legacy landfills (≈8.8 crore t legacy waste, Ghazipur fires)
- <b>C</b>: no <span color="green_bg">segregation at source</span> + low door-to-door collection
- <b>H</b>: overconsumption + FMCG packaging: consumption grew, collection didn't + too few processing units: only 15–20% processed
- <b>F</b>: low municipal finance (poor creditworthiness)
- <b>C</b>: overlapping jurisdiction between agencies

<b>Effects</b>

- Health: landfill fires and disease near dumps
- Environment: <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-815f-8d2c-c047db6f31b7/4251111b-206d-8111-b5d9-001c39150b8c">leachate</span> into groundwater + methane from landfills
- Economy: materials worth crores lost instead of recycled
- Society: waste pickers work unprotected

<b>Solutions</b>

- <b>P</b>: one dedicated, enforced rulebook
  <toggle>
  SWM Rules 2026

  - From 1 Apr 2026, replaced the 2016 Rules: 3-way → 4-stream segregation
  - Bulk generators process their wet waste or buy an <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-813a-a688-edb5c6b16df7/4251111b-206d-81b7-8a45-001c5b0d66e2">EBWGR certificate +</span> <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-813a-a688-edb5c6b16df7/4251111b-206d-8149-b860-001c3c32e773">refuse-derived fuel to cement</span> plants
  - Yearly landfill audits + tourist user fee in hills and islands + polluter-pays compensation
  - Also: <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8117-b3ce-e288dad2fff7/4251111b-206d-811d-82b1-001c6855209d">C&D Waste Rules, 2025</span> + Contaminated Sites Rules 2025
  </toggle>
- <b>I</b>: GPS-tracked door-to-door collection (Bhopal) + waste processors at scale (Mumbai, Bhopal)
- <b>N</b>: designated sites + <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81fa-a371-e44af2385ba8/4251111b-206d-8142-bd49-001c8b855fcd">biomine legacy dumps</span> (<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81fa-a371-e44af2385ba8/4251111b-206d-818c-85d9-001cc5cb4d24">DRAP)</span> + yearly landfill audits
- <b>C</b>: segregation at source: <span color="green_bg">Indore</span> (best example) + Anupam Colony, Delhi + SWaCH, Pune
- <b>H</b>: cut waste at source, treat it as a resource
  <toggle>
  Circular economy

  - Only 7.2% of the world economy is circular (9.1% in 2018) + India could be a \$2 trillion market with 1 crore jobs by 2050
  - Waste to wealth: biogas from wet waste + gasification, pyrolysis + GOBARdhan plants · Indore: Asia's largest Bio-CNG plant (2022)
  - India: Mission LiFE + EPR rule<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8118-945c-eaf9aaf65ef0/4251111b-206d-811e-abe6-001c47d17568">s + Steel Scrap Recycling Policy</span> + NITI Circular Economy Cell
  - Gaps: <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-810e-a66a-f0e9c6fc5972/4251111b-206d-81f3-9d67-001c54e82026">downcycling +</span> informal sector recovers only 10–20% of materials + fake EPR certificates
  - Fix: EPR across sectors (plastic, e-waste, batteries, tyres) + recycled-content mandates + design for reuse · Mixed: <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8172-b8f8-fb70de5df983/4251111b-206d-81ae-b85f-001cfe8ef8de">Alang ship recycling (Hong Kong Convention</span> in force 2025)
  </toggle>
- <b>F</b>: user fees + waste cess (Bengaluru proposal) + Garbage Free City star rating
- <b>C</b>: Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban 2.0 + clear roles for ULBs
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 E-Waste

- Frame: India is 3rd largest after the USA and China: ≈6 million t (2024) → 14 million t by 2030 + only 10% formally recycled (world ≈22%)

<b>Causes</b>

- <b>P</b>: fake recyclers distort the EPR market + EPR covers only gold, copper, iron, aluminium
- <b>I</b>: crude methods: circuit boards stripped with acid
- <b>C</b>: low awareness, old devices go to kabadiwalas
- <b>H</b>: 85% handled by the informal sector
- <b>C</b>: 80% of rich countries' e-waste is shipped to developing countries

<b>Effects</b>

- Health and environment: lead, mercury, cadmium leach into groundwater (Moradabad: Ramganga mercury 8x the standard, CSE 2015)
- Economy: ₹51,000 crore of materials lost (Paryavaran NITI Manthan)

<b>Solutions</b>

- <b>P</b>: widen and police EPR
  <toggle>
  E-waste rules

  - 2011: EPR introduced (producer cleans what he produces) → 2016: Producer Responsibility Organisations
  - 2022: CPCB portal + tradable EPR certificates bought from registered recyclers + items covered 21 → 106
  - <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8106-a4fd-db88c7d9fcec/4251111b-206d-816a-ad81-001c3e0779cd">Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022</span>
  </toggle>
- <b>I</b>: hydrometallurgy + AI-based recovery + <span color="green_bg" discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8148-a677-f1b24de6fc7c/4251111b-206d-81fc-8b69-001c74b593cc">bioleaching</span> (microbes pull metals out of waste)
- <b>C</b>: Kerala's Haritha Karma Sena buys e-waste door to door at fixed rates (2025)
- <b>H</b>: train and certify informal workers
- <b>F</b>: GST-linked checks on recyclers + a recycling wing in th<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8182-bc83-cb4658145fd7/4251111b-206d-81aa-bc5e-001c57d06d2f">e National Critical Mineral Mission</span>
- <b>C</b>: global rules on dumping
  <toggle>
  Basel + Stockholm

  - Basel Convention (1989): controls transboundary movement of hazardous waste, stops rich countries dumping e-waste on poor ones
  - Stockholm Convention (2001): eliminates persistent organic pollutants (the "Dirty Dozen", e.g. DDT)
  </toggle>
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Hazardous & Biomedical Waste

- Frame: hazardous = toxic, flammable, reactive or corrosive + biomedical ≈609 t a day (+101 t a day in COVID)

<b>Causes</b>

- <b>P</b>: small clinics hard to monitor + illegal imports
- <b>C</b>: poor segregation in hospitals + informal recyclers without safety gear + people oppose new TSDFs near them
- <b>H</b>: industry, hospitals, coal plants, gold mining + few treatment, storage and disposal facilities (<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81e4-ae2d-eefd20ba699c/4251111b-206d-8148-a130-001cf7b0bc70">TSDFs) + f</span>ew common biomedical facilities (CBWTFs) in rural areas
  <toggle>
  Mercury

  - <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-812b-97cf-f09df84700ab/4251111b-206d-81a3-8c94-001c175f27b6">Methylmercury is the most toxic form: bioaccumulates in fish</span>, harms foetuses and children
  - Failed: Minamata, Japan (1956, factory waste) + Kodaikanal, Tamil Nadu (2001, HUL thermometer factory)
  - India: ratified the Minamata Convention (2018) + mercury limits for coal plants (2015) + mercury thermometers out of hospitals
  - Gap: coal plants slow on controls (≈78% of Category C plants exempted from <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8192-9081-e320eece7534/4251111b-206d-8173-92c0-001c559a22b0">FGD, Jul 2025</span>)
  </toggle>

<b>Effects</b>

- Health: Bhopal: 337 t of Union Carbide toxic waste burnt at Pithampur only in 2025, 40 years later
- Environment: toxins leach into soil and groundwater

<b>Solutions</b>

- <b>P</b>: enforce the 2016 rules
  <toggle>
  Waste rules 2016

  - Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules 2016 (under EPA): SPCB authorisation for generators + duties for TSDF operators
  - Bio-Medical Waste Rules 2016 (amended 2018, 2019): colour-coded bins + common facilities (CBWTFs) + incineration, autoclave, microwave + secured landfill
  </toggle>
- <b>N</b>: clean old toxic sites with <span color="green_bg">bioremediation</span> and phytoremediatio<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81d0-94ac-feac9c03b583/4251111b-206d-813e-9501-001c435252c4">n + Contaminated Sites Rules 2025</span> (189 substances)
- <b>C</b>: IMAGE, Palakkad: doctors' association runs one common biomedical facility for Kerala's private hospitals
- <b>H</b>: cleaner production + formalise informal recyclers + more TSDFs and CBWTFs, especially rural
</toggle>
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h3">
MISC

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Land Degradation

- Frame: fall in land's biological or economic productivity (UNCCD); in drylands = desertification + India ≈30% of land degraded (ISRO Atlas), Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Jharkhand worst

<b>Causes</b>

- <b>P</b>: policies reward over-irrigation and fertiliser (Punjab–Haryana canals → waterlogging, salinity)
- <b>N</b>: water erosion (biggest) + wind erosion (Thar) + invasive Lantana in ≈50% of forest and scrubland (SOE 2026)
- <b>C</b>: overgrazing + shifting cultivation
- <b>H</b>: deforestation + mining

<b>Effects</b>

- Environment: soils are the 2nd largest carbon pool after oceans (2,500 Gt) + dust storms + silted reservoirs + India breached the <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-813c-bf90-ca407fbd27ae/4251111b-206d-8140-b997-001c5240df97">land-system-change boundary (SOE 2026)</span>
- Economy: lower yields
- Society: rural distress and migration (affects 3.2 billion people worldwide)

<b>Solutions</b>

- <b>P</b>: <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8128-bbd8-d5368003e5bc/4251111b-206d-8118-8406-001c53f73949">LDN target:</span> restore 26 million ha by 2030 (≈24 million ha done or under way)
  <toggle>
  Global commitments

  - Bonn Challenge: restore 350 million ha worldwide by 2030 (India pledged 26 million ha)
  - UNCCD COP16, Riyadh 2024: Riyadh Global Drought Resilience Partnership (\$12 billion+) + land tenure for local communities
  - UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration (2021–2030)
  </toggle>
- <b>I</b>: ISRO Desertification Atlas + Soil Health Card
- <b>N</b>: watershed development (<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81d3-81b7-d71ac0d27dc4/4251111b-206d-813f-9fbf-001cc1f2356f">PMKSY-WDC) + afforestation (Green India Mission, A</span>ravalli Green Wall) + restore whole landscapes, not just plant trees · Ralegan Siddhi (watershed revived groundwater and farms)
- <b>C</b>: grazing control + local techniques (<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8142-8692-dce9e91b6a88/4251111b-206d-811c-b072-001c0e41ab1e">Zai pits</span>) + land tenure rights for local communities
- <b>H</b>: change how we farm
  <toggle>
  Natural farming

  - Chemical-free farming with on-farm inputs (organic buys inputs from outside; natural doesn't)
  - Pillars: <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-813e-9b5c-e98271ac0e2c/4251111b-206d-810b-b480-001c77fe24b7">Beejamrit + Jeevamrit</span> + mulching + Whapasa
  - Worked: Andhra Pradesh <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8177-bdff-fc2ed104c05e/4251111b-206d-81dd-85b2-001c95530457">APCNF (</span>lakhs of farmers, lower input costs) · Failed: Sri Lanka 2021 (overnight fertiliser ban → yields crashed)
  - India: National Mission on Natural Farming (2024, ₹2,481 crore, 1 crore farmers)
  - Gaps: yields may dip in early years + needs cattle for inputs + few premium markets → fix: phased shift (Sri Lanka lesson) + certification + market links
  </toggle>

  <toggle>
  Agroforestry

  - Trees with crops or livestock on farms: ≈8.5% of land + National Agroforestry Policy 2014 (India first in the world)
  - Gains: crop yields up ≈50% + stores 14–27 t CO₂ per ha a year (EAC-PM) + half of fuelwood, 60% of paper-pulp wood
  - Worked: poplar on farm bunds, Punjab–Haryana (feeds the plywood industry)
  - India: <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81c6-b4a9-d25214fdbcea/4251111b-206d-811b-82d8-001c71d3e24e">Trees Outside Forests in India (2023) + SMAF</span> (under NMSA) + NITI's GROW initiative
  - Gap: felling and transit permits → adopt model felling rules in every state
  </toggle>
- <b>F</b><span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8161-958f-c1d6d7d9b038/4251111b-206d-81ab-9f46-001c5ede6641">: Green Credit Programme</span>
</toggle>
</toggle>

<toggle>
OLD way 

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Air

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2022, 2021, 2020, 2014

- <b>2022 Q7 (10 marks):</b> Discuss in detail the photochemical smog emphasizing its formation, effects and mitigation. Explain the 1999 Gothenburg Protocol.
- <b>2021 Q7 (10 marks):</b> Describe the key points of the revised Global Air Quality Guidelines (AQGs) recently released by the World Health Organisation (WHO). Relevance of Coal for India’s Energy Security

- India’s electricity consumption is expected to triple by 2050 \[International Energy Agency (IEA)\]
- Large indigenous availability: India holds 107,727 million tons (MMst) of proven coal reserves as of 2016, ranking 5th in the world.
- Socio-economic relevance: Development of coal-producing region like Bihar; Creation of jobs; etc.

Carbon Capture

- Why: hard-to-abate (means heavy industrial and long distance transport sectors whose GHG cannot be easily or economically eliminated via just using RE) sectors (steel, cement, fertiliser) + blue hydrogen + <span color="green_bg">net zero</span> needs 11.4 Gt stored by 2070

<toggle>
Air Pollution Statistics

- Why Indian air is so bad (factors: No rain in north except monsoon months, dust from that and Sahara, stubble burning, no master plan, unscientific waste disposal eg. Ghazipur landfill burning)
- IQAir 2025: India 6th most polluted country + 66 of world's 100 worst cities + Loni (UP) worst city, Delhi worst capital + about 15% of Delhi deaths linked to air (2023) + about 9.5% of GDP lost (2022, Lancet 2025) + Surat emissions trading (2019) as best practice
- Bad air 2nd largest risk of death after BP (state of global air 2024); So2 and NO2 erode buildings (yellowing of Taj Mahal); <span color="green_bg">urban heat island</span> effect, acid rain
- SMOG TYPES AND GOTHENBURG PROTOCOL
  - Classical smog: coal/SO₂ + smoke + fog → grey haze, cold humid winters
  - Photochemical smog: NOx + VOCs (vehicles, industry) + strong sunlight → ground-level ozone → brown haze, warm sunny cities
  - Gothenburg Protocol (1999, under UNECE Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution): emission ceilings for SO₂, NOx, VOCs and ammonia
</toggle>

<toggle>
Initiatives by India

- <span color="green_bg">National Clean Air Programme</span> (2019)
  - Funds: Central government, states, and urban local bodies fund NCAP.
  - Functions: Reduce particulate pollution by 40% by 2026 (vs 2017) through city action plans and awareness and increased monitoring. It also promotes clean technologies, alternative fuels, and stronger enforcement of pollution laws.
  - Functionaries: CPCB leads monitoring; SPCBs and ULBs implement locally; MoEFCC oversees policy and funding.
  - Goal: Improve air quality in 131 non-attainment cities with multi-sector coordination.
  - Evaluation : focus too much on PM 10 and not PM 2.5, 1600 stations achieved from 25, use of funds is to settle dust by water sprinkling, root causes not addressed.
- WHO AQG 2021 (first update since 2005, tighter for most pollutants):
  | Pollutant | 2005 | 2021 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | PM2.5 annual (µg/m³) | 10 | 5 |
  | PM2.5 24-hour | 25 | 15 |
  | PM10 annual | 20 | 15 |
  | PM10 24-hour | 50 | 45 |
  | NO₂ annual | 40 | 10 |

  <p>
  Also new: 24-hour NO₂, peak-season ozone and 24-hour CO limits
  </p>

  <p>
  India's NAAQS (2009): PM2.5 annual 40 = 8x the new WHO level
  </p>

  <p>
  NCAP changes needed: target PM2.5 not just PM10 + revise NAAQS + airshed / regional plans (not city by city) + source apportionment in every city + health-based targets + more monitors in small towns and villages
  </p>
- Safar portal (real time air pollution tracking)
- DELHI
  - Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM)
    - Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP).
      - 4 stages by AQI: Poor (201–300) → Very poor (301–400) → Severe (401–450) → Severe+ (450+)
    - CAQM Act 2021 (replaced EPCA)
  - costs the Indian economy approximately \$36.8 billion (1.36% of GDP) annually
  - Over 3.3 crore registered vehicles spew NO2 and CO2
  - Construction: Unregulated dust contributes nearly 27% of PM2.5 levels
  - Global precedents : china Beijing model, (cut its average from 144 to 92, 2015–2024)
  - Sources (CAQM): secondary particles 27% + transport 23% + biomass burning 20% + dust 15% + industry 9% → about <span color="green_bg">two-thirds of PM2.5 comes from outside Delhi</span>
  - Winter: north-westerly winds bring dust + temperature inversion + low wind + stubble burning
  - Fix: phase out old vehicles + EV/CNG transport + annual action plans for NCR states + cleaner industrial fuels + environmental compensation (polluter pays; SC, Lodhi Property case)
</toggle>

<toggle>
Availability & Stress

- 18% pop but 4 % water reserves
- 72% of India’s wastewater ends up in rivers and lakes (water reuse tech : membrane bioreactor (biological treatment and membrane filtration ) + ultrafiltration + reverse osmosis + electrodialysis reversal + thermal evaporation)
- Groundwater use: 87% farms, 11% domestic
- CGWB 2025 (6,762 units): over-exploited 10.8% (17.24% in 2017) + critical 2.97% + semi-critical 11.2% + safe 73.2% (62.6% in 2017) + extraction 247.22 BCM + India = about 25% of world groundwater use, 87% for farms
- GW depletion causes: cities seal recharge zones + 1882 Easement Act ties water to land + climate (depletion may triple by 2080) + land subsidence in 5 megacities → steps: <span color="green_bg">Atal Bhujal</span> + <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4221111b-206d-8131-9e96-ef40f6fe551b/4251111b-206d-80cb-82fa-001c8390e976">NAQUIM</span> (National Aquifer Mapping & Management Programme) + Master Plan for Artificial Recharge 2020 + <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4221111b-206d-8131-9e96-ef40f6fe551b/4251111b-206d-8018-8286-001cfb41ebca">IN-GRES</span> (India Groundwater Resource Estimation System) → next: National Water Commission (<span color="green_bg">Mihir Shah</span>) + groundwater rights apart from land
- GW pollution (CGWB 2025): 28.3% of samples exceed a BIS limit + nitrate most widespread (Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra) + fluoride (Rajasthan) + arsenic (Ganga–Brahmaputra plains) + uranium (Punjab, Haryana) + lead (Delhi) → <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4221111b-206d-816e-b49e-e64c35ac6664/4251111b-206d-803b-8fe5-001c280c54b0">blue-baby syndrome</span>, <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4221111b-206d-816e-b49e-e64c35ac6664/4251111b-206d-8097-b205-001cd5370393">fluorosis</span>, cancers, kidney damage → fix: phytoremediation (arsenic) + Nalgonda technique (fluoride) + less nitrogen fertiliser
- Threat to 75 % of wheat and 65% of rice production (composite water management index Niti Aayog 2019)
- Demand expected to double by 2030
- Women and girls spend 200 million hours collecting water (UNICEF)
- Cause of stress : CC + AGRI + Unsustainbel use + indiscriminate festivals + 20% households lack tap water connections + uranium pollution found in 12 states + low treatment capacity of sewage (18% only) bc high operational and capital costs
- <span color="green_bg">Water bankruptcy</span> (UNU-INWEH report, world has entered it): long-term use > what nature refills → damage can't be undone
  - Bank analogy: "current account" = rivers, wetlands, reservoirs (refill yearly) + "savings account" = groundwater, glaciers, aquifers → both drained
  - Stress (reversible) → crisis (short shock: drought, flood) → bankruptcy (permanent)
  - Why: wetlands and floodplains converted + slow overuse ignored (\~70% of major aquifers falling) + dams, cities and industry overbuilt + climate change
  - India: 18% of people, 4% of fresh water + per-capita availability → 1,140 m³ by 2050 + 70% of surface water polluted (NITI)
  - Fix: name bankruptcy in SDG 6 and Rio Conventions + satellite monitoring + basin-level diagnosis + water-thrifty farming and industry
- <span color="green_bg">Urban water governance</span> (Indore contaminated tap water crisis): water = State subject; inter-state rivers = Union (Art 262, ISRWD Act 1956, River Boards Act 1956)
  - Problems: many agencies (Gurugram) + \~38% of water lost as non-revenue water (leaks, theft) + Chennai 2019, Bengaluru 2024 crises + poor sewage treatment (Yamuna) + borewell and tanker dependence
  - BIS drinking-water limits (IS 10500): fluoride 1.5 mg/l, arsenic 0.05 mg/l, nitrate 45 mg/l
  - Best practice: Rajasthan's Mukhyamantri Jal Swavlamban Abhiyan ("four waters") → groundwater up \~4%
  - Way forward: national urban wastewater reuse policy (100% treatment) + Integrated Urban Water Management + merge CWC and CGWB into a National Water Commission (Mihir Shah) + water budgeting + Jan Bhagidari
- Water tech: AI + GIS to site farm ponds and check dams + drones + IoT sensors + drip/sprinkler + IN-GRES (CGWB) + GRACE satellite for groundwater + <span color="green_bg">Ganga digital twin</span> (NMCG)
</toggle>

<toggle>
rivers

<ul>
<li>
RIVERS: CPCB 2025 = 296 polluted stretches on 271 rivers (Maharashtra most) + 1+ toxic metal over limit at 112 of 434 CWC stations (2024)
</li>
<li>
Sources: untreated sewage (>60% enters rivers) + industry (sugar, paper, tanneries) + heavy metals (arsenic, chromium) + solid waste, farm runoff, microplastics
</li>
<li>
Impact: cholera, typhoid + eutrophication, dead zones + toxins in crops + \~3% of GDP lost (World Bank)
</li>
<li>
Law and schemes: Art 21 clean-environment right (MC Mehta 1987) + Water Act 1974 + EPA 1986 + NGT + Namami Gange + National River Conservation Plan + AMRUT
</li>
<li>
Namami Gange (NMCG implements): 127 STPs working (Mar 2025) + CETPs for industry + but NGT (2022): untreated waste still in 60% of the Ganga + only 69% of funds used till 2024–25
</li>
<li>
Why earlier schemes faltered (Ganga Action Plan 1985, GAP-II, NGRBA): only sewage, not whole basin + states didn't run STPs after building them + no e-flow + weak industry checks
</li>
<li>
Way forward: basin-level management with minimum e-flow (EU Water Framework Directive) + stronger, autonomous pollution boards + real-time AI tracking
</li>
<li>
INDUSTRIAL RIVER POLLUTION 

- Industry dumps heavy metals (lead, mercury, chromium) + dyes, phenols + hot water
- Cases: Kali river, UP (Muzaffarnagar–Meerut–Ghaziabad; sugar mills, distilleries, paper mills → black water, no aquatic life) + Noyyal and Bhavani, Tamil Nadu (Tiruppur dyeing units → farmland infertile, groundwater salty and toxic)
- Fix: zero liquid discharge for textile units + CETPs + online effluent monitoring
</li>
</ul>
</toggle>

<toggle>
Schemes & Missions

- National water mission (The National Water Mission (NWM) is funded by the Government of India through the Ministry of Jal Shakti, with additional support from state governments and external agencies when needed. Its key functions include promoting integrated water resource management, improving water use efficiency by 20%, encouraging rainwater harvesting and groundwater recharge, developing basin-level water plans, enhancing water data systems, raising public awareness, and addressing water scarcity and climate change impacts. The Ministry of Jal Shakti leads policy and coordination, supported technically by the Central Water Commission. State Water Departments handle local implementation, while Basin Authorities manage river basins, with local bodies and communities actively participating in water conservation efforts.)
- Jal Jeevan mission (The Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) is funded by the Government of India with budget allocations from the Ministry of Jal Shakti, along with contributions from state governments and local bodies. Its main functions focus on providing potable tap water to every rural household by promoting sustainable water supply systems, enhancing water quality monitoring, encouraging community participation in water management, and ensuring operation and maintenance of water supply infrastructure. The mission also emphasizes capacity building and awareness generation. The Ministry of Jal Shakti leads the policy direction and overall coordination, state governments are responsible for implementation and fund management, local bodies (like Panchayats) manage on-ground execution and community involvement, while technical agencies provide support for planning, monitoring, and capacity building.)
- PMKSY + mission Amrit Sarovar (The mission aims to construct and rejuvenate 75 water bodies in each district across the country, thereby fostering water conservation, ensuring sustainability, and reviving traditional community water bodies through public participation + As on March 2025, over 68,000 Sarovars have been completed, enhancing surface and groundwater availability across various regions. Under Mahatma Gandhi NREGS, over 46,000 Sarovars were constructed/rejuvenated)
- jal sanchay jan bhaghidari (community participation)
- AMRUT 2.0 (Atal mission of rejuvenation and urban transformation) (Making cities “water secure” and providing functional water tap connections to all households, Funding: Outcome based funding to cities who will submit roadmap for outcomes to be achieved by them, will be done via establish circular economy of water + in 500 “AMRUT” cities.
- National Perspective Plan 1980 (NWDA): 30 links = 14 Himalayan + 16 Peninsular
  - For: moves water from surplus to deficit basins → drought and flood relief + more irrigation + hydropower + inland navigation
  - Against: forests and wildlife drowned (Ken–Betwa: Panna Tiger Reserve; \~20,000 people affected) + less silt to deltas → delta sinking and seawater intrusion + costly, slow + states fight over water
  - Ken–Betwa = first link under NPP (MP + UP, Bundelkhand)
</toggle>

<toggle>
Way Forward & Innovations

- one water approach + same emissions trading apply to water + innovative agri practices + teleganas mission kakatiya (Launched in 2014, its primary goal was the restoration of 46,531 minor irrigation tanks to their original capacity. Core Strategy: De-silting tank beds, strengthening bunds, and repairing sluices/channels. It followed a decentralized approach, encouraging farmers to take the silt (rich in nutrients) to their fields. 2026 Evaluation: The program has been highly lauded in the Economic Survey 2026 for its synergy with the Kaleshwaram Project.)and Andhra Pradesh’s Neeru-chettu (Launched in 2015, this is a broader inter-departmental convergence mission (Water + Trees) aimed at making the state drought-proof. Core Strategy: Beyond just tank de-silting, it includes check dams, farm ponds, cascading tank systems, and massive afforestation (aiming for 33% green cover).
- 2026 Status: While the program was a centerpiece of the 2014–2019 administration, it faced scrutiny and legal delays regarding pending payments and contractor bills.
  - Update: As of February 2026, vigilance clearances have settled long-standing disputes, clearing hundreds of engineers of wrongdoing and allowing for the closure of old projects.
  - Impact: Successfully repaired over 1.2 lakh structures and stabilized roughly 3.6 lakh acres. It is particularly noted for its success in the Rayalaseema region, where it helped mitigate extreme groundwater depletion.)
</toggle>

<toggle>
Legislation

- Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974 (amendment : Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) (Manner of Holding Inquiry and Imposition of Penalty) rules, 2024. (The 2024 Amendment Act centralizes key powers like SPCB chairman nomination and industrial exemptions, introduces penalties for government departments’ violations, and empowers adjudicating officers to impose fines credited to the Environment Protection Fund
- National Water Policy 2012 (earlier 1987, 2002): drinking water and sanitation first + then water treated as an economic good + minimum ecological flow for rivers + basin-level planning + Water Regulatory Authority in each state + pricing to save water + national framework law + water-use efficiency
- Draft NWP 2020 (Mihir Shah committee) still not adopted: shift from building dams to demand management + groundwater as common resource
