<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Land Degradation

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: fall in land's biological or economic productivity (UNCCD); in drylands = <span color="green_bg">desertification</span> → India's figures in toggle 3
- <b>Examples</b>: Ralegan Siddhi, Maharashtra (worked: village watershed work revived groundwater and farms) + Punjab–Haryana canal areas (failed: over-irrigation → waterlogging and salinity)

<toggle>
Significance: 1. Global Context & Impact

- Carbon Sink: Soils are the 2nd largest carbon pool (2,500 Gt) after oceans; essential for climate regulation.
- Current Status: \~40% of global land is degraded (UNCCD 2024/25).
- Projection: 95% of land could be degraded by 2050 if current trends continue (Global Environment Facility/UNESCO 2026).
- Human Impact: Directly affects 3.2 billion people; drives migration and food insecurity.
</toggle>

<toggle>
Pillars / key features: 2. International Frameworks

- UNCCD COP16 (Riyadh, 2024): Launched the Riyadh Global Drought Resilience Partnership (\$12B+ fund); focus on "land tenure" rights for local communities.
- <span color="green_bg">Bonn Challenge</span>: Global goal to restore 350 million hectares of degraded landscapes by 2030. (<b>26 million hectares</b> is <b>India's</b> national pledge under the same initiative.)
- UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration (2021–2030): Aiming to prevent, halt, and reverse the degradation of ecosystems worldwide.
</toggle>

<toggle>
India's response + challenges (causes): 3. India’s Commitments & Status

- <span color="green_bg">LDN Target</span>: Restore 26 million hectares of degraded land by 2030 (Target 15.3 of SDGs).
- Progress: <span color="red">India has restored approx. 24.1 million hectares or are under restoration (as per MoEFCC/IUCN reports).</span>
- Planetary Boundaries: According to SOE Report 2026, India has breached the "Land System Change" and "Biosphere Integrity" boundaries.
- Schemes: NAPCC, Desertification & Land Degradation Atlas (by ISRO), Soil Health Card, PM-KSY (Per Drop More Crop), and Green Credit Program.
- India: \~97.85 Mha (\~29.7% of land) degraded (ISRO Desertification & Land Degradation Atlas, 2018–19 data) + Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Jharkhand worst
- Causes: water erosion (biggest) + vegetation loss (deforestation, overgrazing) + wind erosion (Thar) + salinity and waterlogging from over-irrigation (Punjab, Haryana canals) + mining + shifting cultivation
- Effects: lower yields + dust storms + silted reservoirs + rural distress and migration
- Remedies: watershed development (PMKSY-WDC) + afforestation (Green India Mission, <span color="green_bg">Aravalli Green Wall</span>) + Soil Health Card and less fertiliser + agroforestry + grazing control + LDN target of 26 Mha by 2030
</toggle>

<toggle>
Way forward: 4. The "Way Forward" & Local Wisdom

- Forest Landscape Restoration (FLR): Shifting from just "planting trees" to restoring the ecological functionality of the entire landscape.
- Local Techniques:
  - Milpa (Mayan): Sustainable "slash-and-burn" (swidden) agriculture that uses polyculture (maize, beans, squash).
  - Zai Pits (Burkina Faso): Small pits to catch rain and concentrate nutrients.
  - Invasive Species Management: Addressing Lantana camara, which now occupies nearly 50% of India's forest/scrublands (SOE 2026).
</toggle>
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Plastic Pollution

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: 4.12 million tonnes (CPCB’s Annual report) + world: >460 MMT made a year, \~20 MMT leaks into nature (WEF)
- Per capita plastic waste generation doubled over last 5 years
- 3rd globally in single use plastic
- <b>Pillars / key features</b>: Types of plastic :
- TABLE

<toggle>
How to learn this table

- Link the acronym directly to its most common use and a visual image:
- PET: Imagine a pet dog drinking from a plastic water bottle. It's everywhere, so it's Highly recyclable.
- PVC: You probably already know of PVC pipes from plumbing. Pipes are industrial, which can help you remember they often contain toxins and have Low recyclability.
- PP (Polypropylene): Notice the double "P". Associate it with Tupperware. Tupperware goes in the microwave, which helps you remember it is heat resistant.
- PS (Polystyrene): The word itself sounds exactly like Styrofoam. Styrofoam snaps and crumbles easily, helping you remember it is fragile, bulky, and has Very Low recyclability.
</toggle>

- <b>Examples</b>: Sikkim (worked: banned plastic bags in 1998 + bottled water curbs in Lachen) + <span color="green_bg">single-use plastic ban</span>, Jul 2022 (failed: weak enforcement, thin bags back in markets, few cheap alternatives)
- <b>India's response</b>: see Measures below + <span color="green_bg">PWM (Amendment) Rules 2026</span>: producers, importers, brand owners must use more recycled plastic (packaging to IS 14534:2023) + Mandatory Jute Packaging Act 2010 + National Dashboard on SUP

<toggle>
India's response – Measures :

- 1\. India has enforced the <span color="green_bg">Plastic Waste Management</span> Amendment Rules, 2021, banning certain single-use plastics from July 2022, and introduced the <span color="green_bg">Extended Producer Responsibility</span> (EPR) on Plastic Packaging, 2022, which holds producers, importers, and brand owners accountable for the entire lifecycle of plastic products.
- 2\. Further, the Plastic Waste Management (Amendment) Rules, 2024 assign Panchayats the responsibility to assess local plastic waste, while initiatives like Project REPLAN by KVIC focus on reducing plastic pollution,
- 3\. private sector efforts include the India Plastics Pact (IPP) and Un-Plastic Collective (UPC) to promote sustainable plastic use.
- 4\. Plastic Parks have become a key part of India’s strategy to manage plastic waste, promote recycling, and support the chemical industry. Under the New Scheme of Petrochemicals, the government of India offers grant funding of up to 50% of the project cost, with a maximum limit of Rs. 40 crore per project. So far, 10 Plastic Parks have been approved across various states.
</toggle>

- <b>Challenges</b>: weak enforcement of the SUP ban + informal recycling + global plastics treaty talks stalled (INC adjourned without consensus) + bio-based/compostable only 1.5% of plastic + tariffs on plastics cut to 7.2%, alternatives (bamboo) still \~14.4% + microplastics harm health
- <b>Way forward</b>: strict <span color="green_bg">EPR</span> audits + cheap alternatives (<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4221111b-206d-818a-adb1-c7c45802190a/4251111b-206d-80b0-bc00-001c1b1dfac6">REPLAN</span>, compostables) + a global treaty that covers the whole life cycle + sector-based reforms + plastic data systems + synergy with BRS Conventions
</toggle>

<b>Maritime disasters</b>

- Maritime disasters: shipwrecks, fires, collisions, oil spills + new risks (hazardous chemicals, nuclear waste)
- Recent: MSC ELSA 3 sank off Kochi + fire on MV Wan Hai 503 (Kerala coast), 2025
- Problems: cargo not declared honestly + hazardous goods mishandled + tangled ownership (Liberian flag, German owner, Cyprus manager) + insurance disputes
- Rules: IMO conventions (SOLAS 1974, IMDG Code, Ballast Water, Hong Kong ship recycling) + Merchant Shipping Act 1958 + EPA 1986 + National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan (Coast Guard) + Admiralty Act 2017
- Way forward: enforce SOLAS + electronic cargo tracking + satellite detection (RISAT) + <span color="green_bg">polluter pays</span>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Solid Waste

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2018

- <b>2018 Q6 (10 marks):</b> What are the impediments in disposing the huge quantities of discarded solid wastes which are continuously being generated? How do we remove safely the toxic wastes that have been accumulating in our habitable environment?
</toggle>

- Annual waste generation 62 million tons + 43 million tones collection + 12 million tons treated (TERI)
- Causes : inadequate segregation at source + under dev storage infra + low door to door collection + low municipal finance (low creditworthiness) + overlapping jurisdiction
- Initiatives : <span color="green_bg">SWM Rules 2026</span> replaced the 2016 Rules (3-way → 4-stream segregation)
- SWM Rules 2026 (from 1 Apr 2026): 4-stream segregation + bulk generators process wet waste or buy an <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4221111b-206d-81b6-aa1a-d046e64d6682/4251111b-206d-8059-9a9f-001c20abb21a">EBWGR certificate</span> + r<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4221111b-206d-81b6-aa1a-d046e64d6682/4251111b-206d-80c7-b075-001c9f59c762">efuse-derived fuel to cement plants</span> + yearly landfill audits + tourist user fee in hills and islands + polluter-pays compensation
- Scale: 165 Mt by 2030, 436 Mt by 2050 + only 15–20% processed
- Also: C&D Waste Rules 2025 + Contaminated Sites Rules 2025 (189 substances) + DRAP for about 8.8 cr t legacy waste + models: Indore, Anupam Colony (Delhi), SWaCH (Pune)
- Schemes : SBA Urban 2.0 + garbage free star rating protocol to access it
- Mumbai and <span color="green_bg">Bhopal</span> used at scale waste processors and Bhopal use GPS for Door to door collection + CSIR-CMERI made advanced facility with advanced sequestration facilities + Bengaluru MC recommended cess on waste
- Indore best example
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 E-Waste

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2018, 2013

- <b>2018 Q6 (10 marks):</b> What are the impediments in disposing the huge quantities of discarded solid wastes which are continuously being generated? How do we remove safely the toxic wastes that have been accumulating in our habitable environment?
- <b>2013 Q20 (10 marks):</b> Enumerate the National Water Policy of India. Taking river Ganges as an example, discuss the strategies which may be adopted for river water pollution control and management. What are the legal provisions of management and handling of hazardous wastes in India?
</toggle>

- 3rd largest after usa and china + 2.76 MMT (2020) → 6.19 MMT (2024) → 14 MMT by 2030 + <span color="green_bg">formal recycling</span> only 10% (world \~22%, USA 56%) + ₹51,000 cr of materials lost (Paryavaran NITI Manthan)
- Challenges Necessitating Action : precious metals are present in e waste (bio leaching: Bio-leaching is an advanced, eco-friendly form of <span color="green_bg">bioremediation</span> (specifically, biomining). It is the process of using specific, naturally occurring microorganisms (bacteria or fungi) to extract valuable metals from solid waste.) + very toxic (Lead (Pb), Mercury (Hg), and Cadmium will leach into groundwater + non biodegradable
- 85 % is produced by unorganised sector
- 80% e waste by developed countries is sent to developing counties
- India legislations and rules :
  - E waste (management and handling) rules, 2011 (introduced concept of extended producer responsibility (producer cleans what he produces)
  - E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2016: Introduced the concept of <span color="green_bg">Producer Responsibility Organization</span> (A Producer Responsibility Organisation (PRO) is a professional entity hired by companies (producers, brand owners, and importers) to help them meet their legal obligations under <span color="green_bg">Extended Producer Responsibility</span> (EPR).)
  - E waste management rules (2022) (It introduced a centralized digital portal by the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) and created a market for EPR Certificates. Producers must now buy these certificates from registered recyclers to prove they have met their targets, completely digitizing and formalizing the sector. It also expanded the list of regulated items from 21 to 106.)
  - Battery Waste Management Rules 2022 + National Critical Mineral Mission (recycling Li-ion batteries, e-waste)
- Basel Convention (1989): Controls the transboundary movement of hazardous wastes. It prevents developed nations from dumping their toxic waste (like old electronics) into developing nations. Includes e-waste
- Stockholm Convention (2001): Aims to eliminate Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs)—the "Dirty Dozen" chemicals (like DDT) that bioaccumulate in the food chain and take decades to break down
- Issues: fake recyclers distort the EPR market + EPR covers only gold, copper, iron, aluminium + low skills and awareness
- Way forward: GST-linked verification + EPR for more metals and critical minerals + hydrometallurgy, AI-based recovery + train and certify informal workers
- <b>Examples</b>: Moradabad, UP (failed: brass city turned <span color="green_bg">informal e-waste</span> hub → circuit boards stripped with acid on the Ramganga banks → CSE 2015: river mercury 8x the Indian standard) + Kerala, Jul 2025 (worked: Haritha Karma Sena buys e-waste door to door at fixed rates → Clean Kerala Company → scientific disposal)
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 HAZARDOUS and BIOMEDICAL WASTE

Hazardous waste: toxic, flammable, reactive or corrosive

- Rule: Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management & Transboundary Movement) Rules 2016 (under EPA) → SPCB authorisation for generators + categories with SOPs + duties for TSDF operators
- Problems: few Treatment, Storage and Disposal Facilities (TSDFs) + people oppose new ones + informal recyclers without safety gear + illegal imports

Biomedical waste: \~609 t/day (+101 t/day extra in COVID)

- Rule: Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules 2016 (amended 2018, 2019) → colour-coded bins + common treatment facilities (CBWTFs) + incineration, autoclave, microwave + secured landfill
- Problems: poor segregation + few CBWTFs in rural areas + small clinics hard to monitor
- Way forward: more TSDFs and CBWTFs + formalise informal recyclers + cleaner production
- <b>Examples</b>: Union Carbide site, <span color="green_bg">Bhopal</span> (failed: 337 t of toxic waste burnt at Pithampur only in 2025, 40 years later) + IMAGE, Palakkad, Kerala (worked: doctors' association runs one <span color="green_bg">common biomedical waste treatment facility</span> for the state's private hospitals)
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 MERCURY EMISSIONS

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2014

- <b>2014 Q15 (12.5 marks):</b> Environmental Impact Assessment studies are increasingly undertaken before a project is cleared by the Government. Discuss the environmental impacts of coal-fired thermal plants located at coal pitheads.
</toggle>

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: A naturally occurring heavy metal that exists as elemental (Hg⁰), inorganic (Hg²⁺) and organic (methylmercury, MeHg) forms. Methylmercury is the most toxic form that bioaccumulates in food chains.
- <b>Pillars / key features</b>: <span color="green_bg">Minamata Convention</span> on Mercury (2013): treaty to curb mercury supply, reduce emissions, control products/processes, and support ASGM alternatives & remediation. Minamata Convention on Mercury
- <b>Significance</b>: Why it matters (toxicity & persistence) : Neurotoxic, especially harmful to foetuses and young children (developmental delays, cognitive deficits), Bioaccumulates & biomagnifies in aquatic food webs → top predators and fish become human exposure pathways, Persists in environment; deposited far from sources (long-range atmospheric transport).
- Main sources
  - Natural: volcanic emissions, weathering of rocks, geothermal activity.
  - Anthropogenic (major): artisanal & small-scale gold mining (ASGM), coal-fired power plants (coal combustion), cement production, metal smelting/refining, waste incineration, some chemical factories and chlor-alkali operations (legacy plants), and improper disposal of mercury-containing products (thermometers, lamps, batteries).
- <b>Examples</b>: Minamata disease (industrial methylmercury poisoning) → <span color="green_bg">Minamata</span>, Japan (1956: methylmercury from the Chisso factory → Minamata disease) + Kodaikanal, Tamil Nadu (2001, failed: HUL thermometer factory dumped mercury waste → workers sick, clean-up disputed for years)
- <b>India's response</b>: ratified Minamata Convention (2018) + mercury limit for coal power plants (2015 norms) + mercury thermometers phased out of hospitals
- <b>Challenges</b>: coal plants slow on pollution controls (FGD; Category C \~78% exempted, Jul 2025) + old contaminated sites (Kodaikanal)
- <b>Way forward</b>: emission controls and <span color="green_bg">mercury monitoring</span> at coal plants + clean up legacy sites + mercury-free products
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
⚪ Waste to Wealth

- Can use anaerobic fermentation to produce biogas (methane and Co2) + incineration, gasification, pyrolysis for production of heat and light +
- Plastic schemes up above and 500 new Gobardhan (waste to wealth plants)
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Circular Economy

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Current 7.2 % of global economy is circular with declining trend (down from 9.1% in 2018)(circularity gap report 2023) + India: \~₹4,000 cr earned from scrap in Swachhata drives + could be a \$2 tn market with 1 crore jobs by 2050
- <b>Significance</b>: Need :, Resource circularity could save 11% of GDP and 30% by 2050 (eco survey 24-25) + from 1970 to 2015 20x increase in annual material consumption + resource dependency on imports
  - Impact : less kharcha more incomes + reduced resource dependence + promotes green and clean production + ensures reusability + carbon neutral production + calls for resource efficiency
- <b>Examples</b>: Indore (worked: 6-way segregation + Asia's largest Bio-CNG plant on wet waste, 2022 → <span color="green_bg">waste to wealth</span>) + Alang, Gujarat (mixed: recycles ships at scale but worker safety and beach pollution; Hong Kong Convention in force 2025)
- <b>India's response</b>: Initiatives : mission Life + SBA + National resource efficiency policy + EPR rules (e-waste, battery, 2022) + Steel Scrap Recycling Policy + NITI Circular Economy Cell + <span color="green_bg">Jaipur Declaration</span> (3R forum, 2025)
- <b>Challenges</b>: need systematic overview + less incentive to do it + profit hungry corporations are concerned with profit only + downcycling (practice of recycling into lower value and qualitiy than orignal + informal sector recovers only 10–20% of materials (formal \~95%) + fake EPR certificates + EPR mostly iron and copper, not lithium or cobalt
- <b>Way forward</b>: <span color="green_bg">EPR</span> across sectors (plastic, e-waste, batteries, tyres, metals) + recycled-content mandates + design for reuse + battery recycling in the carbon market + a recycling wing in the Critical Mineral Mission + South Korea-style penalties
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Natural Farming

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: chemical-free farming with on-farm inputs (Zero Budget Natural Farming idea) + Organic farming is off farm purchase and natural is no need for outside purchases
- <b>Pillars / key features</b>: Beejamrit (cow dung, urine) + Jivaamrit (bio-stimulant for microorganisms activity) + Mulching + Whapasa (using earthworms) + Plant protection (using biological
- <b>Significance</b>: lower input cost + soil health + less fertiliser subsidy
- <b>Examples</b>: Andhra Pradesh <span color="green_bg">APCNF</span> (2016 on, worked: largest natural-farming programme, lakhs of farmers, lower input costs) + Sri Lanka 2021 (failed: overnight ban on chemical fertiliser → yields crashed → reversed)
- <b>India's response</b>: <span color="green_bg">National Mission on Natural Farming</span> (2024, ₹2,481 cr, 1 crore farmers) + BPKP under PKVY
- <b>Challenges</b>: yields may dip in the first years + needs cattle for inputs + few markets paying more
- <b>Way forward</b>: phased shift, not overnight (Sri Lanka lesson) + market links and certification + ICAR trials on yields
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Agroforestry

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: 8.5 % of total land under agro forestry (4x increase in demand for timber from plywood industry alone ) + \~8% of land (EAC-PM paper)
  - 93%
- <b>Pillars / key features</b>: Silvo-pastoral (Trees + livstock) + siloarable (trees + crops) +
- <b>Significance</b>: extra farm income + timber from <span color="green_bg">trees outside forests</span> + carbon sink + gives \~half of fuelwood and 60% of paper-pulp wood + crop yields up \~50% + stores 14–27 t CO₂ per ha a year (EAC-PM)
- <b>Examples</b>: Poplar on farm bunds, Punjab–Haryana (worked: feeds the plywood industry + farm income) + Melia dubia farming, Karnataka–Tamil Nadu (worked: fast timber for plywood) → but felling and transit permits still hold farmers back
- <b>India's response</b>: <span color="green_bg">National Agroforestry Policy</span> 2014 (India first in the world) + Trees Outside Forests in India programme (2023) + model felling and transit rules for states + <span color="green_bg">SMAF</span> (under NMSA) + NITI's GROW initiative + bamboo = grass, not tree (2017)
- <b>Challenges</b>: felling and transit permits + long wait for returns + timber price swings + 82% of transit-pass (NTPS) applications from just 3 states + too much eucalyptus
- <b>Way forward</b>: adopt the model felling rules in every state + buy-back and price support + good planting material
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h1">
4\. RENEWABLE ENERGY

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Energy Transition

- Frame: non-fossil = <span color="green_bg">50% of installed capacity</span>, reached June 2025 (2030 NDC target, 5 years early) + 250 GW RE, 3rd in the world + but under 30% of generation (<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4221111b-206d-8060-b189-e4aa6622b074/4251111b-206d-8109-9ea4-001c66c3e18f">capacity ≠ generation) +</span> <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4221111b-206d-8060-b189-e4aa6622b074/4251111b-206d-8123-ba4b-001c43355a3d">WEF Energy Transition Index 2024: 71 of 118</span>

<toggle>
50% by 2030?

- Capacity: 50% non-fossil reached June 2025, 5 years early → next 60% by 2035
- Generation by using RE is still under 30% + coal still ≈55% of energy needs
- Verdict: the capacity target is met; 50% of energy needs only with storage, grid and green hydrogen
</toggle>

<b>Benefits</b>

- Health: cleaner air (capability approach by amartya sen)(removes a major unfreedom )
- Environment: cuts CO₂, the road to net zero 2070
- Economy: oil and coal import cut + 1.3 million RE jobs (7.7% of world), 2nd in solar PV jobs after China (IRENA 2025)
- Governance: energy security (West Asia crisis)
- Society: energy access<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81b8-8386-c2ad401904a2/4251111b-206d-8149-893e-001cc96903be">: decentralised RE empowers communities (Barefoot Women Solar Engineers</span>)
  <toggle>
  Energy access + UJALA

  - <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81cf-bbe0-f238ab4ddf97/4251111b-206d-8123-a6d3-001cba730a20">SDG 7</span>: affordable, reliable, sustainable, modern energy for all
  - UJALA (2015): 36.87 crore LED bulbs distributed, saving ₹19,153 crore a year (PIB 2025) (new)
  - LEDs use 90% less power than old bulbs, 50% less than <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81db-96d3-cfa6e29cebc9/4251111b-206d-81db-af4b-001c192f7eb3">CFLs</span> → ≈48 billion units saved a year, ≈9,500 MW peak demand avoided (new, PIB)
  </toggle>

<b>Barriers</b>

- <b>P</b>: fossil fuels still get ≈5x the subsidy of clean energy (IISD, FY24)
  <toggle>
  Subsidy shift

  <ul>
  <li>
  Fossil support fell to 5x clean energy in FY24, the smallest gap in 5 years; clean subsidies up 31% to ≈₹32,000 crore (IISD 2025) (new)
  </li>
  <li>
  But 83% of new PSU investment still goes to fossil assets (IISD) 
  </li>
  <li>
  How the shift helps: frees money for storage and grid + makes RE cheaper than coal + steady signal to investors
  </li>
  <li>
  Use fossil tax revenue to fund clean energy (IISD) (new)
  </li>
  </ul>
  </toggle>
- <b>I</b>: storage costly (≈₹5–6 per unit) + lag in latest solar cells
- <b>N</b>: RE cant provide energy 24x7 as solar during day time and wind during blowing winds <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81de-a4d8-d5f0b9b9f5f8/4251111b-206d-81f0-b4e0-001c052f8014">(no BESS)</span> + spread thin: solar needs 300x the land of nuclear
- <b>C</b>: farmers and herders lose land and grazing commons (orans) without consent → protests + coal workers face job loss (150+ districts live off coal and thermal power)
- <b>H</b>: ≈80% of solar modules from China + power lines in the Thar kill Great Indian Bustards
  <toggle>
  GIB conflict

  - Thar and Kutch: power lines kill Great Indian Bustards (under 150 left)
  - SC 2021 ordered lines underground, eased 2024
  </toggle>
- <b>F</b>: \$6.5 trillion needed by 2070 for net zero <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-813b-9a0d-ee9fb98e8c79/4251111b-206d-81e7-b35d-001cf0d23d1d">+ DISCOM deb</span><span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-813b-9a0d-ee9fb98e8c79/4251111b-206d-817d-b7ae-001c5d253167">t + stranded coal assets</span>
- <b>C</b>: weak transmission, states slow on intra-state lines
  <toggle>
  Green Energy Corridor

  <ul>
  <li>
  Lines that carry solar and wind power from RE-rich states into the grid + <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81fb-b42b-f1ef51205ef8/4251111b-206d-81fe-b12f-001c609d635d">Renewable Energy Management Centres</span>; work began 2015 (new, Ministry of Power)
  </li>
  <li>
  Phase I: inter-state part done (Mar 2020); intra-state part in 8 states delayed by right-of-way and GIB court cases 
  </li>
  <li>
  Phase II: 7 states, ≈10,750 km of lines, ≈₹12,000 crore, 33% central aid + Ladakh 13 GW line (2024) 
  </li>
  <li>
  Next: Phases 3 and 4 to cover the whole country (new, DTE)
  </li>
  </ul>
  </toggle>

<b>Fixes</b>

- <b>P</b>: shift subsidies from fossil to clea<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8198-9853-c4a0e6d168c6/4251111b-206d-8179-ac7d-001ce4fe9579">n + Green Energy Open Access Rules 2022</span>
- <b>I</b>: storage (<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8102-a02c-c0b2c9f69349/4251111b-206d-8159-9f27-001c0848b128">ACC battery PLI</span>, pumped storage) + smart grids + new sources: geothermal (first policy 2025, 381 hot springs), <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8102-a02c-c0b2c9f69349/4251111b-206d-8102-963d-001ce9c00e81">CO₂-to-methanol (</span>NTPC Vindhyachal), <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8102-a02c-c0b2c9f69349/4251111b-206d-8199-84e7-001c45718715">coal gasification</span> (100 MT by 2030)
- <b>N</b>: wind-solar hybrids + one cross-border grid <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81b1-9037-c05945088102/4251111b-206d-81e2-a65b-001c34c66e7e">(OSOWOG</span>)
- <b>C</b>: decentralised RE: rooftops (PM Surya Ghar) + farms (PM-KUSUM) (will cause habitual energy storage of solar energy)
- <b>H</b>: domestic manufacturing <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8156-b4be-f26eb85d5959/4251111b-206d-81e9-abdf-001c98728216">(PLI) + a</span> just transition for coal regions
  <toggle>
  PMKKKY

  - <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-817f-a9e0-d00ad928cfbb/4251111b-206d-8196-bde8-001c121fb1b4">Mining companies pay</span> 10% or 30% of royalty into District Mineral Foundations; ≥70% to health, water, education, women and child welfare
  - Mixed: Keonjhar, Odisha (huge fund, spent on roads and buildings) · Worked: Dantewada (education, livelihoods)
  - Problems: large unspent balances + Collector-run trusts, little Gram Sabha say
  - Fix: real Gram Sabha role + social audits (revised guidelines 2024)
  </toggle>
- <b>F</b>: <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81e5-afbe-d9fd03dd1615/4251111b-206d-8124-9008-001c931b65ca">JETP +</span> green bonds + blended finance
- <b>C</b>: independent national body for coal phase-out + Green Energy Corridor Phases 3 and 4
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Solar

- Frame: 150 GW (Mar 2026), 3rd in the world (Rajasthan, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu top) + potential ≈3,343 GW, rooftop alone 750 GW + ≈300 sunny days a year
- Benefits: no fuel to import + no emissions + sits on rooftops and farms + fastest to build
- Examples: Bhadla, Rajasthan (≈2.2 GW on desert land) + Modhera, Gujarat (first 24x7 solar village, 2022)

<b>Barriers</b>

- <b>I</b>: lag in latest cells (<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4221111b-206d-81a9-a435-f1bd2b836b94/4251111b-206d-81c4-91f5-001c9bfe542e">PERC, bifacial</span>, thin-film)
- <b>N</b>: no power after sunset → storage needed
- <b>C</b>: households slow to put up rooftop panels (PM Surya Ghar target: 1 crore homes; upfront ₹40,000–70,000 per kW)
- <b>H</b>: ≈80% of modules from China (≈35 million imported in FY25) + mining for solar minerals scars land (Economic Survey 2023–24)
- <b>F</b>: weak DISCOM finances

<b>Fixes</b>

- <b>P</b>: protect domestic makers
  <toggle>
  ALMM + PLI

  - <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-816a-af1c-d3cab91cd43c/4251111b-206d-81d8-9c61-001c83bc8185">ALMM:</span> only approved (mostly domestic) modules for government projects
  - PLI for solar PV + <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81e9-b3ce-ef9856d71268/4251111b-206d-8109-ac08-001cfca557f9">National Solar Mission, 2010</span> <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81e9-b3ce-ef9856d71268/4251111b-206d-81dc-9e51-001cccba899c">+ Solar Park Scheme</span>
  </toggle>
- <b>I</b>: move to PERC and bifacial cells
- <b>N</b>: one cross-border grid so the sun is always shining somewhere
  <toggle>
  GGI–OSOWOG

  - Launched by India + UK at COP2<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8101-924e-ff57293aea66/4251111b-206d-8123-8ef4-001c6b399f83">6 (2 Nov 2021), run by ISA</span> with the World Bank → round-the-clock clean power, less storage needed
  - First floated by the PM at ISA's First Assembly, Oct 2018
  - Phases: India linked to Middle East, South Asia, South-East Asia → African power pools → global grid
  - Backed by 80+ ISA members (One Sun Declaration)
  </toggle>
- <b>C</b>: solar for homes and farms
  <toggle>
  PM Surya Ghar

  - Rooftop solar + 300 free units a month
  - 1 crore families save ≈₹15,000 crore a year
  </toggle>

  <toggle>
  PM-KUSUM

  - Solar pumps for farmers + grid-connected solar on barren land
  </toggle>
- <b>F</b>: reverse auctions keep tariffs low → now cheaper than coal
  <toggle>
  Solar cost fall

  - Why: Chinese mass production + better cells + <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-810e-a21c-c302bfd1202b/4251111b-206d-818d-9552-001c72280c20">reverse auctions</span> + solar parks with ready land and lines (new)
  - For thermal plants: run fewer hours, old units become stranded assets, coal shifts to backup role (new)
  </toggle>
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Wind

- Frame: ≈56 GW (2026; 21 GW in 2014), 4th in the world + offshore potential ≈36 GW off Gujarat and Tamil Nadu
- Benefits: 70–80% of components made in India → less import dependence than solar
- Example: Muppandal, Tamil Nadu (India's largest wind cluster)

<b>Barriers</b>

- <b>P</b>: <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8107-9122-feadae34d520/4251111b-206d-803f-8fff-001c7c6e0efd">big minimum project size</span>
- <b>N</b>: offshore turbines are noisy for marine life
- <b>H</b>: land acquisition delays + power lines kill Great Indian Bustards (Thar, Kutch)
- <b>F</b>: offshore costly (salt corrosion)
- <b>C</b>: states slow on intra-state transmission lines

<b>Fixes</b>

- <b>P</b>: <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-813a-85e2-d541449e9708/4251111b-206d-8151-912b-001c8448a22d">Green Open Access Rules 2022</span>
- <b>I</b>: <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81db-bf8a-d48a10182d90/4251111b-206d-81dc-a7c3-001cb10d1434">repower old low-height turbines</span>
- <b>N</b>: wind-solar hybrids (<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-819c-9820-c7f307fc24d4/4251111b-206d-812a-9d54-001c20529fb0">Hybrid Policy 2018)</span>
- <b>F</b>: <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8165-9116-f74ec4565e85/4251111b-206d-81ef-9662-001c8bb86ebf">viability gap funding f</span>or offshore
  <toggle>
  Offshore wind

  - <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-817f-8d4a-f2f6b47fcdf7/4251111b-206d-8143-8d39-001ce69347e0">National Offshore Wind Energy Policy 2015</span> + offshore VGF
  - ≈36 GW potential off Gujarat and Tamil Nadu
  - India–UK offshore wind taskforce
  </toggle>
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Hydro

- Frame: hydro gives flexible power that balances solar and wind; pumped storage works as a giant battery

<toggle>
Run-of-river

- <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-818f-9e2e-fd8c6526e02b/4251111b-206d-81b5-adfa-001c2efa71da">Uses the river's natural flow with little</span> or no reservoir: water diverted through a tunnel to turbines, then returned downstream (new)
- vs storage dam: a big reservoir stores water and generates on demand; run-of-river output rises and falls with river flow (new)
- Pros: less submergence and displacement · Cons: dry stretch between intake and outlet + weak in the lean season (new)
</toggle>

- Barriers: <b>N</b> fragile Himalaya (Chamoli 2021 hit the Tapovan project; Sikkim 2023 broke the Chungthang dam) + <b>C</b> displacement and local protests
- Fixes: minimum e-flow + careful siting + pumped storage for RE
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Nuclear

- Frame: 8.18 GW (Jan 2025) → 22.48 GW by 2031–32 → <span color="green_bg">100 GW by 2047</span> (<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4221111b-206d-819e-89c9-fa3e830ecba2/4251111b-206d-81b2-8182-001cf2a34442">Nuclear Energy Mission,</span> Budget 2025–26)
- Benefits: large thorium reserves + low pollution + little land + 24x7 power
- Examples: Kudankulam (largest plant, <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4221111b-206d-8153-960c-de8bf570a8b2/4251111b-206d-813c-bcdd-001c7910db03">Russian VVERs) ·</span> Jaitapur (planned since 2010, stuck on liability, cost, protests)
- Three-stage programme
  <toggle>
  3-stage + FBR

  - Stage 1: <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81ad-8bba-dc1ab79bce85/4251111b-206d-819b-b76c-001caed89da0">heavy-water reactors</span> on natural uranium → plutonium · Stage 2: fast breeders burn plutonium <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81ad-8bba-dc1ab79bce85/4251111b-206d-8194-bb05-001c59592632">(MOX)</span> and breed more fuel than they use · Stage 3: thorium
  - <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81fd-af25-c2e243f47a9b/4251111b-206d-811d-8195-001cb410e925">PFBR, Kalpakkam</span> (500 MWe, <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81fd-af25-c2e243f47a9b/4251111b-206d-815e-8eae-001cce2f0cb1">BHAVINI</span>): first criticality 6 Apr 2026 → India enters stage 2 (new, PIB)
  - Advantage: unlocks India's thorium + fuel security
  - But: ≈16 years late, cost more than doubled (new)
  </toggle>
- Facts vs fears
  <toggle>
  Facts vs fears

  - Facts: 24x7 low-carbon power + little land + thorium future
  - Fears: accidents (Fukushima 2011) + long-lived waste + liability + delays and cost (PFBR) + local protests (Jaitapur, Kudankulam)
  </toggle>
- Fusion
  <toggle>
  ITER

  - ITER, France: 7 members (EU, US, Russia, China, Japan, Korea, India); India's share ≈9%, given in kind (new)
  - India built the 3,850-tonne <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-818b-8570-d1a1d9367eae/4251111b-206d-81f2-84c6-001c6a90ba83">cryostat</span> (its largest of 14 packages) + in-wall shielding, cooling water and cryogenic systems, diagnostics (new, ITER)
  - Domestic base: <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81b9-997f-da6c0a6c97a7/4251111b-206d-81ea-8b81-001c51952b5f">Aditya tokamak</span> at the Institute for Plasma Research
  - If it works: near-limitless fuel from seawater, no long-lived waste, no meltdown risk, but commercial power is decades away
  </toggle>

<b>Barriers</b>

<ul>
<li>
<b>P</b>: liability law (<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8126-8b52-fdf481922d8f/4251111b-206d-816f-887b-001c159a0548">CLNDA 2010)</span> kept suppliers away now shanti act introduced 
</li>
<li>
<b>N</b>: uranium shortfall + extraction needs sulphuric acid
</li>
<li>
<b>C</b>: locals not consulted → protests (Kudankulam)
</li>
<li>
<b>F</b>: high cost, long delays (PFBR ≈16 years late)
</li>
</ul>

<b>Fixes</b>

- <b>P</b>: <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8127-86ef-d0f4ad7c62db/4251111b-206d-8159-affe-001c778c616a">SHANTI Act</span> + amendments to Atomic Energy Act 1962 and CLNDA 2010 for private participation
- <b>I</b>: <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81cd-9ae5-ddfad45241b7/4251111b-206d-8141-8cef-001ccafcd470">Bharat Small Reactors +</span> at least 5 SMRs by 2033
- <b>H</b>: put reactors on retiring coal-plant sites
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Hydrogen

- Frame: India uses ≈6.5 million t of hydrogen a year, mostly grey
- Benefits: clean<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4221111b-206d-814f-ba1d-eb3179042a8b/4251111b-206d-812a-bb52-001cc0ce20a5">s hard-to-abate sectors (steel</span>, cement, fertiliser, refineries) + energy security + 3x the energy of petrol per kg
- Examples: Leh green-hydrogen buses (NTPC, 2023) + NTPC Kawas, Gujarat (hydrogen blended into piped gas, 2023)

<toggle>
Hydrogen colours

- Grey: from natural gas, CO₂ released
- Blue: from gas, CO₂ captured (CCUS); bridge fuel, cheaper now
- <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-812c-aa96-d700da56e5ef/4251111b-206d-8141-b268-001c5673748e">Green: electrolysis</span> of water with RE, zero carbon
- Pink: electrolysis with nuclear power, 24x7 (BARC research)
</toggle>

<b>Barriers</b>

- <b>I</b>: storage and safety (flammable)
- <b>N</b>: up to 9 litres of water per kg
- <b>H</b>: most hydrogen still grey
- <b>F</b>: \$4–7 per kg, still costly

<b>Fixes</b>

- <b>P</b>: demand mandates for fertiliser and refineries
  <toggle>
  NGHM

  <ul>
  <li>
  National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023): 5 million t of green hydrogen a year by 2030 + 1 lakh crore cut in fossil fuel imports  + 50 MMT of GHG averted + 125 GW capacity will be added 
  </li>
  <li>
  <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8186-ba95-db05bc773b02/4251111b-206d-81d5-b53b-001cd0b48ee4">SIGHT incentives</span> + hydrogen hubs + certification scheme
  </li>
  <li>
  Pilots: GAIL blending in CNG and PNG (Indore) + first hydrogen train coach (ICF) + Kandla port plant + Varanasi fuel-cell boat
  </li>
  </ul>
  </toggle>
- <b>H</b>: cheaper electrolysers (PLI)
- <b>C</b>: green hydrogen hubs
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Bioenergy

- Frame: bioenergy ≈11.6 GW (Nov 2025) + waste-to-energy ≈0.85 GW + modern bioenergy = 13% of final energy use
- Benefits: farm waste becomes energy + less stubble burning + farmer income (Annadata to Urjadata) + forex saved

<toggle>
Biofuel generations

- 1st: edible crops (sugarcane, wheat, corn) → food vs fuel
- 2nd: non-edible parts (straw, grass, wood)
- 3rd: algae · 4th: waste to fuel (pyrolysis)
</toggle>

<b>Barriers</b>

- <b>P</b>: ethanol policy leans on cane and grain (1st gen) → food vs fuel
- <b>I</b>: 2G plants run well below capacity (<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-814e-96bc-f6661322543f/4251111b-206d-812e-8a03-001c25014e15">Panipat 2G refinery</span>)
- <b>N</b>: cane is water-heavy → more blending = more cane = more water + biomass has competing uses (fodder, manure)
- <b>C</b>: mixed wet waste burns poorly → waste-to-energy plants underrun + emissions near homes (Okhla, NGT fine 2017)
- <b>H</b>: weak straw supply chain + no organised biomass market (<i>fragmented human coordination</i>—individual smallholders lack the labour, baling capacity, and market intermediaries to aggregate paddy straw.)
- <b>F</b>: low private investment

<b>Fixes</b>

- <b>P</b>: blending mandates
  <toggle>
  E20 / EBP

  - <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81ab-a4cd-db69fcd35289/4251111b-206d-8133-a2bc-001c724bb2f4">EBP (2003) → E20 met in 2025, 5 years early;</span> E20 mandatory with <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81ab-a4cd-db69fcd35289/4251111b-206d-8140-b38f-001cab65af7d">RON 95</span> from 1 Apr 2026
  - ₹1.84 lakh crore forex saved + ₹1.58 lakh crore to farmers + maize share 0% → 42%
  - Cane / maize ethanol cut GHG 65% / 50% vs petrol (NITI)
  - National Policy on Biofuels 2018 (rev. 2022): E20 by 2025 + 2G ethanol, biodiesel, bio-CNG + non-food feedstock
  - Support: Ethanol Interest Subvention + GST 18% → 5%
  - Concerns: food diverted + water-heavy cane + 3–7% lower mileage in older vehicles
  </toggle>
- <b>I</b>: 2G ethanol (<span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-811b-b9d9-ffdf6c53b183/4251111b-206d-8119-a504-001c868baf46">PM JI-VAN)</span> + online emission monitoring at waste-to-energy plants
- <b>C</b>: villages run their own biogas from dung and farm waste (GOBARdhan) + segregation at source so waste-to-energy plants get only dry waste (SWM Rules 2026) + biomethanation for wet waste
  <toggle>
  SATAT + GOBARdhan

  - Lehragaga, Sangrur, Punjab: India's largest <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81de-a555-c281c4b2dc81/4251111b-206d-813e-af94-001c7e525a28">compressed biogas plant</span> on paddy straw <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81de-a555-c281c4b2dc81/4251111b-206d-81a7-8c32-001cd3c80ace">(SATAT, 2022)</span>
  - Indore <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-81c4-b327-f411b4c44102/4251111b-206d-81fe-83f5-001ce7497ac8">GOBARdhan:</span> wet waste → Bio-CNG for city buses (2022)
  - <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8135-95ab-dd2cd8731d51/4251111b-206d-81d1-8ba4-001cb416e16a">National Bioenergy Programme</span> (2022, ₹1,715 crore)
  </toggle>
- <b><span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8166-aa9f-f106a56d23c1/4251111b-206d-80a9-a519-001c295fc7c9">H</span></b>: <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8166-aa9f-f106a56d23c1/4251111b-206d-811a-aa63-001c35512ff9">FPO-run biomass depots</span> + national biomass repository + GIS maps of biomass + plants near the feedstock
- <b>F</b>: viability gap funding
  <toggle>
  Biotech role

  - Enzymes break straw into 2G ethanol + algae for 3rd-gen fuel + microbes for biogas and bio-CNG (new)
  - Turns waste into fuel → less oil import, the path to energy independence by 2047 (new)
  </toggle>
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 EVs

- Frame: EV share 7.6% (2024) → 30% by 2030 (NITI) + <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4221111b-206d-8170-a5bd-cc8d2231a5f0/4251111b-206d-811d-be99-001c2586dab9">India Electric Mobility Index:</span> Delhi 1st
- Benefits: ≈3x less CO₂ even on today's grid + ≈60% energy efficiency vs ≈20% for petrol + 30% EVs by 2030 saves ≈₹1.1 lakh crore of oil imports a year

<b>Barriers</b>

- <b>P</b><span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4221111b-206d-817d-87c4-cc5fd9ac0d8a/4251111b-206d-81b7-b980-001cf2955125">: inverted GST</span> (18% on inputs, 5% on EVs)
- <b>N</b>: battery minerals (lithium, cobalt) imported
- <b>F</b>: e-buses and e-trucks cost 2–3x + public charging ≈4x the cost of home charging

<b>Fixes</b>

- <b>P</b>: battery recycling under EPR (2022 rules) + National Critical Mineral Mission for lithium
- <b>I</b>: EVs as grid batteries
  <toggle>
  V2G

  - <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8192-9a6c-c04235321ccd/4251111b-206d-81c9-b36e-001c64818919">Vehicle-to-grid</span>: EVs send power back to the grid → owner earns, battery lasts longer, helps meet peak demand
  </toggle>
- <b>F</b>: subsidies for EVs and charging
  <toggle>
  PM E-DRIVE

  - 2024, <span discussion-urls="discussion://4221111b-206d-80b0-a97f-e118421fe6d8/4251111b-206d-8114-8bcd-c7eb6c438fe6/4251111b-206d-81d5-88f8-001c48299f02">replaced FAME-II:</span> subsidies for EVs and charging
  - PM e-Bus Sewa (38,000+ buses) + 5% GST on EVs
  </toggle>
</toggle>

<toggle>
OLD way

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Benefits of Renewable Energy (RE):

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2025, 2022, 2018, 2016

- <b>2025 Q6 (10 marks):</b> How can India achieve energy independence through clean technology by 2047? How can biotechnology play a crucial role in this endeavour?
- <b>2022 Q12 (15 marks):</b> Do you think India will meet 50 percent of its energy needs from renewable energy by 2030 ? Justify your answer. How will the shift of subsidies from fossil fuels to renewables help achieve the above objective ? Explain.
- <b>2018 Q1 (10 marks):</b> “Access to affordable, reliable, sustainable and modern energy is the sine qua non to achieve Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)”.Comment on the progress made in India in this regard.
- <b>2016 Q11 (12.5 marks):</b> Give an account of the current status and the targets to be achieved pertaining to renewable energy sources in the country. Discuss in brief the importance of National Programme on Light Emitting Diodes (LEDs).
</toggle>

- <span color="green_bg">Import reduction</span>
- Renewable
- Fossil fuel reserves not exploited (unemployment)
- Climate change mission
- RE jobs: 1.3 million (7.7% of world), 2nd in solar PV and hydro jobs after China (IRENA 2025) + energy security (West Asia crisis) + decentralised RE empowers communities (Barefoot Women Solar Engineers)
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Challenges of RE:

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2022, 2013

- <b>2022 Q12 (15 marks):</b> Do you think India will meet 50 percent of its energy needs from renewable energy by 2030 ? Justify your answer. How will the shift of subsidies from fossil fuels to renewables help achieve the above objective ? Explain.
- <b>2013 Q11 (10 marks):</b> Write a note on India’s green energy corridor to alleviate the problem of conventional energy.
</toggle>

- Fossil fuel will face losses
- High initial cost
- Adaptation and <span color="green_bg">grid integration</span>
- Availability, import, storage, environmental factor
- Figures: <span color="green_bg">\$6.5 tn</span> needed by 2070 for net zero + \~35 mn solar modules imported in FY25 (\$1.6 bn, mostly China) + storage \~₹5–6 per unit + solar needs 300x the land of nuclear + stranded coal assets + energy demand share to double by 2035
- Way forward: JETP, green bonds + storage (ACC batteries, pumped storage) + domestic manufacturing (PLI) + smart grids + an independent national transition body for coal phase-out
</toggle>

- Non-fossil share of installed capacity: 50% reached June 2025 (2030 NDC target, 5 years early) + record 55.3 GW added in FY 2025–26 + 250.52 GW RE, 3rd largest (IRENA 2026) + next: 60% by 2035 + but under 30% of generation (capacity ≠ generation)

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Solar Energy

- <b>Examples</b>: Bhadla Solar Park, Rajasthan (worked: among the world's largest, \~2.2 GW on desert land) + Modhera, Gujarat (2022, worked: India's first <span color="green_bg">24x7 solar village</span>) → conflict: power lines in Thar kill Great Indian Bustards (see Wind)

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2021, 2020, 2015

- <b>2021 Q6 (10 marks):</b> Explain the purpose of the Green Grid Initiative launched at World Leaders Summit of the COP26 UN Climate Change Conference in Glasgow in November, 2021. When was this idea first floated in the International Solar Alliance (ISA) ?
- <b>2020 Q16 (15 marks):</b> Describe the benefits of deriving electric energy from sunlight in contrast to the conventional energy generation. What are the initiatives offered by our Government for this purpose?
- <b>2015 Q9 (12.5 marks):</b> To what factors can be the recent dramatic fall in equipment cost and tariff of solar energy be attributed? What implications does the trend have for thermal power producers and related industry?
</toggle>

- Installed capacity: 150.26 GW (31 Mar 2026), rank 3rd in world; 45 GW added in 2025–26 (Rajasthan, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu top)
- <span color="green_bg">PM Surya Ghar</span>: Muft Bijli Yojana (PMSGMBY):
  - Objective: Install rooftop solar and provide 300 units electricity per month
  - Potential in India: about 3,343 GWp (NISE); rooftop alone 750 GW
  - Factors behind growth: Under PMSGMBY, 1 crore families are expected to save Rs 15,000 crore annually through reduced electricity bills
  - Abundant solar radiation: \~300 sunny days/year, 4–7 kWh/m²/day
  - Indigenous manufacturing of solar components: Through initiatives like Solar Park Scheme
- <span color="green_bg">ALMM</span> (Approved List of Models and Manufacturers): This is a crucial "Defensive" measure. It ensures that only government-approved, high-quality (mostly domestic) modules are used in government projects, protecting Indian manufacturers from cheap imports.
- <span color="green_bg">PM-KUSUM</span>: "Solarizing" the farm sector (Solar pumps + grid-connected solar on barren land).
- Challenges:
  - Environmental concerns: Extraction of minerals needed for solar leaves large scars, requires substantial water, releases \~15 tonnes CO₂ per tonne of mineral (Economic Survey 2023-24)
  - India lags in adoption of latest solar cell technologies:
    - PERC (Passivated Emitter Rear Contact) – improved version, reduces heat loss
    - Bifacial panels – use both sides to generate power
    - Thin-film technologies – lighter and flexible
- More challenges and measures: about 80% of modules from China + DISCOM finances → PLI for solar PV + National Solar Mission 2010
- <b>Green Grids Initiative (GGI–OSOWOG)</b>
  <ul>
  <li>
  GGI–OSOWOG: launched by India + UK at COP26 World Leaders' Summit (2 Nov 2021), run by ISA with the World Bank → one cross-border solar grid so the sun is always shining somewhere = round-the-clock clean power, less  storage needed
  </li>
  <li>
  First floated: PM at ISA's First Assembly, October 2018 
  </li>
  <li>
  Phases: India linked to Middle East + South Asia + South-East Asia → African power pools → global grid
  </li>
  <li>
  Backed by 80+ ISA members (One Sun Declaration)
  </li>
  </ul>
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Wind Energy

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Installed capacity: 54 GW (now 56 GW, 2026; 21 GW in 2014; 2nd after solar) + Offshore wind potential: 36/35 GW off coast of Gujarat and Tamil Nadu + Rank: 4
- <b>Significance</b>: India is a global hub for wind turbine manufacturing. We now have a domestic value chain for about 70–80% of wind components, making us less dependent on imports compared to the solar sector.
- <b>Examples</b>: Muppandal, Tamil Nadu (worked: India's largest <span color="green_bg">wind cluster</span>) + Thar and Kutch (failed: power lines kill Great Indian Bustards → SC 2021 ordered lines underground, eased 2024)
- <b>India's response</b>: Policy: National Offshore Wind Energy Policy, 2015 + National Wind-Solar Hybrid Policy 2018 + offshore <span color="green_bg">VGF</span> + India–UK offshore wind taskforce + Green Energy Open Access Rules 2022
- <b>Challenges</b>: Challenge : Land Acquisitio, Great Indian Bustard (GIB): + weak transmission + big minimum project size + offshore: high cost, salt corrosion, noise for marine life
- <b>Way forward</b>: <span color="green_bg">repowering</span> old low-height turbines + offshore wind with viability gap funding + wind-solar hybrids
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Run-of-river Hydro

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2013

- <b>2013 Q17b (5 marks):</b> What do you understand by Run-of-river hydroelectricity project? How is it different from any other hydroelectricity project?
</toggle>
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Biomass

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Installed capacity: 10.74 GW
  - Status: 11.6 GW bioenergy (Nov 2025) + modern bioenergy = 13% of final energy use
- <b>Pillars / key features</b>: NBP (MNRE, 2022; ₹1,715 cr; Phase 1 2021–22 to 2025–26): surplus farm biomass → power + rural income → 3 parts: waste-to-energy (biogas, bio-CNG, syngas) + biomass (briquettes, pellets, cogeneration) + biogas (clean cooking) + 20% more aid for NE, hill states, SC/ST
  - Revised guidelines: 50% aid after SPCB consent, rest at 80% capacity + no clearances for pellet plants + NCR pellet makers can pick MNRE or CPCB scheme (stubble burning)
- <b>Significance</b>: farm waste → energy + cuts <span color="green_bg">stubble burning</span> + rural income
- <b>Examples</b>: Lehragaga, Sangrur, Punjab (2022, worked: India's largest <span color="green_bg">compressed biogas</span> plant runs on paddy straw under SATAT) + Punjab stubble still burnt each autumn (failed: straw collection chain weak, few buyers)
- <b>India's response</b>: Links: SATAT + GOBARdhan + PM JI-VAN (2G ethanol) + biofuel policy (your Biofuels block)
- <b>Challenges</b>: Problems: biomass has competing uses + weak supply chain + no biomass exchange + private money shy
- <b>Way forward</b>: national biomass repository + GIS maps + FPO-run depots + viability gap funding + plants near the feedstock
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Waste-to-Energy

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Installed capacity: 0.85 GW
  - Global standing: 4th in installed RE capacity (IRENA RE Stats 2025)
- <b>Significance</b>: less landfill + energy from waste
- <b>Examples</b>: Okhla WTE plant, Delhi (failed: residents' complaints over emissions → NGT fine, 2017) + Indore GOBARdhan Bio-CNG (2022, worked: wet waste → fuel for city buses)
- <b>India's response</b>: <span color="green_bg">SATAT</span> + GOBARdhan + waste-to-energy under SBM-Urban 2.0 + <span color="green_bg">SWM Rules 2026</span> (only non-recyclable dry waste to WTE)
- <b>Challenges</b>: mixed, wet waste burns poorly → plants underrun + emissions near homes + Main challenges: Rare earth concentration in China, solar land requirement, batteries as carbon emitters
- <b>Way forward</b>: <span color="green_bg">segregation at source</span> + online emission monitoring + biomethanation for wet waste
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
⚪ WEF Energy Transition Index 2024

- Rank: 71 out of 118 countries
- Need: High import dependence, international obligations, sustainable development
- Challenges: Adaptation expensive, high upfront costs (residential rooftop solar: ₹40,000–₹70,000 per kW; 5 kW system = ₹2–3.5 lakh), worker displacement, unemployment if fossil fuel sector shut down
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Pradhan Mantri Khanij Kshetra Kalyan Yojana (PMKKKY)

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Basic idea : Mining damages local areas. So the government created PMKKKY to use money from mining companies to improve the lives of people living near mines.
- <b>Pillars / key features</b>: Funds:
  - Mining companies contribute 10% or 30% of royalty to DMFs
  - ≥70% funds for high-priority sectors (health, water, education, women/child welfare)
  - ≤30% funds for other sectors
  - 70% spending in directly affected areas
  - Endowment fund (≤10% receipts) for post-mining livelihoods
  - All transfers via DBT
- Function:
  - Implement welfare & development in mining-affected areas
  - Mitigate environmental/health/socio-economic impacts
  - Maintain affected area/person list
  - Prepare baseline survey, 5-year perspective & annual plans
  - Converge with state/central schemes & SDGs
  - PMUs for collections >₹50 crore; yearly audit & grievance redressal
- Functionaries:
  - DMF (non-profit trust under MMDR Act) set up by State Govt
  - Chaired by District Magistrate/Collector
  - <span color="green_bg">Gram Sabha</span> identifies beneficiaries
  - State Govt defines affected area radius & manages endowment investments
  - Executing agencies implement projects via DBT
- <b>Significance</b>: mining money goes back to the people who bear its harm (<span color="green_bg">benefit-sharing</span>)
- <b>Examples</b>: Keonjhar, Odisha (mixed: one of the biggest <span color="green_bg">DMF</span> funds, but spending skewed to roads and buildings over health and nutrition: CSE) + Dantewada, Chhattisgarh (worked: DMF money for education and livelihoods in mining-hit villages)
- <b>India's response</b>: revised PMKKKY guidelines, 2024 (high-priority share raised to 70%)
- <b>Challenges</b>: large unspent balances + Collector-run trusts, little Gram Sabha say + spending on buildings over health
- <b>Way forward</b>: real Gram Sabha role + <span color="green_bg">social audits</span> + spend on health, nutrition and livelihoods
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Nuclear Energy Mission (Budget 2025-26)

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2025, 2018, 2017

- <b>2025 Q5 (10 marks):</b> The fusion energy programme in India has steadily evolved over the past few decades. Mention India’s contributions to the international fusion energy project – International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER). What will be the implications of the success of this project for the future of global energy?
- <b>2018 Q16 (15 marks):</b> With growing energy needs should India keep on expanding its nuclear energy programme? Discuss the facts and fears associated with nuclear energy.
- <b>2017 Q16 (15 marks):</b> Give an account of the growth and development of nuclear science and technology in India. What is the advantage of fast breeder reactor programme in India?
</toggle>

- Target & Roadmap:
  - 100 GW capacity by 2047
  - Current capacity: 8.18 GW (Jan 2025)
  - Plans: 22.48 GW by 2031-32, including ≥5 Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) by 2033
- Private & Indigenous Push:
  - Proposed amendments to Atomic Energy Act, 1962 and Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, 2010 for private sector participation
  - SHANTI ACT
  - Development of <span color="green_bg">Bharat Small Reactors</span> (BSRs) and SMRs using indigenous technology
  - Repurposing retiring coal plants
- Key Relevance & Challenge:
  - Large thorium reserves, low pollution, minimal land use, continuous power supply
  - Uranium extraction depends on sulphuric acid; projected shortfall 100–320 million tonnes by 2040
- <b>Examples</b>: Kudankulam, Tamil Nadu (worked: India's largest nuclear plant, Russian VVERs) + Jaitapur, Maharashtra (failed: planned since 2010, stuck on <span color="green_bg">nuclear liability</span> law, cost and local protests)
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Hydrogen

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Current production: 6.5 million metric tonnes/year
  - Energy density: 3× gasoline
- <b>Pillars / key features</b> (types): Green hydrogen : Green Hydrogen is produced by electrolysis of water using renewable energy, making it a zero-carbon fuel. It is considered a strategic component of India’s clean energy transition to achieve <span color="green_bg">net-zero</span> targets, decarbonize hard-to-abate sectors (steel, cement, ammonia), and enhance energy security.
- Blue hydrogen : Blue Hydrogen: The "Bridge" Fuel
- What it is: Like the highly polluting "Grey Hydrogen," Blue Hydrogen is extracted from natural gas using a process called Steam Methane Reforming (SMR). However, the crucial difference is that the carbon dioxide emitted during the process is captured and stored underground using Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS)technology. Why it's on the rise: It is currently much cheaper to produce than Green Hydrogen and allows countries to utilize existing natural gas infrastructure while still lowering emissions. 🇮🇳 India’s Initiatives
  - CCUS Policy Framework: NITI Aayog has released a comprehensive CCUS policy framework. Without CCUS, Blue Hydrogen cannot exist.
  - PSU Action: State-owned giants like ONGC and Indian Oil Corporation (IOCL) are actively investing in CCUS technologies to retrofit their existing refineries, effectively preparing to transition their captive grey hydrogen production into blue hydrogen.
- Pink (or Red) Hydrogen: The Nuclear Option
- What it is: Pink hydrogen is produced through the exact same process as Green Hydrogen (electrolysis of water), but the electricity comes from nuclear power plants instead of solar or wind. Why it's on the rise: Nuclear power provides 24/7, uninterrupted baseload electricity. Solar and wind are intermittent (the sun sets, the wind stops), which makes running electrolysers inefficient. Pink hydrogen solves this intermittency problem.
- India’s Initiatives:
  - BARC R&D: The Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) is actively researching High-Temperature Steam Electrolysis (HTSE).
  - Future Integration: With India planning to massively scale up its nuclear capacity (including Small Modular Reactors - SMRs), the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) is exploring the co-location of hydrogen production facilities with future nuclear plants to produce clean Pink Hydrogen at scale.
- <b>Examples</b>: Leh, Ladakh (2023, worked: NTPC's green-hydrogen buses at high altitude) + NTPC Kawas, Gujarat (2023: green hydrogen blended into piped natural gas) → under the <span color="green_bg">National Green Hydrogen Mission</span>
- <b>India's response</b>: Initiatives: GAIL 2% H₂ blending in CNG, NTPC H₂ fuel cell, green hydrogen certification scheme + NGHM (2023): 5 MMT green H₂ a year by 2030 (Phase I to 2025–26, Phase II to 2029–30; <span color="green_bg">SIGHT</span> incentives + hubs + certification) + first hydrogen train coach tested (ICF) + Kandla port H₂ plant + Varanasi fuel-cell boat + GAIL 5% H₂ in PNG (Indore)
- <b>Challenges</b>: Requires up to 9 litres water per kg + Cost: \$4.10–\$7 per kg (still high) + most H₂ still grey (from gas) + storage and safety (flammable)
- <b>Way forward</b>: cheaper electrolysers (PLI) + <span color="green_bg">green hydrogen hubs</span> + demand mandates for fertiliser and refineries
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Biofuels

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2025

- <b>2025 Q6 (10 marks):</b> How can India achieve energy independence through clean technology by 2047? How can biotechnology play a crucial role in this endeavour?
</toggle>

- Generations:
  - 1st gen: edible part of plants (sugarcane, wheat, corn)
  - 2nd gen: non-edible part (tree trunk, grass, straw)
  - 3rd gen: microalgae/macroalgae
  - 4th gen: waste-to-fuel (pyrolysis)
- Investment: \$100–270 billion to meet current policy measures
- Concerns: food security (1st gen), low energy density
- Biggest example: ethanol
- <span color="green_bg">National Policy on Biofuels</span> (2018, revised 2022): o Targets 20% ethanol blending by 2025. o Promotes 2G ethanol, biodiesel, and bio-CNG production. o Focus on non-food feedstocks to avoid food security issues
- <span color="green_bg">Ethanol Blended Petrol</span> (EBP) Programme (1st April 2026 : made E20 mandatory and a Research octane number of 95 (The Research Octane Number (RON) measures a fuel's ability to withstand high compression without prematurely getting burnt or "knocking" inside an engine. A higher RON enables greater engine efficiency and lower emissions, which is exactly why high-RON biofuels like ethanol are blended into standard petrol.)
  - EBP (2003) → E20 met in 2025, 5 years early + ₹1.84 lakh cr forex saved since ESY 2014–15 + ₹1.58 lakh cr to farmers (<span color="green_bg">Annadata to Urjadata</span>) + maize share 0% (2021–22) → 42% (2025) + cane / maize ethanol cut GHG 65% / 50% vs petrol (NITI) + E85 at some OMC outlets, E100 rules approved
  - Measures: PM JI-VAN (2G) + Ethanol Interest Subvention + GST 18% → 5% (2018) + IDR Act amended 2016 → Concerns: food diverted + water-heavy cane + mileage drop + feedstock and storage gaps
  - Vehicles built from 2023–2025 are designed for E20, while older vehicles may experience 3-7% lower mileage.
- <b>Examples</b>: E20 reached in 2025 (worked: 5 years early, saved foreign exchange + paid cane farmers) + Panipat <span color="green_bg">2G ethanol</span> refinery, IOCL (2022, failed so far: ran well below capacity, straw supply chain weak)
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
⚪ Methanol

- Made from methane, natural gas, coal
- World’s first CO₂-to-methanol plant: NTPC Vindhyachal
- NITI Aayog Methanol Economy Programme: convert coal reserves & municipal solid waste
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
⚪ Geothermal Energy

- Potential: 10,600 MW
- Existing: \~300 MW in India
- Promising sites: Puga & Chamathang, Eastern Ladakh
- <span color="green_bg">National Policy on Geothermal Energy</span> (2025, MNRE, first ever): 381 hot springs, 10 geothermal provinces (GSI) + only a 20 kW pilot (Manuguru, Telangana), no big plant yet (Mains 365; check the \~300 MW line above) + clean 24/7 baseload + issues: drilling cost, little data + research support up to 100% (RE-RTD)
</toggle>

- Target: 100 MT by 2030
- Draft UCG guidelines (mining and closure plans for UCG blocks) + National Coal Gasification Mission + incentive scheme → coal → <span color="green_bg">syngas</span> for power, methanol, fertiliser + issues: high cost, foreign tech suits low-ash coal (India's is high-ash) → fluidised-bed gasifiers + CCUS + VGF
</toggle>
