<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Earthquakes

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2021, 2015

- <b>2021 Q8 (10 marks):</b> Discuss about the vulnerability of India to earthquake related hazards. Give examples including the salient features of major disasters caused by earthquakes in different parts of India during the last three decades.
- <b>2015 Q16 (12.5 marks):</b> The frequency of earthquakes appears to have increased in the Indian subcontinent. However, India’s preparedness for mitigating their impact has significant gaps. Discuss various aspects.
</toggle>

- <b>Extent</b>: 59% of India is prone to earthquakes + India recorded 159 earthquakes from November 2024 to February 2025
  - Why India is vulnerable: Indian plate pushing into Eurasia (Himalaya, NE) + 59% of land in moderate–very high zones + dense cities on soft soil
  - Zones: IS 1893:2016 → Zones II–V (59%) + BIS 2025 code added Zone VI (whole Himalayan arc, 61%) → withdrawn Mar 2026 after MoHUA flagged 10–15% cost rise + little consultation → 2016 code back in force

<image source="notion-file-block://4221111b-206d-80e8-b2a8-cb0c066178c3/8a025843-59de-43a3-8016-1c5a8ec231d8?space_id=3939cd2d-3e25-404f-9196-d463e4c2e65e&name=Figure_4_Indian_Seismic_Zone_Map_as_per.png" />

- <b>Causes</b>: Reasons : Earthquakes: plate boundary movement (subduction/collision/transform), intraplate stress, fault rupture/lock–release, volcanic activity, reservoir-induced seismicity (dams/mining), hydraulic fracturing, isostatic rebound.
- <b>Effects</b>: building collapse → most deaths (buildings kill, not the shaking) + <span color="green_bg">liquefaction</span>, landslides, tsunamis, dam damage + lifelines (roads, power, hospitals) cut + economic loss
- <b>Examples</b>: Last 3 decades: Latur 1993 (\~10,000 dead, stable Deccan plate) + Jabalpur 1997 + Chamoli 1999 + Bhuj 2001 (M7.7, \~20,000 dead) + Kashmir 2005 (M7.6) + Sikkim 2011 (M6.9) + Nepal 2015 (M7.8, Bihar hit) + Imphal 2016 (M6.7) + Eg. Mayanmar earthquake (cause strike slip faulting)
- <b>NDMA guideline / scheme</b>: India focuses on pre-disaster mitigation, preparedness, and vulnerability reduction for earthquakes, as they cannot be prevented or precisely predicted. Key national institutions include the National Centre for Seismology (earthquake monitoring, hazard reports, “India Quake” app), the National Earthquake Risk Mitigation Project (structural and non-structural vulnerability reduction), and the National Building Code (regulates safe construction). NDMA’s six pillars of earthquake management include: earthquake-resistant new construction, selective retrofitting of priority structures, regulation and enforcement of building codes, awareness and preparedness campaigns, capacity development through training and R&D, and emergency response via Incident Command Systems and Emergency Operations Centres.
  - Seismic observatories increased from 80 in 2014 to 168 by February 2025. Pib
  - The BhooKamp app was launched for real-time earthquake updates Pib (complements the existing "India Quake" app mention — now two apps).
  - NDMA's Earthquake Risk Indexing (EDRI) project assesses earthquake risks in 50 cities, with plans to cover 16 more. Press Information Bureau
  - <span color="green_bg">NDRF</span> has now expanded to 16 Battalions, each with 1,149 personnel
- <b>Gaps → way forward</b>: Gaps: building codes (IS 1893, NBC) not enforced + most houses non-engineered + slow retrofitting of schools, hospitals + earthquake <span color="green_bg">early warning</span> only a pilot (Uttarakhand) + weak urban planning + low awareness → enforce codes + retrofit schools and hospitals + early warning beyond the pilot + drills and awareness
- <b>Related: Pacific Ring of Fire</b>: Ring of Fire: \~40,000 km horseshoe round the Pacific → \~75% of active volcanoes + \~90% of earthquakes + Why: subduction zones (Pacific under Australian plate, Taupo) + transform faults (San Andreas) + ridges (East Pacific Rise) + hotspots + News: M8.8 Kamchatka quake (shallow reverse faulting) → tsunami in Russia, Japan
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Tsunamis

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2017

- <b>2017 Q18 (15 marks):</b> On December 2004, tsumani brought havoc on 14 countries including India. Discuss the factors responsible for occurrence of Tsunami and its effects on life and economy. In the light of guidelines of NDMA (2010) describe the mechanisms for preparedness to reduce the risk during such events.
</toggle>

- <b>Extent</b>: Though tsunamis are rare in the Indian Ocean, 13 were recorded in the last 300 years, with 3 in the Andaman and Nicobar region. The Indian Ocean Tsunami of 26th December 2004 remains one of the most destructive to have hit India
- <b>Causes</b>: Tsunamis: undersea megathrust/submarine earthquakes, submarine landslides, volcanic flank collapse/eruption (caldera collapse), asteroid/meteor impact, coastal subsidence.
- <b>Effects</b>: 2004 → \~2.3 lakh dead in 14 countries, India \~10,700 (Nagapattinam, A&N worst) + boats, harbours and fishing livelihoods lost + coastal farmland salinised + tourism hit
- <b>Examples</b>: 26 Dec 2004: M9.1 Sumatra–Andaman megathrust (Indian plate under Burma plate) + mangroves (Pichavaram) reduced damage
- <b>NDMA guideline (Tsunami Guidelines, Aug 2010)</b>: Since tsunamis cannot be prevented or precisely predicted, India focuses on pre-disaster mitigation, preparedness, and vulnerability reduction. NDMA’s six pillars for tsunami management include: risk assessment and hazard mapping, preparedness through monitoring networks and awareness, structural mitigation using natural and built barriers, regulation and enforcement of safe construction, coordinated emergency response, and implementation via capacity building and drills. The Indian Tsunami <span color="green_bg">Early Warning</span> System (ITEWS), developed by the Department of Space, DST, and CSIR (run by INCOIS, Hyderabad, under MoES since 2007), can detect Indian Ocean earthquakes in under 10 minutes and issue timely advisories using advanced communication and decision support systems. These measures aim to protect lives, infrastructure, and coastal communities.
- <b>Way forward</b>: mangrove and shelterbelt <span color="green_bg">bio-shields</span> + CRZ no-development zones + regular coastal drills + last-mile alerts (<span color="green_bg">SACHET</span>)
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Floods

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2024, 2016

- <b>2024 Q18 (15 marks):</b> Flooding in urban areas is an emerging climate-induced disaster. Discuss the causes of this disaster. Mention the features of two such major floods in the last two decades in India. Describe the policies and frameworks in India that aim at tackling such floods.
- <b>2016 Q15:</b> The frequency of urban floods due to high intensity rainfall is increasing over the years. Discussing the reasons for urban floods, highlight the mechanisms for preparedness to reduce the risk during such events.
</toggle>

- <b>Extent</b>: Around 12% (40 million hectares) of India's land is prone to floods. The country receives an annual rainfall of 1200 mm, with 85% concentrated in just 3-4 months (June to September)
  - Urban floods in India have become a pressing issue, disrupting city life and causing economic losses. The World Bank estimates urban flood damage could reach \$1 trillion annually by 2050 globally, with India highly vulnerable due to its urban density.
- <b>Causes</b>: Floods: extreme/ prolonged rainfall, river overflow/ice-jam release, rapid snowmelt, <span color="green_bg">storm surge</span>/ cyclone, dam/embankment breach, urbanisation/poor drainage, deforestation and siltation.
  - Urban, common cause: encroached drains and wetlands + concrete stops infiltration + no city flood plan
- <b>Effects</b>: deaths, homes and crops lost + water-borne disease + roads, power and transport cut + big urban economic losses
- <b>Examples</b>: Mumbai, 26 July 2005: \~944 mm in 24 hours (Santacruz) + Mithi river encroached + old drains built for 25 mm/hour → \~1,000 dead + Chennai, Dec 2015: extreme rain + sudden release from Chembarambakkam lake + lakes and Adyar floodplain built over → \~340+ dead in Tamil Nadu
- <b>NDMA guideline / scheme</b>: India’s flood management combines structural and non-structural measures. Structural measures include reservoirs, dams, water storage, drainage improvement, river channel desilting, and catchment area treatment to control floods and runoff. Non-structural measures focus on flood plain zoning, comprehensive flood management plans, integrated water resources management, afforestation, and community preparedness. Programs like the Aapada Mitra Scheme train volunteers for immediate relief and rescue during floods. Together, these measures aim to reduce flood impact, protect lives, and safeguard infrastructure.
  - Policy: NDMA Urban Flood Guidelines 2010 + AMRUT stormwater drains + sponge-city ideas
- <b>Way forward</b>: Urban resilience: urban people 480 mn (2020) → 951 mn (2050) + storm-water flood risk 3.6–7x by 2070 (World Bank) + 52% of towns have no master plan + city own revenue about 1% of GDP → tools: Climate Smart Cities Assessment Framework + C-FLOOD (flood forecasting) + MHEW-DSS → way forward: devolve urban planning to ULBs (74th Amendment) + about USD 2.4 tn resilient infrastructure by 2050 + transit-oriented development
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Landslides

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2021, 2019

- <b>2021 Q18 (15 marks):</b> Describe the various causes and the effects of landslides. Mention the important components of the National Landslide Risk Management Strategy.
- <b>2019 Q18 (15 marks):</b> Disaster preparedness is the first step in any disaster management process. Explain how hazard zonation mapping will help disaster mitigation in the case of landslides.
</toggle>

- <b>Extent</b>: Approximately 12.6-15% of India’s landmass (0.42 million sq. km) is prone to landslides, covering the Himalayas, Western Ghats, Northeastern hill ranges, Nilgiris, Eastern Ghats, and Vindhyans.
- <b>Causes</b>: intense rainfall/soil saturation, earthquake shaking, slope undercutting (rivers/roads), removal of vegetation/deforestation, weak geology/clinopyrite or clay layers, mining/blasting, rapid snow/ice melt.
  - In western ghats : reasons : Basalt rocks + High gradient + Deforestation and mining.
- <b>Effects</b>: deaths and buried homes + roads, power lines and hydel projects cut off + debris dams rivers → flash floods downstream + farmland and topsoil lost + tourism and local economy hit
- <b>Examples</b>: Recent instances : Sikkim (unplanned construction and hydel projects) + Uttarkashi landslide (heavy rain) + Wayanad + Aizawl (Mizoram (unscientific earth cutting )) → two to name: Wayanad, 30 July 2024 (Mundakkai–Chooralmala; extreme rain on steep, weathered slopes; 200+ dead) + Malin, Pune, July 2014 (village buried; hill slopes levelled for farming; \~150 dead)
- <b>NDMA guideline / scheme</b>: NDMA’s landslide management focuses on prevention, preparedness, and area-specific solutions. Key measures include hazard zone identification, slope stabilization (no construction if slope 30 degrees and above), and <span color="green_bg">early warning</span> systems, along with detailed hazard mapping. Construction, road building, and large settlements are restricted in high-risk areas, and agriculture is limited to valleys or moderate slopes. Guidelines also cover excavation codes, landslide insurance, and compensation mechanisms to protect communities and infrastructure. + National landslide susceptible mapping + bhusanket web portal.
  - <span color="green_bg">National Landslide Risk Management Strategy</span> (NDMA, Sept 2019): hazard mapping (GSI's National Landslide Susceptibility Mapping) + monitoring and early warning + awareness + capacity building and training + regulations and policies (mountain zone rules) + stabilisation and mitigation (Landslide Risk Mitigation Scheme, 2019)
  - Landslide <span color="green_bg">hazard zonation</span> mapping : LHZ: divide hill terrain into zones by how likely landslides are → inputs: slope + geology + soil + drainage + land use + rainfall + past landslides (inventory) → made with GIS, satellite images, field checks + Scales: macro 1:50,000 (GSI national map) → meso 1:10,000 (town planning) → site level (projects) + Use: where not to build + road and dam alignment + building codes + where to put early warning sensors
- <b>Way forward</b>: Afforestation, bunds, retaining walls, and terrace farming (especially in NE hill states) are promoted to reduce vulnerability.
- <b>Related</b>: An avalanche is the rapid descent of a mass of snow, ice, rock, or debris down a mountain slope, triggered by natural or human-induced factors (causes Continuous snowfall increases snowpack weight, Rising temperatures cause freeze-thaw cycles, wetter snow, and glacier melt, Deforestation) (sol : Structural Measures: Snow Barriers and Fences, Avalanche Control Piles and Terraces, Deflecting Structures and Tunnels, Controlled explosions trigger small avalanches to prevent larger ones,The India Meteorological Department (IMD) and Snow and Avalanche Study Establishment (SASE) use satellite-based monitoring, Zoning and Land-Use Planning: Mapping high-risk areas (e.g., Red, Blue, Yellow Zones
  - Land subsidence: ground sinks as soil or rock below is compressed → groundwater pumping + mining + urbanisation + crustal movement → Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Bengaluru, Chennai sinking (\~80 mn people; Delhi worst, 51 mm a year, >2,000 buildings at risk) + Joshimath, Mussoorie (unregulated building) → fix: artificial aquifer recharge + InSAR satellite monitoring
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Sturzstrom (Hyper-Mobility Rock-Ice Avalanche)

- Definition: A massive, high-velocity mass movement where a large volume of bedrock/slope suddenly collapses and travels over an exceptionally long horizontal runout distance.
- Mechanism: Initial rock-ice slope failure → rapid acceleration and fragmentation → frictional heat melts ice/firn, generating basal water lubrication → resistance drops drastically, transforming the avalanche into a catastrophic debris flow/flash flood within minutes.
- Key Drivers: Permafrost degradation, freeze-thaw cycles, steep structural joints, and climate-induced warming in high-mountain cryosphere zones.
- Examples:
  - Chamoli Disaster, Uttarakhand (2021): Bedrock failure beneath a hanging glacier released ≈25 million m3of rock and ice.
  - Bhotekoshi–Trishuli Flood, Nepal (Langtang Lirung / Border Region): Rock-ice avalanche and <span color="green_bg">permafrost</span> collapse that devastated Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading districts.
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Cloudburst

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2022, 2016

- <b>2022 Q8 (10 marks):</b> Explain the mechanism and occurrence of cloudburst in the context of the Indian subcontinent. Discuss two recent examples.
- <b>2016 Q16 (12.5 marks):</b> With reference to National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) guidelines, discuss the measures to be adopted to mitigate the impact of recent incidents of cloudbursts in many places of Uttarakhand.
</toggle>

- <b>Definition</b>: Specifically, it is classified when rainfall of about 10 cm or above per hour is recorded over an area roughly 20-30 sq km.
- <b>Causes / mechanism</b>: Cloudburst: intense convective convection over short duration, orographic uplift of moist air, stalled mesoscale convective systems, tropical cyclonic moisture influx, climate change-driven extreme events.
  - Mechanism : Cloudbursts occur mainly in mountainous regions like the Himalayas, where orographic lift forces warm, moist air upward. This forms dense cumulonimbus clouds that trap continuous moisture in tall, vertical columns. The cloud cannot release the water gradually because of its structure and constant inflow, so it eventually bursts, releasing an intense, localized downpour. This sudden release often causes flash floods and severe damage, as seen in the 2013 Uttarakhand floods. The process is driven by temperature and pressure differences, windward-leeward dynamics, and thermodynamic principles.
- <b>Effects</b>: flash floods + landslides and debris flows + roads, bridges and hydel projects washed away + pilgrims and tourists trapped
- <b>Examples</b>: eg. In July 2021, Uttarakhand, a northern Indian state, experienced severe cloudbursts across multiple districts, including Chamoli, Uttarkashi, and Pithoragarh. These cloudbursts triggered flash floods + Recent: Mandi, Himachal (June–July 2025, many cloudbursts in one night) + Chasoti, Kishtwar, J&K (Aug 2025, pilgrims on the Machail yatra route, \~65 dead)
- <b>NDMA measures</b>: Safe Settlement: Advise people to settle on hard rock or firm ground, Infiltration Control: Implement measures to control water infiltration, Vigilance and Reporting, Regulating Construction, Develop effective rainwater drainage systems, both surface and sub-surface, and use bioengineering techniques with local vegetation to reduce soil erosion and instability
- <b>Way forward</b>: Way Forward: Cloudburst Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) Strategy – National Disaster Management Plan (2019) • Landslide Hazard Zonation (LHZ): Using remote sensing and different kinds of spatial data (aerial photographs, satellite imagery) along with local knowledge for accurate mapping of landslide-prone area,\\ Inter-agency Coordination: Coordination between central and state agencies for updating rules, adopting new, standards, amending laws, and reviewing policies, Ensure effective <span color="green_bg">early warning</span> dissemination down to the last mile.
  - Structural Measures: o Slope stabilization through bioengineering (plantation, vegetation), and protective structures. o Maintenance and improvement of stormwater drainage, rivulets, and natural water systems to reduce flooding risks.
  - Non-Structural Measures: o Expansion of multi-hazard insurance for life and property. o Integration of risk-sensitive urban planning: amending building by-laws to reduce vulnerability. o Application of multi-level safety planning in expanding and high-risk settlements, Capacity Development: Strengthen ULBs/PRIs to prepare and respond effectively and encourage use of insurance and risk transfer tools, Climate Change Risk Management: Support and promote state-specific and local adaptation efforts.
- <b>Related: monsoon extremes</b>: Changing monsoon: winds weaker but air holds more moisture → short, intense bursts + long dry spells + El Niño–monsoon link weakening + wet areas drier, dry areas wetter (Ganga states less rain; Saurashtra, Rajasthan more)
  - News: Punjab floods + Uttarakhand, HP, J&K landslides and flash floods
  - Impact: disasters + heat and dengue + harder forecasting + monsoon feeds 51% of farm area, 40% of farm output, 47% of livelihoods
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Lightning

- <b>Extent</b>: In March–April 2025, lightning killed over 160 people across 12 states—a 184% increase over the previous year. Bihar and Uttar Pradesh were worst affected, with most deaths concentrated in rural areas.
- <b>Causes</b>: pre-monsoon heat + moisture → tall cumulonimbus clouds → more lightning as the climate warms
- <b>Effects</b>: deaths mostly of farmers and labourers in open fields + livestock lost + power and telecom damage
- <b>Scheme</b>: Indians initiative : India has developed a lightning <span color="green_bg">early warning</span> system, providing forecasts from five days to three hours in advance, Public Awareness Campaigns e.g., avoiding open fields, not sheltering under trees), Lightning Action Plans, Damini App: Developed by IITM, this mobile app provides location-specific lightning warnings within a 20–40 km radius, valid for 40 minutes
- <b>Way forward</b>: now a notified disaster (16th FC) → SDRF money for lightning arresters and shelters + last-mile Damini alerts + awareness in Bihar, UP villages
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Cyclone

- <b>Extent</b>: India exposed to 10% of the world’s tropical cyclones + Over 8,000 km of India's coastline, spanning both east and west, faces the hazards of tropical cyclones, storm surges, and heavy rainfall
- <b>Causes</b>: warm sea (above \~26.5°C) + Coriolis force + low wind shear + the IPCC AR6 Report, which states that the proportion of intense tropical cyclones (Category 4-5) and their peak wind speeds will increase globally with warming.
- <b>Effects</b>: <span color="green_bg">storm surge</span>, high winds and floods → deaths, homes and crops lost + farmland salinised + coastal erosion + power and ports hit
- <b>Examples</b>: Recent occurrences: cyclone Dana (2024) (Odisha), cyclone Fengal (2024) (Tamil Nadu) and Puducherry cyclone Remal (2024)
  - Cyclone Montha (October 2025):
  - Cyclone Shakti (October 2025)
  - Cyclone Ditwah (November–December 2025):
- <b>NDMA guideline / scheme</b>: India follows a multi-sectoral approach to mitigate cyclone risks. The NDMA Guidelines (2008) focus on <span color="green_bg">early warning</span> systems via IMD’s satellite (colour coding) and Doppler radar networks, aircraft probing for cyclone cores, structural safety with shelters, roads, and <span color="green_bg">bio-shields</span>, and a four-color warning code (Green to Red). The National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project (NCRMP) targets 13 cyclone-prone states/UTs, implementing both structural and non-structural measures with coordination between NDMA, state governments, NIDM, and partial World Bank funding. These measures aim to protect lives, infrastructure, and coastal ecosystems.
  - Odisha is the first state to establish state disaster management authority
- <b>Way forward</b>: Odisha's zero-casualty model everywhere + mangrove bio-shields + cyclone-resilient housing and shelters + last-mile warnings
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Drought

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2014

- <b>2014 Q14 (12.5 marks):</b> Drought has been recognized as a disaster in view of its spatial expanse, temporal duration, slow onset and lasting effects on vulnerable sections. With a focus on the September 2010 guidelines from the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), discuss the mechanisms for preparedness to deal with likely El Nino and La Nina fallouts in India.
</toggle>

- <b>Definition & extent</b>: Defined as area where rainfall deficiency is more than or equal to 26% + Around 68% of India's land is prone to drought in varying degrees. Over 500 of India’s 718 districts report meteorological drought conditions, ranging from mildly to extremely dry
- <b>Causes</b>: Drought: prolonged rainfall deficit, persistent high-pressure/blocked circulation, El Niño/large-scale climate modes, over-extraction of groundwater, deforestation/land-use change, poor water management. (El Niño / La Niña → see 🟡 Extreme Weather Events)
  - Cherrapunji paradox (The Cherrapunji Paradox (often called the "Scarcity in Abundance" paradox) refers to the ironic situation where the world’s wettest place on Earth—Cherrapunji (Sohra) and nearby Mawsynram—suffers from acute drinking water shortages and drought-like conditions during the non-monsoon months.)
- <b>Effects</b>: crop failure → farm distress and debt + drinking water and fodder shortage + distress migration + more groundwater pumping
- <b>Examples</b>: Recent examples: Rayalaseema (Andhra Pradesh 2024), South American drought (2024), Europe (2022) + two to name in India: 2015–16 Marathwada (Latur got drinking water by train) + 2002 all-India drought (monsoon \~19% short, El Niño year)
- <b>NDMA guideline / scheme</b>: The NDMA Guidelines focus on state-level Drought Monitoring Cells, real-time vulnerability mapping, and ICT-based control rooms. Measures include watershed development, automatic weather stations, cloud seeding policies (Cloud seeding: silver iodide or dry ice sprayed into clouds → droplets form → rain (IIT Kanpur trial, Delhi) → risks: floods, toxic silver iodide, unclear cost), drought insurance, short-duration seeds, fodder banks, and market support. Afforestation with suitable species and biodiesel plantations are encouraged. Capacity building programs target PRIs and ULBs for effective drought management. The Drought Prone Area Development Programme (DPAP), launched in 1973–74, uses a watershed-based approach to restore ecological balance, improve socio-economic conditions of vulnerable communities, and enhance agricultural productivity through soil, water, and vegetation management
- <b>Way forward</b>: reactive (emergency food and drink), proactive (<span color="green_bg">early warning</span> systems, de-stocking of food), prospective dating with it (Climate smart agriculture systems + DRR strategies).
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Wildfires

- <b>Extent</b>: More than 36% of the country’s forest cover has been estimated to be prone to frequent forest fires. Nearly 4% of the country’s forest cover is extremely prone to fire, whereas 6% of forest cover is found to be very highly fire prone. In 16 years to 2021, forest fires in India rose.
- <b>Causes</b>: Causes: Wildfires are primarily triggered by human activities (like field burning or unattended campfires), dry weather and climate change, flammable invasive species (e.g., lantana camara, pine), and poor forest management (absence of firebreaks, unmaintained forest floors). Shifting cultivation (slash and burn, burn gets outta hand)
  - Wildfires: lightning strikes, human ignition (campfires, arson, agricultural burning), prolonged drought and heatwaves, strong winds, fuel accumulation (dead biomass), poor land/forest management.
- <b>Effects</b>: biodiversity and <span color="green_bg">carbon sink</span> lost + smoke and haze + soil erosion + forest livelihoods hit
- <b>Examples</b>: Uttarakhand forest fires (2024)
- <b>Scheme</b>: Mitigation: India focuses on prevention, <span color="green_bg">early warning</span>, and response. Key initiatives include the Forest Fire Prevention & Management Scheme (community participation and awareness), FSI’s Pre-Warning Alert System, and the Large Forest Fire Monitoring Programme (2019) using SNPP-VIIRS data for real-time alerts. The Burnt Area Assessment uses IRS AWiFS data to map affected zones and guide response measures. National Action Plan on Forest Fires (NAPFF, 2018)
- <b>Way forward</b>: firebreaks + community fire watchers + clear lantana and pine litter + early alerts to the last village
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Industrial Accidents

- <b>Extent</b>: The National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) highlights industrial accidents involving chemical, biological, and radioactive materials as significant hazards. + India has approximately 1861 Major Accident Hazard (MAH) sites
- <b>Causes</b>: Causes: Inadequate safety regulations and enforcement (Factories Act 1948), human error, lack of training, poor maintenance of equipment (2019 Visakhapatnam gas leak), insufficient investment in safety infrastructure.
- <b>Effects</b>: deaths and long-term illness + air, water and soil contamination + economic loss
- <b>Examples</b>: Key industrial disasters: Gujarat Factory Fire (2025), Thane Chemical Unit Explosion (2024), Korba Chimney Collapse (2009)
  - <span color="green_bg">Bhopal</span>, Dec 1984: methyl isocyanate leak from Union Carbide → thousands dead, \~5 lakh affected
  - Vizag LG Polymers, May 2020: styrene vapour leak during COVID restart → 12 dead + plant ran without valid environmental clearance → NGT interim fine ₹50 cr
- <b>Law / scheme</b>: absolute liability (MC Mehta, Oleum gas leak 1986) + EPA 1986 + <span color="green_bg">MSIHC</span> Rules 1989 + Public Liability Insurance Act 1991 + NDMA Chemical Disaster Guidelines 2007
- <b>Way forward</b>: Solutions: same as above (no changes allowed)
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Stampedes

- <b>Extent</b>: Over 79% of stampedes in India occur at religious events, where terrain, infrastructure, and crowd management are particularly challenging e.g., 340 deaths at Mandhardevi temple (MH), 250 deaths at Chamunda Devi temple (Jodhpur, RJ) + \~4,000 stampedes in the last 3 decades (UNDRR: surge of people when danger or loss of space is felt)
- <b>Causes</b>: Causes: Overcrowding (events like Maha Kumbh Mela and RCB celebration), poor crowd management, inadequate infrastructure, panic triggers (rumors or accidents) + <span color="green_bg">Chinnaswamy</span>, Bengaluru (Jun 2025: \~2.5 lakh people vs 34,600 capacity + free-pass post without police coordination) + Mintz (cooperation breaks) and Smelser (craze) theories + little tech (crowd-density analytics)
- <b>Effects</b>: deaths by crushing and asphyxia + injuries + loss of trust in event management
- <b>NDMA guideline</b>: NDMA guide on Managing Crowd at Events and Venues of Mass Gathering (2014) → stampede = man-made disaster; capacity planning + risk and vulnerability analysis + <span color="green_bg">FMEA</span> (severity, frequency, detection) + Art 19(1)(b) + Police Act 1861
- <b>Way forward</b>: Solutions: <span color="green_bg">FIST Model</span> (Crowd Behaviour Analysis): Fruin, a renowned theorist, proposed the <span color="green_bg">FIST model</span> to understand crowd behavior and stampede causes. F: Crowd Force, I: Information upon which the crowd acts, S: Physical Space involved, T: Time. Utility: This model helps in developing proactive strategies by addressing these four elements during event risk management planning. + crowd-density norms per sq m (New York: trained crowd managers for 1,000+) + wide, multiple exits + RFID/IoT (Kumbh, Vaishno Devi), AI CCTV and drones (Hajj) + learn from Mumbai's 2024 T20 roadshow
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Heatwaves

- <b>Definition & extent</b>: Criteria by IMD: plains max temp 40°C, coastal 37°C and 30°C in hills → heatwave if departure from normal is 4.5–6.4°C (severe: above 6.4°C) or actual max is 45°C+ (severe: 47°C+) + must hold at 2 stations in a sub-division for 2 days in a row (declared on day 2) + 13 to 15% of population is highly vulnerable, though latest estimates show over 57% of Indian districts (roughly 75% of the population) face high to very-high heat risk + heat stress = body temp above 37°C; <span color="green_bg">heat risk</span> = chance of illness or death (intensity + exposure + vulnerability) (CEEW, 734 districts)
- <b>Causes</b>: Causes: Anticyclonic conditions + absence of moisture and cloudless sky, reasons for increasing heatwaves (El Nino, <span color="green_bg">urban heat island</span> effect, climate change, westerly winds from Iran/Pakistan), plus rising incidence of very warm nights and relative humidity reducing the body’s recovery ability + warm nights rising faster than warm days (2012–22) + N India humidity 30–40% → 40–50%
- <b>Effects</b>: 10k people dead (2000–2020) though current health surveillance misses the wider burden of heart, lung, and kidney conditions worsened by heat, high energy demand due to cooling facilities, 5.8 work hours lost because of it + 93% of species' ranges exposed by 2085 + rice and wheat at risk (Ganga, Indus basins) + up to 40% fall in work capacity (wet-bulb extremes)
- <b>Examples</b>: Examples: Andhra Pradesh + Telangana, May 2015 (\~2,000+ deaths) + North India, May–June 2024 (Churu 50.5°C, 40,000+ suspected heatstroke cases)
- <b>Scheme</b>: Initiatives: IMD (green, yellow, orange, red), heat action plans by IMD, heat index launched by IMD, newly added as India’s 14th notified natural calamity (removing the 10% SDRF cap and unlocking full State Disaster Response/Mitigation Funds), 16th Finance Commission increased disaster funds by 28% • •
- <b>NDMA guideline → way forward</b>: NDMA guidelines: same as all, mandated <span color="green_bg">Heat Action Plans</span> (HAPs) which need expansion from the current 300 cities to 4,800 urban local bodies, requirement to convert HAPs into fundable projects, link solutions to development schemes, and utilize pre-agreed <span color="green_bg">parametric insurance</span> (automatic payouts on temperature thresholds) + plan for warm nights too + MHA: heatwaves eligible for SDMF projects + declare heat a disaster where >50% districts face high risk + National HAP Repository + heat-tolerant crops and breeds
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Glacier Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF)

- <b>Definition</b>: Definition: Sudden release of large water volume retained in glacier + >31,000 glacial lakes growing in High Mountain Asia (IIT Roorkee) + 34 of 100 lakes over 10 ha growing (CWC) + since 1990 lake number / area / volume up 53% / 51% / 48%
- <b>Causes</b>: Causes: Rapid glacier advance; moraine/ice dam failure, seismic activity; human activities (urbanisation, mining, deforestation, hydropower, GHGs)
- <b>Effects</b>: Vulnerability: >9M people in High Mountain Asia at risk; glaciers may lose 30–50% volume (2015–2100, <span color="green_bg">ICIMOD</span>) + flash floods and debris wipe out villages, roads and hydel dams downstream (Chungthang dam, 2023) + HKH (8 nations): 70–80% of glacier volume may go by 2100 at high emissions (ICIMOD) + 7,500 lakes above 4,500 m, hard to monitor + IHR \~100 mn tourists a year
- <b>Examples</b>: Examples: Uttarkashi (2025), South Lhonak–Sikkim (2023), Kedarnath (2013), Chamoli (2021)
  - Update the Chamoli (2021) was  a Sturzstrom / Rock-Ice Avalanche that transformed into a debris flood, distinguishing it from moraine-dammed breach GLOFs (like South Lhonak, 2023).
- <b>NDMA guideline</b>: Mitigation: NDMA 2020 guidelines; structural (reservoirs, depressions, embankments); <span color="green_bg">early warning</span> at 56 at-risk lakes; CEA hydro slope stability guidelines; risk projects in HP, UK, Sikkim, Arunachal + National GLOF Risk Mitigation Project (same 4 states) + <span color="green_bg">CWC monitors 900+ lakes</span> + risk-indexing criteria + NRSC 24x7 lake watch + GSI landslide mapping + ICIMOD HKH cryosphere initiative
- <b>Way forward</b>: Way Forward: Latest research (Himalayas, Alps, Tian Shan, Andes); collaboration among experts/policymakers; structural + non-structural measures (breaching, siphoning, outlet structures); advanced monitoring & early warning via satellites, GIS, remote sensing
- <b>Related</b>: Sturzstrom → see 🟡 Sturzstrom heading
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Fire Safety

- <b>Extent</b>: Status (2022): 7,435 deaths in 7,500+ fires (NCRB). → <span color="green_bg">5,888 deaths</span> (2024, NCRB)
- <b>Causes</b>: Causes – Non-compliance (examples: Delhi coaching centres, Kumbakonam School 2004, AMRI Hospital 2011)
- <b>Effects</b>: most deaths from smoke + crowded buildings become traps (hospitals, coaching centres) + economic loss
- <b>Examples</b>: Recent: Rajkot gaming zone, Harda firecracker factory, Delhi hospital + Kochi Brahmapuram waste fire (2023) + Mukherjee Nagar coaching centre (2023) + Cuttack hospital and Delhi building fires (2026) + North Goa night club
- <b>Law / standards</b>: Standards – Fire service: state subject; NBC (BIS) central standard; states must adopt. Also: Model Building Bye Laws 2016, Fire & Life Safety guidelines, Model Bill 2019
  - Challenges – No uniform law; NBC advisory; staff/equipment shortage (2019: 5,191 stations, 5,03,365 staff); urban issues (Kamala Mills fire 2017)
  - Fire services = Art 243W, 12th Schedule (ULBs) + NBC 2016 (BIS) + SFAC (MHA) + Scheme for Expansion & Modernisation of Fire Services (15th FC)
- <b>Way forward</b>: Way Forward (NDMA) – <span color="green_bg">State Fire Act</span>; outreach to block/GP level; district-level fire chiefs; indigenous low-water tech R&D + third-party fire audits before NOCs + AI-based HIRA + fire tax + community fire prevention (China)
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Dams

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2023

- <b>2023 Q7 (10 marks):</b> Dam failures are always catastrophic, especially on the downstream side, resulting in a colossal loss of life and property. Analyze the various causes of dam failures. Give two examples of large dam failures.
</toggle>

- <b>Extent</b>: India is the 3rd largest dam-owning nation with 6,628 specified dams (Maharashtra most), after the USA and China
- <b>Causes of failure</b>: Ageing infrastructure: 80% of Indian dams are over 25 years old, raising safety concerns (about 26% over 50 years) + Also: reservoirs lost about 19% storage to silt, average age 42 years (CWC) + GLOF risk (Chungthang dam, Sikkim 2023)
  - Seismic vulnerability: Indian dams can be vulnerable to earthquakes (e.g., Bhuj, 2001)
- <b>Effects</b>: sudden flood wave downstream → deaths, towns wiped out + farmland, power and water supply lost
- <b>Examples</b>: Major dam failures: 1975 (Banqiao dam in China), 1979 (Macchchu dam in Morbi GJ), 2023 (Derna dam, Libya) + South Fork (USA 1889)
- <b>Law / scheme</b>: Dam rehab and improvement, Dam health and rehab monitoring; The <span color="green_bg">Dam Safety Act</span>, 2021 established a 4-tier institutional mechanism at central and state levels
  - Tools: NRLD + DRIP + SHAISYS + DHARMA app + National Centre for Earthquake Safety of Dams (MNIT Jaipur) → next: sediment bypass (Japan) + lifecycle management + IoT sensors
- <b>Way forward</b>: Way forward: advanced technologies like ROVs and drones for underwater inspections, integrated water management, considering alternatives to large dams
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 New Technology for Disaster Management

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2020

- <b>2020 Q18 (15 marks):</b> Discuss the recent measures initiated in disaster management by the Government of India departing from the earlier reactive approach.
</toggle>

- India uses tech-driven disaster measures for cyclone, flood, lightning, and GLOF preparedness through risk mapping tools (Web-DCRA, Flood Hazard Atlas, Glacial Lake Dataset), IMD forecasting with satellites and apps (Damini, Mausam), and integrated <span color="green_bg">early warning</span> systems — Common Alerting Protocol (CAP) for multi-channel alerts, National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project (NCRMP) for cyclone-prone coastal states, and <span color="green_bg">SACHET</span> dashboard/app for localized multilingual alerts
- NDRF & ERSS-112 ensure rapid rescue during emergencies, while public drills build awareness
- Global leadership includes G20 DRR, tsunami warning systems, and humanitarian aid under Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam
- Operation Brahma — India's HADR mission to Myanmar following the 2025 earthquake — in the spirit of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam Press Information Bureau (add alongside the existing Operation Dost mention for Turkiye/Syria).
- 16th Finance Commission (Chair: Arvind Panagariya) — Disaster Management Recommendations
  - Total Corpus — Big Increase
    - Total corpus of ₹2,04,401 crore recommended for SDRF + SDMF for 2026-31. Press Information Bureau This is a 27% increase over the 15th FC's ₹1,60,153 crore.
    - Landmark: Heatwaves and Lightning Added to Notified Disasters
      - The Commission recommended adding heatwaves and lightning to India's national list of notified disasters, citing rising deaths and climate change.
- DRR financing (GP2025: India showed the world's largest DRR finance system): 15th FC (2021–26) allocations over ₹2.32 lakh cr (\~\$28 bn) + <span color="green_bg">Disaster Risk Index</span> (hazard 70 + vulnerability 30, BPL as proxy) to share funds + NDMF/SDMF (mitigation), NDRF (100% Centre, "severe" calamity), SDRF (75:25; 90:10 Himalayan & NE)
  - GAR 2025: only 2% of aid goes to DRR + losses doubled in 20 years + \$1 on DRR saves \$15
  - Issues: DRI one-size (misses hilly, coastal) + "severe" not defined in DM Act + ₹4 lakh per death unchanged for a decade + slow, step-by-step release
  - Way forward: blended finance, debt-for-resilience swaps + layered financing + adaptive DRI / NDMA composite index + FEMA-style per-capita thresholds + review every 5 years
- <b>Examples</b>: Wayanad 2024 (worked: Army built a 190-ft Bailey bridge in about a day and a half for rescue) + <span color="green_bg">cell broadcast</span> alert tests across India (2023)
</toggle>
</toggle>
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h1">
6\. ENVIRONoMENTAL IMPACT ASSESSMENT (EIA)

<toggle color="gray">
PYQ 2024, 2020, 2019, 2016, 2014

- <b>2024 Q8 (10 marks):</b> What role do environmental NGOs and activists play in influencing Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) outcomes for major projects in India? Cite four examples with all important details.
- <b>2020 Q7 (10 marks):</b> How does the draft Environment Impact Assessment (EIA) Notification, 2020 differ from the existing EIA Notification, 2006?
- <b>2019 Q17 (15 marks):</b> Define the concept of carrying capacity of an ecosystem as relevant to an environment. Explain how understanding this concept is vital while planning for sustainable development of a region.
- <b>2016 Q14 (12.5 marks):</b> Rehabilitation of human settlements is one of the important environmental impacts which always attracts controversy while planning major projects. Discuss the measures suggested for mitigation of this impact while proposing major developmental projects.
- <b>2014 Q15 (12.5 marks):</b> Environmental Impact Assessment studies are increasingly undertaken before a project is cleared by the Government. Discuss the environmental impacts of coal-fired thermal plants located at coal pitheads.
</toggle>

<toggle>
ANUDEEP NOTES

<b>Meaning</b>

- EIA : assessment of +ve and -ve impact of a proposed project on env't, social & economic costs (UNEP) + process of <span color="yellow_bg">identifying, predicting, evaluating and mitigating</span> its effects before decisions are taken and commitments made (IAIA)
- Origin : NEPA 1970 (USA) → India: <span color="green_bg">EIA Notification 2006 under EPA 1986</span> + makes policy makers justify decisions on studies and public comments
- Types : <span color="green_bg">Rapid EIA</span> (1 season data, not monsoon) vs <span color="green_bg">Comprehensive EIA</span> (all 4 seasons)
- Categories : A → Centre clears (Expert Appraisal Committee) + B → state SEIAA (B1 needs EIA, B2 exempt) + exempt: border highways within 100 km, solar, wind, hydro \<25 MW

<b>Process (with drawback of each stage)</b>

- Screening : clears projects unlikely to harm, by size/location (school no EIA vs coal mining must) → drawback: even small industrial units (rubber) harm + <span color="green_bg">no study shows projects below a limit are harmless</span>
- Preliminary assessment : if screening doesn't clear → review available data + key impacts + predict extent → <span color="green_bg">early warning system</span>
- EIA team : formed by developer → drawback: no social scientists, anthropologists, ecologists + <span color="green_bg">conflict of interest</span>
- Scoping : study covers all important issues after talking to govt, experts, civil society, locals → drawback: <span color="green_bg">public comments ignored</span> + only major impacts covered
- Main EIA (5 questions) : Identification (what will happen?) + Prediction (how much change?) + Evaluation (does it matter? local acceptance, consultation, standards) + Mitigation (what can be done?) + Documentation (report for decision makers: exec summary, impacts, mitigation measures, gaps + summary for public)
  - Identification → drawback: unreliable data + local knowledge ignored
  - Prediction : maths models → drawback: method not disclosed + uncertainty
  - Mitigation : change site/route/process/raw material + pollution control + restoration, money to displaced, CSR + compare alternatives (cost-benefit, matrix) → drawback: <span color="green_bg">stays on paper</span> + some kept confidential (nuclear) + community left out + no disaster plan (Uttarakhand floods)
- Public hearing : panel = SPCB rep + DC + state env't ministry rep + project's ministry rep + ≤3 local body reps (PRI/ULB) + ≤3 senior citizens picked by DC + <span color="green_bg">exempt: mining ≤25 ha, highway widening, irrigation modernisation, SEZ/EPZ units</span>
- Appraisal : EIA → SPCB review → public hearing → IAA (MoEF) → Expert Appraisal Committee (site visit if needed) → MoEF final review → clearance (<span color="green_bg">too many layers of bureaucracy</span>)
  <image source="notion-file-block://4221111b-206d-80be-a503-ec3b3ec717ba/048995f0-760e-4da9-9b8c-bb24b2a9e1d3?space_id=3939cd2d-3e25-404f-9196-d463e4c2e65e&name=image.png" />
- After clearance : <span color="green_bg">Environment Audit Rules 2025</span> → certified, randomly assigned third-party auditors check compliance (EIA = before project, audit = after it starts)

<b>2006 vs Draft 2020 (PYQ 2020)</b>

|  | 2006 | Draft 2020 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Public hearing | 30 days | 20 days |
| Post-facto clearance | Not allowed | Allowed |
| Compliance reports | Twice a year | Once a year |
| Exemptions | Few | Many (highways, defence, "strategic") |

- Pushback : UN Special Rapporteurs objected + <span color="green_bg">courts rejected post-facto clearance</span> (LG Polymers, Vizag)

<b>Problems</b>

- Reports : <span color="green_bg">incomplete, false data</span> (no central data bank) + single season data + <span color="green_bg">bulky, technical, only in English</span> + <span color="green_bg">consultant paid by proponent</span> + <span color="green_bg">doubtful expertise</span> (Odisha: Reliance project EIA by Berhampur Univ, no Olive Ridley expertise; Mithivirdi nuclear EIA questioned by Greenpeace) + copy-paste reports (Sterlite)
- Public hearing : many exemptions (now critical minerals too) + <span color="green_bg">opinions ignored</span> + <span color="green_bg">low literacy in tribal areas</span> (Niyamgiri palli sabha) + <span color="green_bg">documents late</span> + <span color="green_bg">minutes lack fidelity</span> + <span color="green_bg">local admin sides with project</span>
- Public consultation (EIA 2006): for Category A and B1 → public hearing near the site + written responses → run by SPCB/UTPCC → proceedings to the regulator within 45 days + now exempt: mining of atomic, critical, strategic minerals (thorium from monazite, rare earths for defence) → concerns: weakens Art 21 and 48A + Silkyara tunnel (Char Dham) was exempt and collapsed in 2023 + Sterlite + Aarhus Convention 1998
- Clearance : site work starts before EIA + <span color="green_bg">clearance despite objection, no reasons given</span> + closed-door after hearing + <span color="green_bg">\~238 days delay</span>
- After clearance : MoEF regional offices <span color="green_bg">lax in monitoring</span> (people don't know the standards, SPCB has its own) + weak follow-up (Vizhinjam) + appeals: <span color="green_bg">NEAA heard only \~15 cases in 8 yrs</span> (NEAA replaced by NGT, 2010)
- Dilution now : <span color="green_bg">Vanashakti 2025 ban on post-facto clearance recalled</span> (May 2025 struck down ex-post ECs → Nov 2025 recalled 2:1 on review → Vanashakti III, Jul 2026: prior EC mandatory + 2017 one-time window upheld + 2021 OM quashed for the future, old ex-post ECs stay) + <span color="green_bg">land before EIA for non-coal mining</span> (Dec 2025) + Aravalli 100 m definition + no transboundary EIA (India not in Espoo 1991)

<b>Way forward</b>

- <span color="green_bg">Independent EIA authority</span> (judicial officers + civil society, env't, scientists) + central fund deposited by developers + accredited list of consultants
- Public hearing in 3 phases : <span color="green_bg">explaining → discussing → voting</span> + video recording + true minutes + local language
- <span color="green_bg">Reasons for approval/rejection in clear terms</span> + expert meeting minutes public + balanced expert committee (env't experts, sociologists)
- <span color="green_bg">MoEF regional offices with experts</span> + local communities in monitoring + info desk on clearance status + <span color="green_bg">capacity building</span> of communities, NGOs, judges
- <span color="green_bg">Trim exemptions</span> + no rapid EIA + <span color="green_bg">assess biodiversity</span> + <span color="green_bg">disaster plan</span> + <span color="green_bg">Strategic Env't Assessment</span> (sector-wide) + cumulative, regional EIA + standalone EIA law + independent post-clearance audit (UK model)

<b>Cases</b>

- MC Mehta 1986 (<span color="green_bg">absolute liability</span>) + Godavarman 1995 + Vellore Citizens 1996 (<span color="green_bg">polluter pays, precautionary principle</span>) + MC Mehta v Kamal Nath 1996 (<span color="green_bg">public trust</span>) + Arts 21, 48A, 51A(g)

<b>NGOs and activists (PYQ 2024)</b>

- Role : translate reports + bring people to hearings + file objections + go to NGT/SC + expose copy-paste reports and violations
- <span color="green_bg">Silent Valley</span> : KSSP campaign → Kunthipuzha dam dropped → National Park 1984
- <span color="green_bg">Niyamgiri 2013</span> : Dongria Kondh vs Vedanta bauxite → SC let gram sabhas decide → <span color="green_bg">all 12 said no</span>
- <span color="green_bg">Goa Foundation</span> : exposed illegal iron-ore mining (Shah Commission) → SC cancelled 88 lease renewals (2018)
- <span color="green_bg">Save Mon Region Federation</span> : NGT 2016 suspended Nyamjang Chhu hydro clearance (black-necked crane site ignored)

<b>Coal pithead plants (PYQ 2014)</b>

- Plant at the mine (no rail haul) but <span color="green_bg">pollution piles up in one place</span> (Singrauli, Korba) + fly-ash dyke breaches (Sasan 2020) + SO₂, NOx, PM, mercury + heavy water use, hot water discharge + forest and farmland lost + fluorosis, lung disease → 2015 emission norms (scrubber deadlines extended → Jul 2025: Category C plants, \~78%, away from big cities and critically polluted areas, exempted from FGD; only stack height) + <span color="green_bg">Fly Ash Notification 2021 (100% use)</span> + cumulative EIA + green belts

<b>Rehabilitation (PYQ 2016)</b>

- <span color="green_bg">Tribals \~40% of people displaced</span> by projects (Ken-Betwa \~20,000, Hasdeo Arand, Mumbai Coastal Road) + land, community ties, livelihood lost → <span color="green_bg">RFCTLARR 2013</span>: social impact assessment + consent (80% private, 70% PPP) + compensation up to 4x rural, 2x urban → <span color="green_bg">land for land</span> + job or annuity + skill training + resettle whole village together + gram sabha consent (PESA, FRA)

<b>SDGs</b>

- 17 goals, 169 targets → <span color="green_bg">only 17% on track</span> (SDR 2025), India 99th + \~\$4 tn a year finance gap → <span color="green_bg">Sevilla Commitment</span> (FfD4, 2025)
</toggle>
</toggle>
